question: What happens to a collective agreement or arbitral award when a portion of the federal public administration is established as or becomes a part of a corporation or business to which the Part applies?
answer:
**Section 47 of the Canada Labour Code**

When a portion of the federal public administration is established as or becomes a part of a corporation or business to which the Part applies, a collective agreement or arbitral award that applies to any employees in that portion of the federal public administration and that is in force at the time of the establishment or severance continues in force, subject to certain conditions.

**Continuation of Collective Agreement or Arbitral Award
"...a collective agreement or arbitral award that applies to any employees in that portion of the federal public administration and that is in force at the time the portion of the federal public administration is established as or becomes a part of such a corporation or business continues in force, subject to subsections (3) to (7), until its term expires..."

This means that the collective agreement or arbitral award will continue to apply to the employees until its term expires, unless it is terminated or modified by the parties involved.

**Application of the Federal Public Sector Labour Relations Act
"...the Federal Public Sector Labour Relations Act applies in all respects to the interpretation and application of the collective agreement or arbitral award."

This means that the Federal Public Sector Labour Relations Act will govern the interpretation and application of the collective agreement or arbitral award, in addition to the Canada Labour Code.

**Board's Role in Determining Collective Agreement or Arbitral Award**

The Board may make an order determining whether the employees of the corporation or business who are bound by a collective agreement or arbitral award constitute one or more units appropriate for collective bargaining, and which trade union shall be the bargaining agent for the employees in each such unit.

**Effect of Board's Order
"Where the Board has made an order pursuant to paragraph (4)(c), this Part applies to the interpretation and application of any collective agreement or arbitral award affected thereby."

This means that the Board's order will have a significant impact on the interpretation and application of the collective agreement or arbitral award, and will govern the relationship between the employer, employees, and bargaining agent.

{"id": "CLC-47.1", "type": "Canada Labour Code", "title": "Successor Rights and Obligations: Where notice to bargain collectively given prior to deletion", "section": "47.1"}, "text": "Section 47.1 Where, before the deletion or severance referred to in subsection 47(1), notice to bargain collectively has been given in respect of a collective agreement or arbitral award binding on employees of a corporation or business who, immediately before the deletion or severance, were part of the federal public administration, (a) the terms and conditions of employment contained in a collective agreement or arbitral award that, by virtue of section 107 of the Federal Public Sector Labour Relations Act , are continued in force immediately before the date of the deletion or severance or that were last continued in force before that date, in respect of those employees shall continue or resume in force on and after that date and shall be observed by the corporation or business, as employer, the bargaining agent for those employees and those employees until the requirements of paragraphs 89(1)(a) to (d) have been met, unless the employer and the bargaining agent agree otherwise; (b) the Federal Public Sector Labour Relations Act applies in all respects to the interpretation and application of any term or condition continued or resumed by paragraph (a); (c) on application by the corporation or business, as employer, or the bargaining agent for those employees, made during the period beginning on the one hundred and twentieth day and ending on the one hundred and fiftieth day after the date of the deletion or severance, the Board shall make an order determining (i) whether the employees of the corporation or business who are represented by the bargaining agent constitute one or more units appropriate for collective bargaining, and (ii) which trade union shall be the bargaining agent for the employees in each such unit; (d) where the Board makes the determinations under paragraph (c), the corporation or business, as employer, or the bargaining agent may, by notice, require the other to commence collective bargaining under this Act for the purpose of entering into a collective agreement; and (e) this Part, other than section 80, applies in respect of a notice given under paragraph (d). 1996, c. 18, s. 9 1998, c. 26, s. 23(F) 2003, c. 22, ss. 109, 223(E) 2017, c. 9, s. 55 Previous Version Marginal note: Order"

question: What happens to the terms and conditions of employment for employees who move from the federal public administration to a corporation or business in terms of collective agreements and arbitral awards?
answer:
**Successor Rights and Obligations**

**Continuation of Collective Agreements and Arbitral Awards**

Before the deletion or severance of a portion of the federal public administration, notice to bargain collectively has been given in respect of a collective agreement or arbitral award binding on employees of a corporation or business who, immediately before the deletion or severance, were part of the federal public administration.
"Where, before the deletion or severance referred to in subsection 47(1), notice to bargain collectively has been given in respect of a collective agreement or arbitral award binding on employees of a corporation or business who, immediately before the deletion or severance, were part of the federal public administration, (a) the terms and conditions of employment contained in a collective agreement or arbitral award that, by virtue of section 107 of the Federal Public Sector Labour Relations Act , are continued in force immediately before the date of the deletion or severance or that were last continued in force before that date, in respect of those employees shall continue or resume in force on and after that date and shall be observed by the corporation or business, as employer, the bargaining agent for those employees and those employees until the requirements of paragraphs 89(1)(a) to (d) have been met, unless the employer and the bargaining agent agree otherwise..."

This means that the terms and conditions of employment contained in the collective agreement or arbitral award will continue or resume in force on and after the date of the deletion or severance, and will be observed by the corporation or business, as employer, the bargaining agent for those employees, and those employees until the requirements of paragraphs 89(1)(a) to (d) have been met.

**Federal Public Sector Labour Relations Act
"...the Federal Public Sector Labour Relations Act applies in all respects to the interpretation and application of any term or condition continued or resumed by paragraph (a)..."

This indicates that the Federal Public Sector Labour Relations Act will apply to the interpretation and application of any term or condition continued or resumed by paragraph (a), ensuring that the collective agreement or arbitral award is enforced in accordance with the Act.

**Board's Role
"...on application by the corporation or business, as employer, or the bargaining agent for those employees, made during the period beginning on the one hundred and twentieth day and ending on the one hundred and fiftieth day after the date of the deletion or severance, the Board shall make an order determining (i) whether the employees of the corporation or business who are represented by the bargaining agent constitute one or more units appropriate for collective bargaining, and (ii) which trade union shall be the bargaining agent for the employees in each such unit..."

The Board will make an order determining whether the employees of the corporation or business who are represented by the bargaining agent constitute one or more units appropriate for collective bargaining, and which trade union shall be the bargaining agent for the employees in each such unit. This ensures that the collective bargaining process is established and the bargaining agent is determined.

{"id": "CLC-47.2", "type": "Canada Labour Code", "title": "Successor Rights and Obligations: Order", "section": "47.2"}, "text": "Section 47.2 The Governor in Council may, by order, exclude from the operation of sections 47 and 47.1 any portion of the federal public administration that is deleted or severed as described in subsection 47(1) where the Governor in Council, on the recommendation of the Minister after consultation with the Treasury Board and the Minister responsible for that portion of the federal public administration, is of the opinion that it is in the public interest to do so. 1996, c. 18, s. 9 2003, c. 22, s. 224(E)"

question: Under what circumstances can the Governor in Council exclude a portion of the federal public administration from the operation of sections 47 and 47.1?
answer:
**Exclusion from Operation of Sections 47 and 47.1**

The Governor in Council can exclude a portion of the federal public administration from the operation of sections 47 and 47.1
"...where the Governor in Council, on the recommendation of the Minister after consultation with the Treasury Board and the Minister responsible for that portion of the federal public administration, is of the opinion that it is in the public interest to do so."

**Source:** CLC-47.2

This quote indicates that the Governor in Council has the authority to exclude a portion of the federal public administration from the operation of sections 47 and 47.1, but only if it is deemed to be in the public interest. This decision is made after consultation with the Minister and the Treasury Board, and is subject to the Minister's recommendation.

**Conditions for Exclusion**

The exclusion is contingent upon the Governor in Council's opinion that it is in the public interest. This implies that the decision to exclude is not arbitrary, but rather based on a careful consideration of the potential impact on the public interest.

**Source:** CLC-47.2

In this context, the public interest is likely to be considered in terms of the potential benefits or drawbacks of excluding a portion of the federal public administration from the operation of sections 47 and 47.1. The Governor in Council and the Minister must weigh these factors and make a decision that is in the best interests of the public.

question: What are the requirements for an employer who takes over providing services from a previous contractor under a contract or arrangement?
answer:
**Contract Retendering and Successor Rights**

The question pertains to the requirements for an employer who takes over providing services from a previous contractor under a contract or arrangement. This scenario is governed by the Canada Labour Code, specifically Section 47.3.

**Definition of Successor Contractor**

A successor contractor is defined as an employer who, under the terms of a contract or other arrangement,
"...provided services at an airport to another employer, or to a person acting on behalf of that other employer, in an industry referred to in paragraph (e) of the definition federal work, undertaking or business in section 2..."

**Equal Remuneration Obligations**

The successor contractor is required to pay to the employees providing services under the contract or arrangement
"...remuneration not less than that which the employees of the previous contractor who provided the same or substantially similar services were entitled to receive under the terms of a collective agreement to which this Part applied."

**Source of the Quote**

This quote is from Section 47.3 of the Canada Labour Code, which outlines the requirements for an employer who takes over providing services from a previous contractor under a contract or arrangement.

**Implications for Employers**

The requirements outlined in Section 47.3 have significant implications for employers who take over providing services from a previous contractor. They must ensure that they pay employees the same or higher remuneration than the previous contractor, in order to maintain the rights and benefits of the employees. This includes ensuring that wages and access to seniority entitlements are treated as continuous, even in cases of contract retendering.

question: What can a certified bargaining agent or an employer do to initiate collective bargaining when no collective agreement is in force?
answer:
**Initiating Collective Bargaining**

A certified bargaining agent or an employer can initiate collective bargaining when no collective agreement is in force by giving notice to each other.

**Certified Bargaining Agent's Notice**

A certified bargaining agent may, by notice, require the employer to commence collective bargaining for the purpose of entering into a collective agreement.
"Where the Board has certified a bargaining agent for a bargaining unit and no collective agreement binding on the employees in the bargaining unit is in force, the bargaining agent may, by notice, require the employer of those employees, or the employer may, by notice, require the bargaining agent to commence collective bargaining for the purpose of entering into a collective agreement."

**Employer's Notice**

Alternatively, the employer may, by notice, require the bargaining agent to commence collective bargaining for the purpose of entering into a collective agreement.

**Notice to Bargain**

The bargaining agent or the employer may give notice to each other to initiate collective bargaining. This notice is a requirement under the Canada Labour Code.

**Source**
CLC-48:
"Where the Board has certified a bargaining agent for a bargaining unit and no collective agreement binding on the employees in the bargaining unit is in force, the bargaining agent may, by notice, require the employer of those employees, or the employer may, by notice, require the bargaining agent to commence collective bargaining for the purpose of entering into a collective agreement."

question: What are the requirements for a party to a collective agreement to initiate collective bargaining for the purpose of renewing, revising, or entering into a new collective agreement?
answer:
**Initiating Collective Bargaining for Renewal, Revision, or New Collective Agreement**

**Timeframe for Initiation**

A party to a collective agreement may initiate collective bargaining for the purpose of renewing or revising the collective agreement or entering into a new collective agreement
"...within the period of four months immediately preceding the date of expiration of the term of the collective agreement, or within the longer period that may be provided for in the collective agreement..."

**Notice Requirement**

Either party to a collective agreement must provide notice to the other party to initiate collective bargaining for the purpose of renewing or revising the collective agreement or entering into a new collective agreement (CLC-49(1)). The notice must be given
"...within the period of four months immediately preceding the date of expiration of the term of the collective agreement, or within the longer period that may be provided for in the collective agreement..."

**Notice Period**

The notice period for initiating collective bargaining for renewal, revision, or new collective agreement is four months prior to the expiration of the term of the collective agreement (CLC-49(1)). However, the notice period may be longer if provided for in the collective agreement (CLC-49(1)).

**Source**

CLC-49: Section 49 of the Canada Labour Code.

CLC-50:

{"id": "CLC-50", "type": "Canada Labour Code", "title": "Obligation to Bargain Collectively: Duty to bargain and not to change terms and conditions", "section": "50"}, "text": "Section 50 Where notice to bargain collectively has been given under this Part, (a) the bargaining agent and the employer, without delay, but in any case within twenty days after the notice was given unless the parties otherwise agree, shall (i) meet and commence, or cause authorized representatives on their behalf to meet and commence, to bargain collectively in good faith, and (ii) make every reasonable effort to enter into a collective agreement; and (b) the employer shall not alter the rates of pay or any other term or condition of employment or any right or privilege of the employees in the bargaining unit, or any right or privilege of the bargaining agent, until the requirements of paragraphs 89(1)(a) to (d) have been met, unless the bargaining agent consents to the alteration of such a term or condition, or such a right or privilege. R.S., c. L-1, s. 148 1972, c. 18, s. 1 1977-78, c. 27, s. 51"

question: What are the obligations of the bargaining agent and the employer once notice to bargain collectively has been given under this Part of the Canada Labour Code (PART I - Industrial Relations)?
answer:
**Obligations of the Bargaining Agent and the Employer**

Once notice to bargain collectively has been given under this Part of the Canada Labour Code (PART I - Industrial Relations), the bargaining agent and the employer have specific obligations.

**Good Faith Bargaining**

The bargaining agent and the employer are required to
"...meet and commence, or cause authorized representatives on their behalf to meet and commence, to bargain collectively in good faith..." This means that they must engage in constructive dialogue and make every reasonable effort to reach a collective agreement.

**Timeframe for Bargaining**

The bargaining agent and the employer must
"...make every reasonable effort to enter into a collective agreement..." within twenty days after the notice was given, unless the parties otherwise agree (CLC-50.1). This timeframe is non-negotiable, and the parties must make a concerted effort to negotiate a collective agreement.

**Protection from Alterations**

The employer is prohibited from altering the rates of pay or any other term or condition of employment or any right or privilege of the employees in the bargaining unit, or any right or privilege of the bargaining agent, until the requirements of paragraphs 89(1)(a) to (d) have been met, unless the bargaining agent consents to the alteration of such a term or condition (CLC-50.1). This means that the employer cannot unilaterally change the terms of employment or the bargaining agent's rights until the parties have reached a collective agreement.

**Source**

CLC-50.1: Section 50 of the Canada Labour Code.

{"id": "CLC-51", "type": "Canada Labour Code", "title": "Technological Change", "section": "51"}, "text": "Section 51 (1) In this section and sections 52 to 55, means (a) the introduction by an employer into their work, undertaking or business of equipment or material of a different nature or kind than that previously utilized by the employer in the operation of the work, undertaking or business; and (b) a change in the manner in which the employer carries on the work, undertaking or business that is directly related to the introduction of that equipment or material. Marginal note: Application of sections 52, 54 and 55 (2) Sections 52, 54 and 55 do not apply, in respect of a technological change, to an employer and a bargaining agent who are bound by a collective agreement where (a) the employer has given to the bargaining agent a notice in writing of the technological change that is substantially in accordance with subsection 52(2), (i) prior to the day on which the employer and the bargaining agent entered into the collective agreement, if the notice requiring the parties to commence collective bargaining for the purpose of entering into that collective agreement was given pursuant to section 48, or (ii) not later than the last day on which notice requiring the parties to commence collective bargaining for the purpose of entering into the collective agreement could have been given pursuant to subsection 49(1), if the notice was given under that subsection; (b) the collective agreement contains provisions that specify procedures by which any matters that relate to terms and conditions or security of employment likely to be affected by a technological change may be negotiated and finally settled during the term of the agreement; or (c) the collective agreement contains provisions that (i) are intended to assist employees affected by any technological change to adjust to the effects of the technological change, and (ii) specify that sections 52, 54 and 55 do not apply, during the term of the collective agreement, to the employer and the bargaining agent. R.S., 1985, c. L-2, s. 51 1999, c. 31, s. 162(E) Marginal note: Notice of technological change"

question: Under what conditions do sections 52, 54, and 55 of the Canada Labour Code not apply to an employer and a bargaining agent who are bound by a collective agreement in the context of a technological change?
answer:
**Exemptions from Sections 52, 54, and 55**

According to Section 51(2) of the Canada Labour Code, sections 52, 54, and 55 do not apply to an employer and a bargaining agent who are bound by a collective agreement in the context of a technological change under the following conditions:

* The employer has given to the bargaining agent a notice in writing of the technological change that is substantially in accordance with subsection 52(2), prior to the day on which the employer and the bargaining agent entered into the collective agreement, if the notice requiring the parties to commence collective bargaining for the purpose of entering into that collective agreement was given pursuant to section 48, or
* The collective agreement contains provisions that specify procedures by which any matters that relate to terms and conditions or security of employment likely to be affected by a technological change may be negotiated and finally settled during the term of the agreement, or
* The collective agreement contains provisions that are intended to assist employees affected by any technological change to adjust to the effects of the technological change, and specify that sections 52, 54, and 55 do not apply, during the term of the collective agreement, to the employer and the bargaining agent.

**Source:** Section 51(2) of the Canada Labour Code

Marginal note: Details of proposed change (3) An employer who has given notice under subsection (1) to a bargaining agent shall, on request from the bargaining agent, provide the bargaining agent with a statement in writing setting out (a) a detailed description of the nature of the proposed technological change; (b) the names of the employees who will initially be likely to be affected by the proposed technological change; and (c) the rationale for the change. R.S., 1985, c. L-2, s. 52 1999, c. 31, s. 152(E) Marginal note: Application for order respecting technological change"

question: What are the requirements for an employer bound by a collective agreement to implement a technological change that is likely to affect the terms and conditions or security of employment of a significant number of employees?
answer:
**Section 52: Notice of Technological Change**

To implement a technological change that is likely to affect the terms and conditions or security of employment of a significant number of employees, an employer bound by a collective agreement must give notice to the bargaining agent at least one hundred and twenty days prior to the date on which the technological change is to be effected.
"An employer who is bound by a collective agreement and who proposes to effect a technological change that is likely to affect the terms and conditions or security of employment of a significant number of the employer’s employees to whom the collective agreement applies shall give notice of the technological change to the bargaining agent bound by the collective agreement at least one hundred and twenty days prior to the date on which the technological change is to be effected."

**Section 52: Contents of Notice**

The notice must be in writing and must state the following information:

* The nature of the technological change
* The date on which the employer proposes to effect the technological change
* The approximate number and type of employees likely to be affected by the technological change
* The effect that the technological change is likely to have on the terms and conditions or security of employment of the employees affected
* Such other information as is required by the regulations made pursuant to subsection (4)
"The notice referred to in subsection (1) shall be in writing and shall state (a) the nature of the technological change; (b) the date on which the employer proposes to effect the technological change; (c) the approximate number and type of employees likely to be affected by the technological change; (d) the effect that the technological change is likely to have on the terms and conditions or security of employment of the employees affected; and (e) such other information as is required by the regulations made pursuant to subsection (4)."

**Section 52: Details of Proposed Change**

The employer must also provide the bargaining agent with a statement in writing setting out:

* A detailed description of the nature of the proposed technological change
* The names of the employees who will initially be likely to be affected by the proposed technological change
* The rationale for the change
"An employer who has given notice under subsection (1) to a bargaining agent shall, on request from the bargaining agent, provide the bargaining agent with a statement in writing setting out (a) a detailed description of the nature of the proposed technological change; (b) the names of the employees who will initially be likely to be affected by the proposed technological change; and (c) the rationale for the change."

{"id": "CLC-53", "type": "Canada Labour Code", "title": "Technological Change: Application for order respecting technological change", "section": "53"}, "text": "Section 53 (1) Where a bargaining agent alleges that sections 52, 54 and 55 apply to an employer in respect of an alleged technological change and that the employer has failed to comply with section 52, the bargaining agent may, not later than thirty days after the bargaining agent became aware, or in the opinion of the Board ought to have become aware, of the failure of the employer to comply with section 52, apply to the Board for an order determining the matters so alleged. Marginal note: Order respecting technological change (2) On receipt of an application for an order determining the matters alleged under subsection (1) and after affording an opportunity for the parties to make representations, the Board may, by order, (a) determine that sections 52, 54 and 55 do not apply to the employer in respect of the alleged technological change; or (b) determine that sections 52, 54 and 55 apply to the employer in respect of the alleged technological change and that the employer has failed to comply with section 52 in respect of the technological change. Marginal note: Idem (3) The Board may, in any order made under paragraph (2)(b), or by order made after consultation with the parties pending the making of any order under subsection (2), (a) direct the employer not to proceed with the technological change or alleged technological change for such period, not in excess of one hundred and twenty days, as the Board considers appropriate; (b) require the reinstatement of any employee displaced by the employer as a result of the technological change; and (c) where an employee is reinstated pursuant to paragraph (b), require the employer to reimburse the employee for any loss of pay suffered by the employee as a result of their displacement. Marginal note: Order deemed notice (4) An order of the Board made under paragraph (2)(b) in respect of an employer is deemed to be a notice of technological change given by the employer pursuant to section 52, and the Board shall concurrently, by order, grant leave to the bargaining agent to serve on the employer a notice to commence collective bargaining for the purpose referred to in subsection 54(1). R.S., 1985, c. L-2, s. 53 1998, c. 26, s. 26 1999, c. 31, s. 162(E) Marginal note: Application for order to serve notice to bargain"

question: What can a bargaining agent do if they allege that an employer has failed to comply with the requirements related to technological changes, and what are the potential outcomes of such an action?
answer:
**Application for Order Respecting Technological Change**

If a bargaining agent alleges that an employer has failed to comply with the requirements related to technological changes, they can apply to the Board for an order determining the matters so alleged.

According to Section 53 of the Canada Labour Code,
"Where a bargaining agent alleges that sections 52, 54 and 55 apply to an employer in respect of an alleged technological change and that the employer has failed to comply with section 52, the bargaining agent may, not later than thirty days after the bargaining agent became aware, or in the opinion of the Board ought to have become aware, of the failure of the employer to comply with section 52, apply to the Board for an order determining the matters so alleged."

**Potential Outcomes of Such an Action**

The Board may, by order, determine that sections 52, 54 and 55 do not apply to the employer in respect of the alleged technological change, or that sections 52, 54 and 55 apply to the employer in respect of the alleged technological change and that the employer has failed to comply with section 52 in respect of the technological change.

The Board may also direct the employer not to proceed with the technological change or alleged technological change for a period not in excess of one hundred and twenty days, require the reinstatement of any employee displaced by the employer as a result of the technological change, and require the employer to reimburse the employee for any loss of pay suffered by the employee as a result of their displacement.

**Notice of Technological Change**

An order of the Board made under paragraph (2)(b) is deemed to be a notice of technological change given by the employer pursuant to section 52, and the Board shall concurrently, by order, grant leave to the bargaining agent to serve on the employer a notice to commence collective bargaining for the purpose referred to in subsection 54(1).

question: What recourse does a bargaining agent have when it receives notice of a technological change that may adversely affect the terms and conditions or security of employment of a significant number of employees bound by a collective agreement?
answer:
**Application for Order to Serve Notice to Bargain**

A bargaining agent has the recourse to apply to the Board for an order granting leave to serve on the employer a notice to commence collective bargaining for the purpose of revising the existing provisions of the collective agreement or including new provisions that relate to terms and conditions or security of employment.

According to Section 54(1) of the Canada Labour Code,
"Where a bargaining agent receives notice of a technological change pursuant to section 52, the bargaining agent may, in order to assist the employees affected by the change to adjust to the effects of the change, apply to the Board, within thirty days after the date on which it receives the notice, for an order granting leave to serve on the employer a notice to commence collective bargaining for the purpose of (a) revising the existing provisions of the collective agreement by which they are bound that relate to terms and conditions or security of employment; or (b) including new provisions in the collective agreement that relate to terms and conditions or security of employment."

This provision allows the bargaining agent to seek the Board's intervention to negotiate and finalize agreements that address the potential adverse effects of the technological change on the employees' terms and conditions or security of employment.

**Granting Leave to Serve Notice to Bargain**

If the Board is satisfied that the technological change is likely, substantially, and adversely to affect the terms and conditions or security of employment of a significant number of employees to whom the collective agreement applies, it may grant leave to the bargaining agent to serve on the employer a notice to commence collective bargaining.

According to Section 54(2) of the Canada Labour Code,
"Where the Board has received from a bargaining agent an application for an order under subsection (1), and it is satisfied that the technological change in respect of which the bargaining agent has received notice given pursuant to section 52 is likely, substantially and adversely, to affect the terms and conditions or security of employment of a significant number of employees to whom the collective agreement between the bargaining agent and the employer applies, the Board may, by order, grant leave to the bargaining agent to serve on the employer a notice to commence collective bargaining for the purpose referred to in subsection (1)."

question: What happens to an employer's ability to effect a technological change when a bargaining agent applies to the Board for an order under subsection 54(1)?
answer:
**Effect of Bargaining Agent's Application on Technological Change**

When a bargaining agent applies to the Board for an order under subsection 54(1), the employer's ability to effect a technological change is temporarily suspended.

**Section 55: Conditions Precedent to Technological Change
"Where a bargaining agent applies to the Board for an order under subsection 54(1), the employer in respect of whom the application is made shall not effect the technological change in respect of which the application is made until (a) the Board has made an order refusing to grant leave to the bargaining agent to serve on the employer a notice to commence collective bargaining; or (b) the Board has made an order granting leave to the bargaining agent to serve on the employer a notice to commence collective bargaining and (i) an agreement has been reached as a result of collective bargaining, or (ii) the requirements of paragraphs 89(1)(a) to (d) have been met."

This subsection indicates that the employer's ability to effect a technological change is contingent on the outcome of the Board's decision on the bargaining agent's application. If the Board grants the order, the employer must wait for an agreement to be reached or for the requirements to be met before proceeding with the technological change. If the Board refuses the order, the employer is free to proceed with the technological change.

**Content and Interpretation of Collective Agreements**

**Provision for Final Settlement of Differences**

According to Section 57 of the Canada Labour Code,
"Every collective agreement shall contain a provision for final settlement without stoppage of work, by arbitration or otherwise, of all differences between the parties to or employees bound by the collective agreement, concerning its interpretation, application, administration or alleged contravention."

This provision requires that collective agreements include a mechanism for resolving disputes between parties, ensuring that differences are settled in a fair and timely manner.

**Appointment of Arbitrator or Arbitration Board Chairperson**

If the parties are unable to agree on an arbitrator or arbitration board chairperson, either party or its nominee may make a written request to the Minister to appoint an arbitrator or arbitration board chairperson. (CLC-57)

The Minister shall then appoint an arbitrator or arbitration board chairperson, after such inquiry, if any, as the Minister considers necessary. (CLC-57)

This provision ensures that the Minister can intervene in disputes where the parties are unable to agree on the appointment of an arbitrator or arbitration board chairperson, providing a neutral third-party solution to resolve the dispute.

question: What is the status of an arbitrator or arbitration board's decision under the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
**Status of an Arbitrator or Arbitration Board's Decision**

**Finality of Decisions**

According to Section 60 of the Canada Labour Code,
"Every order or decision of an arbitrator or arbitration board is final and shall not be questioned or reviewed in any court." [CLC-60]

This means that the decisions of an arbitrator or arbitration board are not subject to review or appeal in any court, including the Federal Court of Canada.

As stated in Section 58 of the Canada Labour Code,
"No order shall be made, process entered or proceeding taken in any court, whether by way of injunction, certiorari , prohibition, quo warranto or otherwise, to question, review, prohibit or restrain an arbitrator or arbitration board in any of their proceedings under this Part." [CLC-58]

This provision ensures that the decisions of an arbitrator or arbitration board are not subject to review or challenge in any court, and that they are given effect as final and binding decisions.

**No Statutory Authority to Proceed Beyond the Decision**

As stated in Section 18 of the Labour-Reports document,
"Once a decision is filed with the Court, the Labour Program  has no statutory authority to proceed beyond this point. The party may now seek  enforcement of the order through other avenues as with any judgment of the  Federal Court." [LABOUR-REPORTS-12_8]

This means that once an arbitrator or arbitration board's decision is filed with the Federal Court, the Labour Program is no longer able to take any further action to enforce the decision, and the party must seek enforcement through other means.

question: What are the general powers and authorities granted to an arbitrator or arbitration board in the context of labor disputes and collective agreements under the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
**General Powers and Authorities of Arbitrators and Arbitration Boards**

The Canada Labour Code grants arbitrators and arbitration boards significant powers and authorities in the context of labor disputes and collective agreements.

**Powers Conferred by the Board**

An arbitrator or arbitration board has the powers conferred on the Board by paragraphs 16(a), (b), (c), and (f.1) of the Canada Labour Code. 

**Interpretation and Application of Statutes and Collective Agreements**

An arbitrator or arbitration board has the power to interpret, apply, and give relief in accordance with a statute relating to employment matters, whether or not there is conflict between the statute and the collective agreement. 

**Making Interim Orders**

An arbitrator or arbitration board has the power to make the interim orders that the arbitrator or arbitration board considers appropriate. 

**Considering Submissions and Expediting Proceedings**

An arbitrator or arbitration board has the power to consider submissions provided in the form that the arbitrator or the arbitration board considers appropriate or to which the parties agree. The arbitrator or arbitration board also has the power to expedite proceedings and to prevent abuse of the arbitration process by making the orders or giving the directions that the arbitrator or arbitration board considers appropriate for those purposes. 

**Determining Arbitrability**

An arbitrator or arbitration board has the power to determine any question as to whether a matter referred to the arbitrator or arbitration board is arbitrable.

question: What are the key responsibilities of an arbitrator or arbitration board in terms of procedure and fairness during a proceeding?
answer:
**Key Responsibilities of an Arbitrator or Arbitration Board**

The key responsibilities of an arbitrator or arbitration board in terms of procedure and fairness during a proceeding are outlined in the Canada Labour Code.

**Determining Procedure**

An arbitrator or arbitration board
"...shall determine their own procedure, but shall give full opportunity to the parties to the proceeding to present evidence and make submissions to the arbitrator or arbitration board."

This means that the arbitrator or arbitration board has the authority to decide on the procedures to be followed during the proceeding, but they must also ensure that the parties have a fair opportunity to present their evidence and make submissions.

**Principles of Administrative Fairness**

The arbitrator or arbitration board must also adhere to principles of administrative fairness, which include:

* Having an unbiased decision-maker
* Giving the parties an opportunity to present their evidence and arguments
* Receiving a decision in a timely manner
* Having the reasons for the decision clearly explained

These principles are essential to ensuring that the proceeding is fair and that the parties receive a just outcome.

**Giving Full Opportunity to Parties**

The arbitrator or arbitration board must give
"...full opportunity to the parties to the proceeding to present evidence and make submissions to the arbitrator or arbitration board."

This means that the parties must be given a fair chance to present their case and make their arguments, and that the arbitrator or arbitration board must consider all relevant evidence and submissions before making a decision.

**No Error of Jurisdiction**

The arbitrator or arbitration board must not make a decision or finding outside of the area of law that they have the authority to interpret and apply. (CLC-61)

This means that the arbitrator or arbitration board must be mindful of their jurisdiction and ensure that their decisions are based on the relevant law and evidence.

question: What are the rules and exceptions surrounding the timeframe for an arbitrator or arbitration board to make or give an order or decision in a labour dispute?
answer:
**Timeframe for Making or Giving an Order or Decision**

The Canada Labour Code sets out the rules and exceptions surrounding the timeframe for an arbitrator or arbitration board to make or give an order or decision in a labour dispute.

**Section 64: Order or Decision within Sixty Days**

According to Section 64 of the Canada Labour Code,
"Every order or decision of an arbitrator or arbitration board shall be made or given within sixty days after, in the case of an arbitrator, their appointment as arbitrator, and, in the case of an arbitration board, the appointment of the arbitration board chairperson, unless..."

**Exceptions to the Sixty-Day Rule**

There are two exceptions to the sixty-day rule. Firstly, if the collective agreement otherwise provides or the parties otherwise agree, the order or decision can be made or given outside of the sixty-day timeframe (CLC-64). Secondly, if owing to circumstances beyond the control of the arbitrator or arbitration board, it is not practicable to make or give the order or decision within those sixty days, the order or decision can also be made or given outside of the timeframe (CLC-64).

**Suspension of Arbitration Proceedings**

The sixty-day rule does not apply if the arbitration proceedings are suspended pursuant to subsection 65(2) of the Canada Labour Code. In such cases, any day included in the suspension period is not counted as one of the sixty days referred to in subsection 64(1) (CLC-64).

**Late Order or Decision**

The failure of an arbitrator or arbitration board to make or give an order or decision within the sixty-day timeframe does not affect the jurisdiction of the arbitrator or arbitration board to continue with and complete the arbitration proceedings. Any order or decision made or given by the arbitrator or arbitration board after the expiration of those sixty days is not for that reason invalid (CLC-64).

question: What are the implications for a collective agreement that contains no provision as to its term or is for a term of less than one year, and how can its term be altered or revised?
answer:
**Term of Collective Agreement**

A collective agreement that contains no provision as to its term or is for a term of less than one year is deemed to be for a term of one year from the date on which it comes into force.
"Where a collective agreement contains no provision as to its term or is for a term of less than one year, the collective agreement shall be deemed to be for a term of one year from the date on which it comes into force and shall not, except as provided by subsection 36(2) or with the consent of the Board, be terminated by the parties thereto within that term of one year."

**Revision of Collective Agreement**

The parties to a collective agreement can agree to revise any provision of the collective agreement, except for the provision relating to the term of the collective agreement.
"Nothing in this Part prohibits the parties to a collective agreement from agreeing to a revision of any provision of the collective agreement other than a provision relating to the term of the collective agreement."

**Alteration of Termination Date**

The Board may order that the termination date of the collective agreement be altered for the purpose of establishing a common termination date for two or more collective agreements binding a single employer.
"The Board may, on application made jointly by both parties to a collective agreement, order that the termination date of the collective agreement be altered for the purpose of establishing a common termination date for two or more collective agreements binding a single employer."

**Provision for Settlement of Differences**

The provision required to be contained in a collective agreement, as set out in subsection 57(1), shall remain in force after the termination of the collective agreement and until the requirements of paragraphs 89(1)(a) to (d) have been met.
"Notwithstanding anything contained in a collective agreement, the provision required to be contained therein by subsection 57(1) shall remain in force after the termination of the collective agreement and until the requirements of paragraphs 89(1)(a) to (d) have been met."

**Powers of Arbitrator**

Where a difference between the parties to a collective agreement relating to a provision contained in the collective agreement arises during the period from the date of its termination to the date the requirements of paragraphs 89(1)(a) to (d) have been met, an arbitrator or arbitration board may hear and determine the difference.
"Where a difference between the parties to a collective agreement relating to a provision contained in the collective agreement arises during the period from the date of its termination to the date the requirements of paragraphs 89(1)(a) to (d) have been met, (a) an arbitrator or arbitration board may hear and determine the difference; and (b) sections 57 to 66 apply to the hearing and determination."

**Revision of Term
"Despite subsection (2), if a notice to bargain referred to in subsection 65.12(1) of the Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act has been served, the parties may agree to revise the term of the collective agreement without approval of the Board."
"Despite subsection (2), if a notice to bargain referred to in subsection 65.12(1) of the Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act has been served, the parties may agree to revise the term of the collective agreement without approval of the Board."

**Canada Labour Code: Provisions in Collective Agreements**

question: What happens when a trade union requests that union dues be deducted from the wages of employees in a bargaining unit, and are there any exceptions for employees who object to paying these dues?
answer:
**Trade Union Request for Union Dues Deduction**

**Section 70 of the Canada Labour Code**

When a trade union requests that union dues be deducted from the wages of employees in a bargaining unit, the employer is required to include a provision in the collective agreement that requires the employer to deduct the union dues from the wages of each employee in the unit affected by the collective agreement, whether or not the employee is a member of the union. [1]

**Religious Objections**

The Canada Labour Code also provides for exceptions for employees who object to paying union dues due to religious convictions or beliefs. [2] In such cases, the Board may order that the provision in the collective agreement requiring membership in a trade union or payment of regular union dues does not apply to the employee, as long as an amount equal to the regular union dues is paid by the employee, either directly or by way of deduction from their wages, to a registered charity mutually agreed on by the employee and the trade union. [3]

**Designation of a Registered Charity**

If the employee and the trade union are unable to agree on a registered charity, the Board may designate any such charity as the charity to which payment should be made. [4]

**Definitions**

The Canada Labour Code defines "registered charity" as an organization that is registered under the Income Tax Act, and "regular union dues" as the dues uniformly and regularly paid by a member of the union in accordance with the constitution and by-laws of the union, or the dues referred to in paragraph (a), other than any amount that is for payment of pension, superannuation, sickness insurance, or any other benefit available only to members of the union. [5]

question: What steps must be taken by a party to a collective bargaining agreement when they are unable to reach an agreement or when collective bargaining has not commenced within the required timeframe?
answer:
**Notice of Dispute**

When a party to a collective bargaining agreement is unable to reach an agreement or when collective bargaining has not commenced within the required timeframe, they must inform the Minister of their failure to enter into, renew or revise a collective agreement.

According to Section 71 of the Canada Labour Code,
"Where a notice to commence collective bargaining has been given under this Part, either party may inform the Minister, by sending a notice of dispute, of their failure to enter into, renew or revise a collective agreement where (a) collective bargaining has not commenced within the time fixed by this Part; or (b) the parties have bargained collectively for the purpose of entering into or revising a collective agreement but have been unable to reach agreement."

**Procedure for Filing a Notice of Dispute**

To file a notice of dispute, the party must send a notice to the Minister, who must then be copied on any subsequent communication with the other party. This ensures that the Minister is aware of the dispute and can provide guidance or intervention if necessary.

**Options for the Minister**

The Minister has options for addressing the dispute, including providing guidance to the parties, intervening in the collective bargaining process, or referring the dispute to a conciliation officer. The Minister's role is to facilitate a resolution to the dispute and ensure that the parties return to collective bargaining.

question: What are the possible actions the Minister can take upon receiving a notice or considering it necessary to assist parties in entering into or revising a collective agreement?
answer:
**Conciliation Procedures: Options of Minister**

The Minister has several options upon receiving a notice or considering it necessary to assist parties in entering into or revising a collective agreement.

**Appointing a Conciliation Officer**

The Minister may appoint a conciliation officer to assist the parties in entering into or revising a collective agreement. This is stated in section 72(1)(a) of the Canada Labour Code:
"The Minister shall, not later than fifteen days after receiving a notice in writing under section 71, (a) appoint a conciliation officer..."

**Appointing a Conciliation Commissioner**

Alternatively, the Minister may appoint a conciliation commissioner to assist the parties in entering into or revising a collective agreement. This is also stated in section 72(1)(b) of the Canada Labour Code:
"The Minister shall, not later than fifteen days after receiving a notice in writing under section 71, (a) appoint a conciliation officer; (b) appoint a conciliation commissioner..."

**Establishing a Conciliation Board**

The Minister may also establish a conciliation board to assist the parties in entering into or revising a collective agreement. This is stated in section 72(1)(c) of the Canada Labour Code:
"The Minister shall, not later than fifteen days after receiving a notice in writing under section 71, (a) appoint a conciliation officer; (b) appoint a conciliation commissioner; (c) establish a conciliation board in accordance with section 82..."

**Notifying the Parties**

If the Minister does not receive a notice under section 71, but considers it advisable to take action, the Minister may notify the parties in writing of their intention not to appoint a conciliation officer or conciliation commissioner or establish a conciliation board. question: What is the primary role of a conciliation officer appointed during a labour dispute under the Canada Labour Code, and what are their key responsibilities?
answer:
**Conciliation Officer's Role and Responsibilities**

The primary role of a conciliation officer appointed during a labour dispute under the Canada Labour Code is to assist the parties to the dispute in entering into or revising a collective agreement.

According to Section 73(1) of the Canada Labour Code,
"Where a conciliation officer has been appointed under section 72, the conciliation officer shall (a) forthwith after the appointment, confer with the parties to the dispute and endeavour to assist them in entering into or revising a collective agreement..."

This indicates that the conciliation officer's primary responsibility is to facilitate negotiations between the parties to the dispute, with the goal of reaching a collective agreement.

**Key Responsibilities**

The conciliation officer's key responsibilities include:

* Confering with the parties to the dispute and endeavouring to assist them in entering into or revising a collective agreement (Section 73(1))
* Reporting to the Minister within fourteen days of the appointment or within the longer period agreed to by the parties or allowed by the Minister, as to whether or not the officer has succeeded in assisting the parties in entering into or revising a collective agreement (Section 73(2))

This suggests that the conciliation officer's role is to act as a neutral third-party mediator, facilitating negotiations and providing guidance and support to the parties to the dispute, in order to reach a mutually acceptable collective agreement.

question: What are the primary duties of a conciliation commissioner or a conciliation board when appointed or established to resolve a labor dispute?
answer:
**Primary Duties of a Conciliation Commissioner or a Conciliation Board**

According to the Canada Labour Code, the primary duties of a conciliation commissioner or a conciliation board when appointed or established to resolve a labor dispute are as follows:

**To Assist Parties in Entering into or Revising a Collective Agreement
"...conciliation board shall (a) immediately endeavour to assist the parties to the dispute in entering into or revising a collective agreement..."

This duty is a fundamental aspect of the conciliation process, as it aims to facilitate negotiations between the parties to resolve the dispute.

**To Report to the Minister on Success or Failure in Assisting Parties
"...within fourteen days after the date of appointment or establishment, or within the longer period that may be agreed to by the parties or allowed by the Minister, report to the Minister as to the commissioner’s or board’s success or failure in assisting the parties to the dispute and as to their findings and recommendations."

This duty requires the conciliation commissioner or board to provide a report to the Minister, outlining their efforts to resolve the dispute and any outcomes or recommendations that may have been made.

**To Determine Their Own Procedure
"A conciliation commissioner or a conciliation board (a) may determine their own procedure..."

This duty highlights the flexibility and autonomy that conciliation commissioners and boards have in conducting their proceedings, as long as they remain within the bounds of the law and the Canada Labour Code.

**To Have Powers Conferred by the Board
"...conciliation commissioner or a conciliation board (a) may determine their own procedure; (b) has, in relation to any proceeding before them, the powers conferred on the Board, in relation to any proceeding before the Board, by paragraphs 16(a), (b), (c), (f) and (h)..."

This duty emphasizes the significant powers that conciliation commissioners and boards have in resolving labor disputes, including the ability to investigate and gather evidence, and to make recommendations or orders.

question: What are the implications if a conciliation officer, commissioner, or board does not submit a report within the specified time limit, and what are the exceptions to this rule?
answer:
**Conciliation Procedures: Late Report Not Invalid**

**Failure to Submit Report within Time Limit**

According to Section 113 of the Canada Labour Code,
"The failure of a conciliation officer, conciliation commissioner or conciliation board to report to the Minister within a period limited by this Part does not invalidate the proceeding or terminate the authority of the conciliation officer, conciliation commissioner or conciliation board."

This means that even if a conciliation officer, commissioner, or board fails to submit a report within the specified time limit, the proceeding or authority of the officer, commissioner, or board is not affected.

**Exceptions to the Rule**

Section 75 of the Canada Labour Code outlines the exceptions to the rule. According to Section 75,
"Except with the consent of the parties, the Minister may not extend the time for a conciliation officer to report, or for a conciliation commissioner or conciliation board to submit a report, beyond sixty days after the date of appointment or establishment."

This means that if the parties to the dispute agree to extend the time limit, the Minister may do so. However, if the parties do not consent to an extension, the time limit of sixty days must be adhered to.

**Deemed Reporting and Receipt**

In the event that the parties do not consent to an extension, the conciliation officer is deemed to have reported sixty days after the date on which that officer was appointed or at the end of the extended time limit to which the parties consent, unless she or he actually reports earlier. (CLC-75)

Similarly, the Minister is deemed to have received the report of the conciliation commissioner or conciliation board sixty days after the date on which the conciliation commissioner was appointed or the board was established or at the end of the extended time limit to which the parties consent, unless the Minister actually receives the report earlier. (CLC-75)

This means that even if the conciliation officer or commissioner/board fails to submit a report within the specified time limit, the Minister is still deemed to have received the report on the specified date, unless the report is actually received earlier.

**Conciliation Procedures: Release of Report**

According to Section 77 of the Canada Labour Code, the Minister has the following actions with respect to a report submitted by a conciliation commissioner or conciliation board:

The Minister shall, after receiving the report of a conciliation commissioner or conciliation board,
"...a copy of the report to the parties to the dispute; and (b) may make the report available to the public in a manner that the Minister considers advisable."

This quote highlights the Minister's obligation to release the report to the parties involved in the dispute, as well as to make it available to the public. This action is a crucial step in ensuring that the report is accessible to all stakeholders and that the parties can review and consider the findings and recommendations.

**Reconsideration of Report**

Additionally, Section 76 of the Canada Labour Code provides that the Minister may direct the conciliation commissioner or conciliation board to reconsider the report and clarify or amplify any part of it. This action allows the Minister to request further clarification or additional information from the conciliation commissioner or conciliation board, which can be useful in ensuring that the report is accurate and comprehensive.

question: What happens if an employer and a bargaining agent fail to enter into a first collective agreement after being required to commence collective bargaining, and the Minister considers it necessary or advisable to intervene?
answer:
**Minister's Intervention in Collective Bargaining Dispute**

If an employer and a bargaining agent fail to enter into a first collective agreement after being required to commence collective bargaining, the Minister may intervene to assist the parties in entering into or revising a collective agreement.

**Section 80 of the Canada Labour Code**

According to Section 80 of the Canada Labour Code,
"Where an employer or a bargaining agent is required, by notice given under section 48, to commence collective bargaining for the purpose of entering into the first collective agreement between the parties with respect to the bargaining unit for which the bargaining agent has been certified and the requirements of paragraphs 89(1)(a) to (d) have otherwise been met, the Minister may, if the Minister considers it necessary or advisable, at any time thereafter direct the Board to inquire into the dispute and, if the Board considers it advisable, to settle the terms and conditions of the first collective agreement between the parties."

In this scenario, the Minister has the authority to direct the Board to inquire into the dispute and settle the terms and conditions of the first collective agreement between the parties.

**Board's Role in Settling Collective Agreement**

The Board's role in settling the terms and conditions of a first collective agreement is outlined in Section 80 of the Canada Labour Code. The Board shall
"...proceed as directed by the Minister under subsection (1) and, if the Board settles the terms and conditions of a first collective agreement referred to in that subsection, those terms and conditions shall constitute the collective agreement between the parties and shall be binding on them and on the employees in the bargaining unit, except to the extent that such terms and conditions are subsequently amended by the parties by agreement in writing."

The Board's settlement of the terms and conditions of a first collective agreement is considered binding on the parties and the employees in the bargaining unit, unless the parties agree to amend the agreement in writing.

**Considerations in Settling Collective Agreement**

When settling the terms and conditions of a first collective agreement, the Board considers several factors, including
"...the extent to which the parties have, or have not, bargained in good faith in an attempt to enter into the first collective agreement between them; (b) the terms and conditions of employment, if any, negotiated through collective bargaining for employees performing the same or similar functions in the same or similar circumstances as the employees in the bargaining unit; and (c) such other matters as the Board considers will assist it in arriving at terms and conditions that are fair and reasonable in the circumstances."

By considering these factors, the Board aims to arrive at terms and conditions that are fair and reasonable in the circumstances, ensuring that the collective agreement is equitable and beneficial to all parties involved.

question: What is the process for establishing a conciliation board under the Canada Labour Code, and who is responsible for appointing its members?
answer:
**Establishment of Conciliation Boards**

The process for establishing a conciliation board under the Canada Labour Code involves several steps.

**Notification to Parties**

The Minister shall give notice to the parties of the establishment of the conciliation board, as stated in Section 83 of the Canada Labour Code:
"When the members of a conciliation board have been appointed under section 82 in respect of a dispute, the Minister shall forthwith give notice to the parties of the names of the members of the board, and thereupon it shall be conclusively presumed that the conciliation board described in the notice has been established in accordance with this Part as of the date the notice is given."

**Nomination of Members**

The parties to the dispute are required to nominate a person to be a member of the conciliation board within seven days after receiving the notice from the Minister. If either party fails to nominate a person, the Minister shall appoint a qualified person to be a member of the conciliation board. (CLC-82)

**Appointment of Chairperson**

The members of the conciliation board shall nominate a third person, who is willing and ready to act, to be a member and chairperson of the conciliation board within five days after the appointment of the second member. If the members fail to nominate a chairperson, the Minister shall appoint a qualified person to be a member and chairperson of the conciliation board. (CLC-82)

**Responsibility for Appointing Members**

The Minister is responsible for appointing the members of the conciliation board, as stated in Section 82 of the Canada Labour Code:
"...the Minister shall immediately, by notice in writing, require each of the parties to the dispute to nominate, within seven days after receipt by the party of the notice, one person to be a member of the conciliation board and, on receipt of the nomination within those seven days, the Minister shall appoint the nominee to be a member of the conciliation board."

question: What are the requirements that must be met by a trade union or an employers' organization before declaring or authorizing a strike or lockout under the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
**Requirements for Declaring or Authorizing a Strike or Lockout**

**Section 89: No Strike or Lockout until Certain Requirements Met**

In order to declare or authorize a strike or lockout, a trade union or an employers' organization must meet the requirements outlined in Section 89 of the Canada Labour Code.
"No employer shall declare or cause a lockout and no trade union shall declare or authorize a strike unless (a) the employer or trade union has given notice to bargain collectively under this Part..."
*   This requirement ensures that the parties have made an effort to negotiate a collective agreement before resorting to strike or lockout action.

**Section 87.1: Strike Notice**

A trade union must give notice to the employer, at least seventy-two hours in advance, indicating the date on which a strike will occur, and must provide a copy of the notice to the Minister.
"Unless a lockout not prohibited by this Part has occurred, a trade union must give notice to the employer, at least seventy-two hours in advance, indicating the date on which a strike will occur, and must provide a copy of the notice to the Minister."
*   This requirement ensures that the employer is given adequate notice before the strike can take place.

**Section 87.3: Secret Ballot - Strike Vote
"...a trade union may not declare or authorize a strike unless it has, within the previous sixty days, or any longer period that may be agreed to in writing by the trade union and the employer, held a secret ballot vote among the employees in the unit and received the approval of the majority of the employees who voted."
"...a trade union may not declare or authorize a strike unless it has, within the previous sixty days, or any longer period that may be agreed to in writing by the trade union and the employer, held a secret ballot vote among the employees in the unit and received the approval of the majority of the employees who voted."
*   This requirement ensures that the employees have given their consent to the strike before it can take place.

**Section 89: No Strike or Lockout until Certain Requirements Met**

In addition to the requirements outlined in Section 87.1 and 87.3, a trade union or an employers' organization must also meet the requirements outlined in Section 89.
"No employer shall declare or cause a lockout and no trade union shall declare or authorize a strike unless (a) the employer or trade union has given notice to bargain collectively under this Part; (b) the employer and the trade union (i) have failed to bargain collectively within the period specified in paragraph 50(a), or (ii) have bargained collectively in accordance with section 50 but have failed to enter into or revise a collective agreement..."
*   This requirement ensures that the parties have made an effort to negotiate a collective agreement before resorting to strike or lockout action.

**Section 89: No Strike or Lockout until Certain Requirements Met**

The requirements outlined in Section 89 must be met before a trade union or an employers' organization can declare or authorize a strike or lockout.
"No employee shall participate in a strike unless (a) the employee is a member of a bargaining unit in respect of which a notice to bargain collectively has been given under this Part; and (b) the requirements of subsection (1) have been met in respect of the bargaining unit of which the employee is a member."
*   This requirement ensures that the employees are part of a bargaining unit and have given their consent to the strike before it can take place.

question: What are the obligations of employers, trade unions, and employees in the bargaining unit during a strike or lockout under the Canada Labour Code, and what role does the Board play in ensuring public safety and health?
answer:
**Obligations of Employers, Trade Unions, and Employees**

During a strike or lockout, the Canada Labour Code imposes specific obligations on employers, trade unions, and employees in the bargaining unit.

**Employer Obligations**

The employer must continue to provide services, operation of facilities, or production of goods to the extent necessary to prevent an immediate and serious danger to the safety or health of the public. This is stated in Section 87.4(1) of the Canada Labour Code:
"During a strike or lockout not prohibited by this Part, the employer, the trade union and the employees in the bargaining unit must continue the supply of services, operation of facilities or production of goods to the extent necessary to prevent an immediate and serious danger to the safety or health of the public."

**Trade Union Obligations**

The trade union must also continue to provide services, operation of facilities, or production of goods to the extent necessary to prevent an immediate and serious danger to the safety or health of the public. This is stated in Section 87.4(2) of the Canada Labour Code:
"An employer or a trade union may, no later than fifteen days after notice to bargain collectively has been given, give notice to the other party specifying the supply of services, operation of facilities or production of goods that, in its opinion, must be continued in the event of a strike or a lockout in order to comply with subsection (1) and the approximate number of employees in the bargaining unit that, in its opinion, would be required for that purpose."

**Employee Obligations**

Employees in the bargaining unit must continue to provide services, operation of facilities, or production of goods to the extent necessary to prevent an immediate and serious danger to the safety or health of the public. This is stated in Section 87.4(1) of the Canada Labour Code.

**Board's Role**

The Board plays a crucial role in ensuring public safety and health during a strike or lockout. The Board may:

* Determine any question with respect to the application of Section 87.4(1) and make any orders it considers appropriate to ensure compliance with that subsection (Section 87.4(4) and (6) of the Canada Labour Code).
* Review and confirm, amend or cancel an agreement entered into, or a determination or order made, under Section 87.4(7) of the Canada Labour Code.
* Direct a binding method of resolving the issues in dispute between the parties for the purpose of ensuring settlement of a dispute (Section 87.4(8) of the Canada Labour Code).

In the event that the Board determines that a strike or lockout could pose an immediate and serious danger to the safety or health of the public, it may, by order, designate the supply of services, operation of facilities, and production of goods that it considers necessary to continue, and specify the manner and extent to which the employer, the trade union, and the employees in the bargaining unit must continue that supply, operation, and production (Section 87.4(6) of the Canada Labour Code).

question: What are the main restrictions imposed on an employer during a dispute resolution process and after a strike or lockout under the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
**Restrictions on Employers During a Dispute Resolution Process**

The Canada Labour Code imposes several restrictions on employers during a dispute resolution process. One of the main restrictions is that an employer must give notice to the trade union, at least seventy-two hours in advance, indicating the date on which a lockout will occur, and must provide a copy of the notice to the Minister.
"...an employer must give notice to the trade union, at least seventy-two hours in advance, indicating the date on which a lockout will occur, and must provide a copy of the notice to the Minister."

This restriction is intended to provide the trade union with sufficient time to prepare for the lockout and to allow for a peaceful resolution of the dispute.

**Restrictions on Employers After a Strike or Lockout**

After a strike or lockout, the employer is subject to several restrictions. One of the main restrictions is that the employer must reinstate employees in the bargaining unit who were on strike or locked out, in preference to any person who was not an employee in the bargaining unit on the date on which notice to bargain collectively was given and was hired or assigned after that date to perform all or part of the duties of an employee in the unit on strike or locked out.
"At the end of a strike or lockout not prohibited by this Part, the employer must reinstate employees in the bargaining unit who were on strike or locked out, in preference to any person who was not an employee in the bargaining unit on the date on which notice to bargain collectively was given and was hired or assigned after that date to perform all or part of the duties of an employee in the unit on strike or locked out."

This restriction is intended to ensure that employees who were on strike or locked out are given preference in the event of a dispute resolution process.

**Restrictions on Employers Regarding Services to Grain Vessels**

During a strike or lockout, the employer in the long-shoring industry, or other industry included in paragraph (a) of the definition in section 2, must continue to provide the services they normally provide to ensure the tie-up, let-go and loading of grain vessels at licensed terminal and transfer elevators, and the movement of the grain vessels in and out of a port.

This restriction is intended to ensure that the supply of services, operation of facilities, or production of goods is maintained to prevent an immediate and serious danger to the safety or health of the public.

question: What are the requirements for employers and employees in the long-shoring industry during a strike or lockout, with respect to services related to grain vessels?
answer:
**Section 87.7: Obligations of Employers and Employees in the Long-Shoring Industry**

During a strike or lockout not prohibited by this Part, an employer in the long-shoring industry, or other industry included in paragraph (a) of the definition in section 2, its employees and their bargaining agent shall continue to provide the services they normally provide to ensure the tie-up, let-go and loading of grain vessels at licensed terminal and transfer elevators, and the movement of the grain vessels in and out of a port.
"...an employer in the long-shoring industry, or other industry included in paragraph (a) of the definition in section 2, its employees and their bargaining agent shall continue to provide the services they normally provide..."

This quote highlights the specific requirements for employers and employees in the long-shoring industry during a strike or lockout. The employer and employees must continue to provide the services they normally provide to ensure the tie-up, let-go and loading of grain vessels at licensed terminal and transfer elevators, and the movement of the grain vessels in and out of a port.

**Continuation of Services**

Unless the parties otherwise agree, the rates of pay or any other term or condition of employment, and any rights, duties or privileges of the employees, the employer or the trade union in effect before the requirements of paragraphs 89(1)(a) to (d) were met, continue to apply with respect to employees who are members of the bargaining unit and who have been assigned to provide services pursuant to subsection (1).

This quote emphasizes that the continuation of services is not limited to the specific services mentioned in subsection (1), but also includes any other services that the employer and employees normally provide.

**Board Order**

On application by an affected employer or trade union, or on referral by the Minister, the Board may determine any question with respect to the application of subsection (1) and make any order it considers appropriate to ensure compliance with that subsection.

This quote highlights the role of the Board in ensuring compliance with the requirements of subsection (1) during a strike or lockout. The Board may make orders to ensure that the employer and employees continue to provide the necessary services to ensure the tie-up, let-go and loading of grain vessels at licensed terminal and transfer elevators, and the movement of the grain vessels in and out of a port.
