question: Under what conditions are strikes and lockouts allowed to occur during the term of a collective agreement?
answer:
**Section 88: Strikes and Lockouts Prohibited during Term of Collective Agreement**

According to Section 88 of the Canada Labour Code,
"Strikes and lockouts are prohibited during the term of a collective agreement except if (a) a notice to bargain collectively has been given pursuant to a provision of this Part, other than subsection 49(1); and (b) the requirements of subsection 89(1) have been met."

**Section 89: Requirements for Strikes and Lockouts**

The requirements for strikes and lockouts to occur during the term of a collective agreement are outlined in Section 89. According to this section,
"No employer shall declare or cause a lockout and no trade union shall declare or authorize a strike unless (a) the employer or trade union has given notice to bargain collectively under this Part; (b) the employer and the trade union (i) have failed to bargain collectively within the period specified in paragraph 50(a), or (ii) have bargained collectively in accordance with section 50 but have failed to enter into or revise a collective agreement; (c) the Minister has (i) received a notice, given under section 71 by either party to the dispute, informing the Minister of the failure of the parties to enter into or revise a collective agreement, or (ii) taken action under subsection 72(2); (d) twenty-one days have elapsed after the date on which the Minister (i) notified the parties of the intention not to appoint a conciliation officer or conciliation commissioner, or to establish a conciliation board under subsection 72(1), (ii) notified the parties that a conciliation officer appointed under subsection 72(1) has reported, (iii) released a copy of the report to the parties to the dispute pursuant to paragraph 77(a), or (iv) is deemed to have been reported to pursuant to subsection 75(2) or to have received the report pursuant to subsection 75(3); (e) the Board has determined any application made pursuant to subsection 87.4(4) or any referral made pursuant to subsection 87.4(5); and (f) sections 87.2 and 87.3 have been complied with."

**Conclusion**

In order for strikes and lockouts to be allowed to occur during the term of a collective agreement, a notice to bargain collectively must have been given, and the requirements outlined in Section 89 must have been met. This includes the employer or trade union having given notice to bargain collectively, the parties having failed to bargain collectively within the specified period, or having bargained collectively but failed to enter into or revise a collective agreement.

question: What conditions must be met by an employer or a trade union before declaring a lockout or authorizing a strike?
answer:
**Definitions**

Before declaring a lockout or authorizing a strike, an employer or a trade union must meet certain conditions.

**Section 89: No strike or lockout until certain requirements met**

To declare a lockout or authorize a strike, an employer or a trade union must give notice to bargain collectively under this Part. This is stated in subsection 89(1) as follows:
"No employer shall declare or cause a lockout and no trade union shall declare or authorize a strike unless (a) the employer or trade union has given notice to bargain collectively under this Part..."

**Section 89(1) Conditions for declaring a lockout or authorizing a strike**

The conditions for declaring a lockout or authorizing a strike are as follows:
"(a) the employer or trade union has given notice to bargain collectively under this Part..."

This means that the employer or trade union must have given notice to bargain collectively under the Canada Labour Code before declaring a lockout or authorizing a strike.

**Section 89(1) Additional conditions**

In addition to giving notice to bargain collectively, the employer or trade union must also meet the following conditions:
"(b) the employer and the trade union (i) have failed to bargain collectively within the period specified in paragraph 50(a), or (ii) have bargained collectively in accordance with section 50 but have failed to enter into or revise a collective agreement..."

This means that the employer and the trade union must have either failed to bargain collectively within the specified period or have bargained collectively but failed to enter into or revise a collective agreement.

**Section 89(1) Minister's involvement**

The Minister must also be involved in the process. The conditions for declaring a lockout or authorizing a strike are as follows:
"(c) the Minister has (i) received a notice, given under section 71 by either party to the dispute, informing the Minister of the failure of the parties to enter into or revise a collective agreement, or (ii) taken action under subsection 72(2)..."

This means that the Minister must have either received a notice from either party to the dispute informing them of the failure to enter into or revise a collective agreement or taken action under subsection 72(2).

**Section 89(1) Time period**

The conditions for declaring a lockout or authorizing a strike are also subject to a time period. The conditions are as follows:
"(d) twenty-one days have elapsed after the date on which the Minister (i) notified the parties of the intention not to appoint a conciliation officer or conciliation commissioner, or to establish a conciliation board under subsection 72(1), (ii) notified the parties that a conciliation officer appointed under subsection 72(1) has reported, (iii) released a copy of the report to the parties to the dispute pursuant to paragraph 77(a), or (iv) is deemed to have been reported to pursuant to subsection 75(2) or to have received the report pursuant to subsection 75(3)..."

This means that twenty-one days must have elapsed after the Minister has notified the parties of their intention not to appoint a conciliation officer or conciliation commissioner, or to establish a conciliation board.

**Section 89(1) Board's involvement**

The conditions for declaring a lockout or authorizing a strike are also subject to the involvement of the Board. The conditions are as follows:
"(e) the Board has determined any application made pursuant to subsection 87.4(4) or any referral made pursuant to subsection 87.4(5)..."

This means that the Board must have determined any application made pursuant to subsection 87.4(4) or any referral made pursuant to subsection 87.4(5).

**Section 89(1) Compliance with sections 87.2 and 87.3**

The conditions for declaring a lockout or authorizing a strike are also subject to compliance with sections 87.2 and 87.3. The conditions are as follows:

"(f) sections 87.2 and 87.3 have been complied with."

This means that sections 87.2 and 87.3 must have been complied with before declaring a lockout or authorizing a strike.

**Section 89(2): No employee to strike until certain requirements met**

In addition to the conditions for declaring a lockout or authorizing a strike, no employee shall participate in a strike unless they meet the following conditions:
"(a) the employee is a member of a bargaining unit in respect of which a notice to bargain collectively has been given under this Part..."

This means that the employee must be a member of a bargaining unit in respect of which a notice to bargain collectively has been given under the Canada Labour Code.
"(b) the requirements of subsection (1) have been met in respect of the bargaining unit of which the employee is a member."

This means that the requirements of subsection 89(1) must have been met in respect of the bargaining unit of which the employee is a member.

question: Under what circumstances can the Governor in Council intervene to defer a strike or lockout, and what is the purpose of such intervention?
answer:
**Circumstances for Intervention**

The Governor in Council can intervene to defer a strike or lockout under the following circumstances:
"Where a strike or lockout not prohibited by this Part occurs or may occur during the time commencing on the date of a dissolution of Parliament and ending on the date fixed for the return of the writs at the next following general election and, in the opinion of the Governor in Council, adversely affects or would adversely affect the national interest..."

This intervention is triggered by the Governor in Council's opinion that the strike or lockout may adversely affect the national interest.

**Purpose of Intervention**

The purpose of the Governor in Council's intervention is to prevent a strike or lockout from having a negative impact on the national interest.
"...the Governor in Council may during that time make an order deferring the strike or lockout during the period commencing on the day the order is made and ending on the twenty-first day following the date fixed for the return of the writs."

This order defers the strike or lockout for a specified period, allowing the Governor in Council to assess the potential impact on the national interest and take steps to mitigate any adverse effects.

question: What recourse does an employer have under the Canada Labour Code if they believe a trade union has called or authorized a strike, or employees are participating in a strike, that contravenes the Code?
answer:
**Recourse for Employers Under the Canada Labour Code**

**Application for a Declaration that a Strike is Unlawful**

According to Section 91 of the Canada Labour Code, an employer has the right to apply to the Board for a declaration that a strike is unlawful. This is stated in the following passage:
"Where an employer alleges that a trade union has declared or authorized a strike, or that employees have participated, are participating or are likely to participate in a strike, the effect of which was, is or would be to involve the participation of an employee in a strike in contravention of this Part, the employer may apply to the Board for a declaration that the strike was, is or would be unlawful."

**Consequences of a Declaration that a Strike is Unlawful**

If the Board grants the employer's application, it may make a declaration that the strike is unlawful and take various measures to prevent the strike from continuing. These measures may include:

* Requiring the trade union to revoke the declaration or authorization to strike and give notice of such revocation to the employees to whom it was directed
* Enjoining any employee from participating in the strike
* Requiring any employee who is participating in the strike to perform the duties of their employment
* Requiring any trade union, of which any employee with respect to whom an order is made under paragraph (b) or (c) is a member, and any officer or representative of that union, to give notice of any order made under paragraph (b) or (c) to any employee to whom it applies.

These measures are outlined in the following passage:
"Where an employer applies to the Board under subsection (1) for a declaration that a strike was, is or would be unlawful, the Board may, after affording the trade union or employees referred to in subsection (1) an opportunity to make representations on the application, make such a declaration and, if the employer so requests, may make an order (a) requiring the trade union to revoke the declaration or authorization to strike and to give notice of such revocation forthwith to the employees to whom it was directed; (b) enjoining any employee from participating in the strike; (c) requiring any employee who is participating in the strike to perform the duties of their employment; and (d) requiring any trade union, of which any employee with respect to whom an order is made under paragraph (b) or (c) is a member, and any officer or representative of that union, forthwith to give notice of any order made under paragraph (b) or (c) to any employee to whom it applies."

question: What recourse does a trade union have if it alleges that an employer has declared or caused a lockout in contravention of the Part of the Canada Labour Code (PART I - Industrial Relations), and what actions can be required of the employer as a result?
answer:
**Recourse for a Trade Union**

A trade union has the right to apply to the Board for a declaration that a lockout was, is or would be unlawful and the Board may, after affording the employer an opportunity to make representations on the application, make such a declaration.

**Section 92 of the Canada Labour Code
"Where a trade union alleges that an employer has declared or caused or is about to declare or cause a lockout of employees in contravention of this Part, the trade union may apply to the Board for a declaration that the lockout was, is or would be unlawful and the Board may, after affording the employer an opportunity to make representations on the application, make such a declaration and, if the trade union so requests, may make an order (a) enjoining the employer or any person acting on behalf of the employer from declaring or causing the lockout; (b) requiring the employer or any person acting on behalf of the employer to discontinue the lockout and to permit any employee of the employer who was affected by the lockout to return to the duties of their employment; and (c) requiring the employer forthwith to give notice of any order made against the employer under paragraph (a) or (b) to any employee who was affected, or would likely have been affected, by the lockout."

**Possible Orders Against the Employer**

The Board may make an order requiring the employer to discontinue the lockout and to permit any employee of the employer who was affected by the lockout to return to the duties of their employment. The employer may also be required to give notice of any order made against the employer to any employee who was affected, or would likely have been affected, by the lockout.

question: What are the considerations and procedures involved when the Board makes an order, and how can the order be adjusted over time?
answer:
**Considerations and Procedures for Making an Order**

The Canada Labour Code outlines the considerations and procedures involved when the Board makes an order. According to Section 19, the Board may make any decision or issue any order, prescribe any term or condition, or do any other thing in relation to any person or organization,
"...generally or in any particular case or class of cases."

**Interim Orders**

For interim orders, the Board may make an order
"...on application by a trade union, an employer or an affected employee..." This suggests that the Board considers the application of the parties involved and makes an order to ensure the fulfillment of the objectives of the Act.

**Finality of Orders**

Every order of the Board is final and shall not be questioned or reviewed in any court (CLC-247.991(1)). This means that the Board's decisions are binding and cannot be challenged in court.

**Adjusting Orders Over Time**

The Board may make supplementary orders to continue or modify an existing order (CLC-93(2)). This allows the Board to adjust the order over time in response to changing circumstances.

**Notice and Application Process**

The application for a supplementary order must be made by the employer or trade union that requested the original order, or by any employer, trade union, employee, or other person affected by the order (CLC-93(2)). The Board must be notified of the application, and the parties must be given notice of the application.

**Enforcement of Orders**

The Board's orders are enforceable in the Federal Court, and the Board may register the order in the Court (CLC-247.991(3)). This provides a mechanism for enforcing the Board's orders and ensuring compliance with the Act.

question: What are the main restrictions on employers when it comes to their interactions with trade unions and their employees' participation in union activities?
answer:
**Employer Interference in Trade Union Activities**

The Canada Labour Code imposes several restrictions on employers when it comes to their interactions with trade unions and their employees' participation in union activities.

**Participation in Trade Union Formation and Administration**

No employer or person acting on behalf of an employer shall
"...participate in or interfere with the formation or administration of a trade union or the representation of employees by a trade union..."(a)). This means that employers cannot influence or control the activities of a trade union or its representatives.

**Contributing to Trade Unions**

Employers are also prohibited from contributing financial or other support to a trade union (CLC-94(1)(b)). This includes providing financial support to a trade union's pension, health, or other welfare trust fund.

**Prohibited Employer Conduct**

Employers are prohibited from engaging in certain conduct that could be seen as intimidating or coercing employees into joining or participating in a trade union. For example, employers cannot
"...seek, by intimidation, threat of dismissal or any other kind of threat, by the imposition of a financial or other penalty or by any other means, to compel a person to refrain from becoming or to cease to be a member, officer or representative of a trade union..."

**Restrictions on Replacement Workers**

Employers are also prohibited from using replacement workers to undermine a trade union's representational capacity. Specifically, employers cannot use a person who was not an employee in the bargaining unit on the date on which notice to bargain collectively was given and was hired or assigned after that date to perform all or part of the duties of an employee in the bargaining unit on strike or locked out (CLC-94(2.1)).

**Prohibition on Discrimination**

Employers are prohibited from discriminating against employees who participate in union activities. For example, employers cannot
"...refuse to employ or to continue to employ or suspend, transfer, lay off or otherwise discriminate against any person with respect to employment, pay or any other term or condition of employment..."(a)) because the person is or proposes to become a member of a trade union or participates in the promotion, formation or administration of a trade union.

**Source:**
CLC-94: Unfair Practices: Employer interference in trade union
CLC-95: Unfair Practices: Prohibitions relating to trade unions

question: What types of actions are prohibited for trade unions and their representatives under the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
**Prohibited Actions for Trade Unions and Their Representatives**

The Canada Labour Code sets out various prohibitions for trade unions and their representatives. These prohibitions aim to protect employees and ensure fair collective bargaining practices.

**Participating in or Interfering with the Formation or Administration of an Employer's Organization**

A trade union or person acting on behalf of a trade union shall not participate in or interfere with the formation or administration of an employers' organization. (Source: CLC-95, section 95(c))

**Seeking to Compel Bargaining with an Employer**

A trade union or person acting on behalf of a trade union shall not seek to compel an employer to bargain collectively with the trade union if the trade union is not the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit that includes employees of the employer. (Source: CLC-95, section 95(a))

**Bargaining for a Bargaining Unit Where Another Union is the Bargaining Agent**

A trade union or person acting on behalf of a trade union shall not bargain collectively for the purpose of entering into a collective agreement or enter into a collective agreement with an employer in respect of a bargaining unit, if that trade union or person knows or, in the opinion of the Board, ought to know that another trade union is the bargaining agent for that bargaining unit. (Source: CLC-95, section 95(b))

**Discriminatory Membership Rules and Discipline**

A trade union or person acting on behalf of a trade union shall not apply membership rules or standards of discipline in a discriminatory manner to an employee. (Source: CLC-95, section 95(f))

**Intimidation and Coercion**

A trade union or person acting on behalf of a trade union shall not intimidate or coerce an employee because that employee has testified or otherwise participated or may testify or otherwise participate in a proceeding under the Canada Labour Code, made or is about to make a disclosure that the person may be required to make in a proceeding under the Canada Labour Code, or made an application or filed a complaint under the Canada Labour Code. (Source: CLC-95, section 95(i))

question: What are the consequences for an employer or individual who uses intimidation or coercion to influence an individual's decision regarding trade union membership or their employment status?
answer:
**Consequences of Intimidation or Coercion**

According to the Canada Labour Code, an employer or individual who uses intimidation or coercion to influence an individual's decision regarding trade union membership or their employment status can face severe consequences.

**Section 96: Prohibition
"No person shall seek by intimidation or coercion to compel a person to become or refrain from becoming or to cease to be a member of a trade union."

This section explicitly prohibits the use of intimidation or coercion to influence an individual's decision regarding trade union membership.

**Section 96.1: Employer's Prohibition
"An employer is prohibited from treating an employee as if they were not their employee."

This section specifically prohibits employers from using intimidation or coercion to influence an individual's employment status.

**Consequences for Contravention**

If an employer or individual contravenes these sections, the Canada Labour Board may impose various consequences, including:

* Paying compensation to the affected individual (Source: CLC-99, subsection (c))
* Reinstating an employee who was unfairly dismissed or denied employment (Source: CLC-99, subsection (b.2))
* Rescinding disciplinary action taken against an employee (Source: CLC-99, subsection (f))
* Paying compensation to an employee affected by the contravention (Source: CLC-99, subsection (g))

These consequences aim to deter employers and individuals from using intimidation or coercion to influence individuals' decisions regarding trade union membership or their employment status.

question: What is the procedure for filing a complaint under the Canada Labour Code, and what are the key requirements that must be met?
answer:
**Overview of Filing a Complaint under the Canada Labour Code**

To file a complaint under the Canada Labour Code, individuals must follow a specific procedure. The procedure involves several steps, including providing records to support the complaint, submitting the complaint, and meeting certain eligibility and timelines.

**Eligibility and Timelines**

According to the Canada Labour Code, there are different timelines for filing complaints depending on the type of complaint. For monetary complaints, the deadline is 6 months from the last day the employer was required to pay the employee. For non-monetary complaints, the deadline is 6 months from the day the employee became aware of the issue. For unjust dismissal complaints, the deadline is 90 days from the date of dismissal.

**Key Requirements for Filing a Complaint**

To file a complaint, individuals must meet certain key requirements. For monetary complaints, relevant documents to provide include pay stubs, employment contracts, and employee records or receipts. For non-monetary complaints, relevant documents may include pay stubs, employment contracts, and employee records or receipts. For unjust dismissal complaints, a copy of the written reasons for dismissal must be provided.

**Procedure for Filing a Complaint**

The procedure for filing a complaint involves several steps. First, individuals must complete a complaint form. Next, they must provide relevant records to support their complaint. After that, they must submit their complaint to the Labour Program. Finally, they must meet the eligibility and timelines requirements.

**Submission of Complaint**

The Canada Labour Code requires that complaints be submitted within the specified timelines. Individuals should not delay filing their complaint form within the timelines to obtain supporting documents. They can submit these documents at a later date.

**Exception for Trade Unions**

The Canada Labour Code also provides an exception for trade unions. If an individual has not presented a grievance or appeal to the trade union, they can file a complaint with the Board if the Board is satisfied that the action or circumstance giving rise to the complaint is such that the complaint should be dealt with without delay.

**Section 97 of the Canada Labour Code
"Section 97 (1) Subject to subsections (2) to (5), any person or organization may make a complaint in writing to the Board that (a) an employer, a person acting on behalf of an employer, a trade union, a person acting on behalf of a trade union or an employee has contravened or failed to comply with subsection 24(4) or 34(6) or section 37, 47.3, 50, 69, 87.5 or 87.6, subsection 87.7(2) or section 94, 95 or 96.1; or (b) any person has failed to comply with section 96."

question: What is the process for handling a complaint made under section 97 of the Canada Labour Code, and what factors influence the Board's decision to assist parties or determine the complaint?
answer:
**Process for Handling a Complaint under Section 97 of the Canada Labour Code**

According to Section 97 of the Canada Labour Code, a complaint can be made to the Board by any person or organization that alleges an employer, a person acting on behalf of an employer, a trade union, or an employee has contravened or failed to comply with certain provisions of the Code.

**Time Limit for Making a Complaint**

A complaint must be made to the Board within 90 days after the date on which the complainant knew, or in the opinion of the Board, ought to have known, of the action or circumstances giving rise to the complaint. [CLC-97(2)]

**Factors Influencing the Board's Decision**

The Board may assist the parties to the complaint to settle the complaint, but it may refuse to do so if the matter could be referred by the complainant pursuant to a collective agreement to an arbitrator or arbitration board. [CLC-98(3)]

The Board may also refuse to determine a complaint if it determines that the complainant has not presented a grievance or appeal in accordance with any procedure established by the trade union to which the complainant has been given ready access. [CLC-97(4)(a)]

In addition, the Board may refuse to determine a complaint if the complainant has not given the trade union ready access to a grievance or appeal procedure. [CLC-97(5)(b)]

**Board's Duty and Power**

On receipt of a complaint, the Board may assist the parties to the complaint to settle the complaint. If the complaint is not settled within a reasonable period, the Board may determine the complaint. [CLC-98(1)]

The Board's decision to assist parties or determine the complaint is influenced by the factors mentioned above, as well as the fact that the complaint is made in writing and the complainant has given the Board notice of the action or circumstances giving rise to the complaint. [CLC-97(2)]

question: What can the Board do if it determines that a party to a complaint has contravened or failed to comply with certain provisions of the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
**Board Orders**

According to Section 99 of the Canada Labour Code, if the Board determines that a party to a complaint has contravened or failed to comply with certain provisions, the Board may make an order requiring the party to comply with or cease contravening that provision.

For example, the Board may require an employer to pay compensation to an employee,
"...by order, require an employer to pay to any employee compensation not exceeding such sum as, in the opinion of the Board, is equivalent to the remuneration that would, but for that failure, have been paid by the employer to the employee..."(a)).

The Board may also require a trade union to take and carry on on behalf of an employee,
"...require a trade union to take and carry on on behalf of any employee affected by the contravention or to assist any such employee to take and carry on such action or proceeding as the Board considers that the union ought to have taken and carried on on the employee’s behalf or ought to have assisted the employee to take and carry on..."(b)).

In addition, the Board may require an employer to rescind any disciplinary action taken against an employee,
"...action taken in respect of and pay compensation to any employee affected by the failure, not exceeding such sum as, in the opinion of the Board, is equivalent to any financial or other penalty imposed on the employee by the employer..."(c)).

**Certification**

In certain circumstances, the Board may certify a trade union despite a lack of evidence of majority support,
"The Board may certify a trade union despite a lack of evidence of majority support if (a) the employer has failed to comply with section 94; and (b) the Board is of the opinion that, but for the unfair labour practice, the trade union could reasonably have been expected to have had the support of a majority of the employees in the unit."

**Duty and Power of the Board**

The Board has the power to determine complaints and make orders to remedy or counteract any consequences of a contravention or failure to comply with certain provisions,
"...the Board may assist the parties to the complaint to settle the complaint and shall, where it decides not to so assist the parties or the complaint is not settled within a period considered by the Board to be reasonable in the circumstances, determine the complaint."

question: Under what circumstances can the Board certify a trade union even if there is no evidence that it has the support of a majority of employees?
answer:
**Certification of Trade Unions Despite Lack of Majority Support**

The Canada Labour Code provides that the Board may certify a trade union despite a lack of evidence of majority support under certain circumstances.

**Section 99.1: Certification Despite Unfair Labour Practice**

The Board may certify a trade union despite a lack of evidence of majority support if the employer has failed to comply with section 94, and the Board is of the opinion that, but for the unfair labour practice, the trade union could reasonably have been expected to have had the support of a majority of the employees in the unit.
"Section 99.1 The Board may certify a trade union despite a lack of evidence of majority support if (a) the employer has failed to comply with section 94; and (b) the Board is of the opinion that, but for the unfair labour practice, the trade union could reasonably have been expected to have had the support of a majority of the employees in the unit."

This provision suggests that the Board may take into account the employer's unfair labour practice as a mitigating factor in determining whether to certify the trade union. In other words, the Board may consider the circumstances surrounding the employer's failure to comply with section 94 and determine that the trade union could have reasonably been expected to have had the support of a majority of employees, even if there is no direct evidence to support this claim.

**Section 25: Certification Prohibited in Certain Circumstances**

However, the Code also provides that the Board shall not certify a trade union if it is satisfied that the trade union is so dominated or influenced by an employer that the fitness of the trade union to represent employees of the employer for the purpose of collective bargaining is impaired.
"Notwithstanding anything in this Part, where the Board is satisfied that a trade union is so dominated or influenced by an employer that the fitness of the trade union to represent employees of the employer for the purpose of collective bargaining is impaired, the Board shall not certify the trade union as the bargaining agent for any unit comprised of employees of the employer and any collective agreement between the trade union and the employer that applies to any such employees shall be deemed not to be a collective agreement for the purposes of this Part."

This provision suggests that the Board may consider the relationship between the trade union and the employer as a factor in determining whether to certify the trade union. If the Board is satisfied that the trade union is dominated or influenced by the employer, it may refuse to certify the trade union, even if there is no evidence of majority support.

**Conclusion**

In summary, the Board may certify a trade union despite a lack of evidence of majority support if the employer has failed to comply with section 94 and the Board is of the opinion that, but for the unfair labour practice, the trade union could reasonably have been expected to have had the support of a majority of employees. However, the Board shall not certify a trade union if it is satisfied that the trade union is dominated or influenced by an employer that impairs its fitness to represent employees for collective bargaining purposes.

question: What are the potential consequences for employers, trade unions, and other individuals or entities that fail to comply with the provisions of a specific part of the Canada Labour Code (PART I - Industrial Relations)?
answer:
**Consequences of Non-Compliance**

The Canada Labour Code (CLC) outlines the potential consequences for employers, trade unions, and other individuals or entities that fail to comply with its provisions.

**Employers**

Employers who contravene or fail to comply with the provisions of the CLC, other than sections 50, 94, or 95, are guilty of an offence and liable on summary conviction to a fine not exceeding \$10,000. (CLC-101(2))

**Trade Unions**

Trade unions who contravene or fail to comply with the provisions of the CLC, other than sections 50, 94, or 95, are also guilty of an offence and liable on summary conviction to a fine not exceeding \$10,000. (CLC-101(2))

**Individuals or Entities**

Individuals or entities other than employers or trade unions who contravene or fail to comply with the provisions of the CLC, other than sections 50, 94, or 95, are guilty of an offence and liable on summary conviction to a fine not exceeding \$1,000. (CLC-101(1))

**Specific Offences**

Certain specific offences, such as refusing to employ or continue to employ an employee, or refusing to pay wages, can result in more severe penalties, including fines not exceeding \$400 for individuals and \$4,000 for employers. (CLC-102)

**Prosecution of Employers' Organizations, Trade Unions, and Councils of Trade Unions**

The CLC also provides that employers' organizations, trade unions, and councils of trade unions can be prosecuted for certain offences, including those related to the formation or administration of a trade union or the representation of employees by a trade union. (CLC-94)

**Failure to Attend or Produce Documents**

According to Section 102 of the Canada Labour Code,
"Every person who (a) being required to attend to give evidence pursuant to paragraph 16(a), fails, without valid excuse, to attend accordingly, (b) being commanded to produce, pursuant to paragraph 16(a), any document or thing in their possession or under their control, fails to produce the document or thing, (c) refuses to be sworn or to affirm, as the case may be, after being required to do so pursuant to paragraph 16(a), or (d) refuses to answer any proper question put to them, pursuant to paragraph 16(a), by the Board, a conciliation board, a conciliation commissioner, an arbitrator or an arbitration board, is guilty of an offence and liable on summary conviction to a fine not exceeding four hundred dollars."

**Source:** Section 102, Canada Labour Code

**Fines for Non-Compliance**

The Canada Labour Code specifies that the fine for non-compliance is not exceeding \$400. This fine is liable on summary conviction, meaning that it can be imposed by a court without a trial.

**Source:** Section 102, Canada Labour Code

**Prosecution of Employers' Organizations, Trade Unions, and Councils of Trade Unions**

It is worth noting that the Canada Labour Code also applies to employers' organizations, trade unions, and councils of trade unions. These organizations can be prosecuted for non-compliance with the requirements outlined in Section 102.

question: Under what circumstances can a mediator be appointed to assist in settling a labour dispute, and what actions can they take?
answer:
**Mediator Appointment and Role**

A mediator can be appointed by the Minister under Section 105 of the Canada Labour Code.

**Circumstances for Mediator Appointment**

A mediator can be appointed "where the Minister deems it expedient" (CLC-105(1)).

**Mediator's Role**

A mediator's role is to
"...confer with the parties to a dispute or difference and endeavour to assist them in settling the dispute or difference." They can also make recommendations for settlement of the dispute or difference at the request of the parties or the Minister (CLC-105(2)).

**Limitations of Mediator's Power**

A mediator does not create the resolution; the parties determine the resolution together (LABOUR-REPORTS-10_2, Section 5). The mediator is neutral and cannot make a ruling that decides whether the dismissal was just or unjust (LABOUR-REPORTS-10_2, Section 5).

**Mediator's Authority**

A mediator's decision is not binding, and the parties can still choose to pursue other forms of dispute resolution, such as adjudication (LABOUR-REPORTS-10_2, Section 11).

The Minister can initiate inquiries into industrial relations matters under two circumstances.

**On Application or on the Minister's Own Initiative**

The Minister may make inquiries regarding matters that may affect industrial relations "on application or on the Minister's own initiative" (CLC-106). **On the Minister's Own Initiative**

The Minister may also initiate inquiries into industrial relations matters "where the Minister deems it expedient" (CLC-106). This implies that the Minister has the discretion to initiate inquiries into matters that may affect industrial relations, even if there is no prior application or request from either employers or employees.

question: What actions can the Minister take to maintain or secure industrial peace and promote conditions favourable to the settlement of industrial disputes?
answer:
**Actions of the Minister to Maintain or Secure Industrial Peace**

The Minister has the authority to take various actions to maintain or secure industrial peace and promote conditions favourable to the settlement of industrial disputes.

**Appointing a Mediator**

The Minister may appoint a mediator to confer with the parties to a dispute or difference and endeavour to assist them in settling the dispute or difference. This is stated in Section 105 of the Canada Labour Code:
"The Minister, on request or on the Minister’s own initiative, may, where the Minister deems it expedient, at any time appoint a mediator to confer with the parties to a dispute or difference and endeavour to assist them in settling the dispute or difference."

**Making Inquiries**

The Minister may also make inquiries regarding matters that may affect industrial relations. This is stated in Section 106 of the Canada Labour Code:
"The Minister, on application or on the Minister’s own initiative, may, where the Minister deems it expedient, make any inquiries that the Minister considers advisable regarding matters that may affect industrial relations."

**Referencing the Board**

The Minister may refer any question to the Board or direct the Board to do such things as the Minister deems necessary. This is stated in Section 107 of the Canada Labour Code:
"The Minister, where the Minister deems it expedient, may do such things as to the Minister seem likely to maintain or secure industrial peace and to promote conditions favourable to the settlement of industrial disputes or differences and to those ends the Minister may refer any question to the Board or direct the Board to do such things as the Minister deems necessary."

**Composition of the Industrial Inquiry Commission**

The Minister may also appoint an Industrial Inquiry Commission to inquire into matters referred to it by the Minister and endeavour to carry out its terms of reference. This is stated in Section 108 of the Canada Labour Code:
"An Industrial Inquiry Commission shall consist of one or more members to be appointed by the Minister."

**Distribution and Publication of Report**

The Minister may also furnish a copy of the report of an Industrial Inquiry Commission to each employer and trade union involved in the dispute or difference, and publish the report in such manner as the Minister considers advisable. This is stated in Section 108 of the Canada Labour Code:
"On receipt of a report of an Industrial Inquiry Commission relating to any dispute or difference between any employer and employees, the Minister shall (a) furnish a copy of the report to each employer and trade union involved in the dispute or difference; and (b) publish the report in such manner as the Minister considers advisable."

question: What is the role of an Industrial Inquiry Commission in the event of a labour dispute or difference between an employer and employees, and how does it report its findings?
answer:
**Role of an Industrial Inquiry Commission**

In the event of a labour dispute or difference between an employer and employees, an Industrial Inquiry Commission is appointed by the Minister to investigate and report on the matter.

**Composition and Functions**

An Industrial Inquiry Commission is composed of one or more members appointed by the Minister. Its functions include inquiring into the matter referred to it, endeavouring to carry out its terms of reference, and making its report and recommendations to the Minister within a specified period.

**Reporting Requirements**

On receipt of a report from the Industrial Inquiry Commission, the Minister shall furnish a copy of the report to each employer and trade union involved in the dispute or difference, and publish the report in a manner considered advisable.

**Powers of the Commission**

An Industrial Inquiry Commission has all the powers of a person appointed as a Commissioner under Part I of the Inquiries Act.

**Example of a Report**

According to the Canada Labour Code, an Industrial Inquiry Commission shall make its report and recommendations to the Minister within fourteen days after its appointment or within such longer period as the Minister may allow.

question: Under what conditions can a trade union's authorized representative be granted access to employees living in isolated locations on an employer's premises or those of another person?
answer:
**Access to Employees in Isolated Locations**

According to the Canada Labour Code, a trade union's authorized representative can be granted access to employees living in isolated locations on an employer's premises or those of another person under the following conditions:

**Section 109.1**

The Board may, by order, require an employer to give an authorized representative of the trade union access to employees whose normal workplace is not on premises owned or controlled by their employer and authorize the trade union to communicate with those employees, if the Board is of the opinion that such communication is required for purposes relating to soliciting trade union memberships, the negotiation or administration of a collective agreement, the processing of a grievance or the provision of a trade union service to employees.

**Specific Conditions**

The Board must determine that access to the employees is
"...impracticable unless permitted on premises owned or controlled by their employer or by such other person..." Additionally, the Board must be of the opinion that access is "reasonably required" for the purposes mentioned above.

**Method of Access and Communication**

The Board must specify the method of access to the employees, the times at which access is permitted, and the periods of its duration in every order made under subsection (1) (CLC-109.1(2)).

**Source:** Canada Labour Code, Section 109.1

answer:
**Request for Employee Contact Information**

A trade union can request that an employer provide employee contact information to facilitate communication under the following circumstances:

*   The trade union is seeking to solicit trade union memberships, negotiate or administer a collective agreement, process a grievance, or provide a trade union service to employees.
*   The Board is of the opinion that such communication is required for the purposes mentioned above.

According to Section 109.1(1) of the Canada Labour Code,
"On application by a trade union, the Board may, by order, require an employer to give an authorized representative of the trade union mentioned in the order, or the Board, or both, the names and addresses of employees whose normal workplace is not on premises owned or controlled by their employer..."

**Protecting Employee Privacy and Safety**

To ensure the protection of employee privacy and safety, the Board may include conditions in the order, such as:

*   Specifying the method of communication
*   Establishing times of day and periods during which communication is authorized
*   Requiring the employer to transmit information to the union by means of the employer's existing electronic communications system
*   Providing employees with the opportunity to refuse the giving of their name and address to the union representative
*   Transmitting information to employees in a manner that protects their privacy and safety

According to Section 109.1(3) of the Canada Labour Code,
"If the Board is of the opinion that the privacy and safety of affected employees cannot otherwise be protected, the Board may (a) provide each employee with the opportunity to refuse the giving of their name and address to the representative of the trade union that the Board authorizes and, if the employee does not so refuse, may transmit that name and address to the authorized representative; or (b) transmit the information that the union wishes to communicate to the employees in the manner it considers appropriate."

**Protections for Employees**

Employees have the right to refuse the giving of their name and address to the union representative, and their information will not be used unless it is for a purpose consistent with this section.

According to Section 109.1(4) of the Canada Labour Code,
"The names and addresses of employees provided under subsection (1) shall not be used unless it is for a purpose consistent with this section."

question: What are the obligations of trade unions and employers' organizations regarding financial statements and their disclosure to members?
answer:
**Financial Statement Obligations of Trade Unions and Employers' Organizations**

**Disclosure Requirements**

Every trade union and employers' organization is required to provide a financial statement of their affairs to their members upon request. According to Section 110(1) of the Canada Labour Code,
"Every trade union and every employers’ organization shall, forthwith on the request of any of its members, provide the member, free of charge, with a copy of a financial statement of its affairs to the end of the last fiscal year, certified to be a true copy by its president and treasurer or by its president and any other officer responsible for the handling and administration of its funds."

**Content Requirements**

The financial statement must contain information in sufficient detail to disclose accurately the financial condition and operations of the trade union or employers' organization for the fiscal year for which it was prepared. (CLC-110)

**Complaint Procedure**

If a member complains that a trade union or employers' organization has failed to comply with the disclosure requirements, the Board may make an order requiring the organization to file a statement with the Board. (CLC-110)

**Board's Discretion**

The Board may also make an order requiring a trade union or employers' organization to provide a copy of a statement filed under subsection (3) to such members of the trade union or employers' organization as the Board in its discretion directs. (CLC-110)

question: What type of regulations can the Governor in Council make according to section 111 of the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
**Regulations under Section 111 of the Canada Labour Code**

According to section 111 of the Canada Labour Code, the Governor in Council may make regulations in the following areas:

### Prescribing Forms and Content of Notices

The Governor in Council may prescribe the form and content of notices, such as:

*   A notice to commence collective bargaining
*   A notice under section 71
*   A notice under section 87.2
*   A written request to the Minister under subsection 57(2) or (4)

These regulations may also include additional information that is to be furnished with such notices.

### Delegation of Powers

The Governor in Council may delegate to the head of the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service their powers of appointment under this Act.

### Service of Notices

The Governor in Council may also prescribe the manner in which and the time within which a copy of an order or decision referred to in section 59 shall be filed with the Minister.

### Examination of Copies of Orders and Decisions

The Governor in Council may prescribe the circumstances in which copies of orders and decisions filed with the Minister pursuant to section 59 may be examined by members of the public and the fees, if any, to be charged for providing copies thereof.

### Release of Reports

The Governor in Council may also prescribe the manner in which a report of a conciliation commissioner or a conciliation board may be released by the Minister to the parties to a dispute pursuant to paragraph 77(a).

These regulations are made under section 111 of the Canada Labour Code, which gives the Governor in Council the power to make regulations in these areas.

answer:
**Evidentiary Status of Documents**

**Documents Purporting to be Orders or Decisions of the Board**

According to Section 112 of the Canada Labour Code,
"Any document purporting to contain or to be a copy of any order or decision of the Board and purporting to be signed by a member of the Board is admissible in any court in evidence without proof of the signature or official character of the person appearing to have signed the document and without further proof thereof."

This means that in a court of law, a document that appears to be an order or decision of the Board and is signed by a member of the Board can be accepted as evidence without needing to prove the authenticity of the signature or the official character of the person who signed it.

**Certificates from the Minister or an Official of the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service**

Similarly, a certificate from the Minister or an official of the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service stating that a report, request, or notice was or was not received or given by the Minister is admissible in court as evidence. The certificate is admissible
"...without proof of the signature or official character of the person appearing to have signed the certificate and without further proof thereof."

This means that a certificate from the Minister or an official of the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service can be accepted as evidence in court without needing to prove the authenticity of the signature or the official character of the person who signed it.

question: What is the purpose of an agreement that can be made between the Government of Canada and a provincial government under the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
**Purpose of Agreement Under the Canada Labour Code**

The Canada Labour Code allows for agreements to be made between the Government of Canada and a provincial government under Section 120.

**Administration of Provincial Legislation**

According to Section 120(1),
"Where this Part and legislation enacted by the legislature of a province are substantially uniform, the Minister may, on behalf of the Government of Canada, with the approval of the Governor in Council, enter into an agreement with the government of the province to provide for the administration of the legislation of the province by officers and employees employed in the federal public administration."

This section outlines the purpose of an agreement between the Government of Canada and a provincial government, which is to provide for the administration of the provincial legislation by federal officers and employees.

**Scope of Agreement**

The agreement can provide for the administration of the provincial legislation in various ways, including:

* The administration by Canada of the legislation of the province with respect to a particular work, undertaking, or business (Section 120(2)(a))
* The exercise of powers conferred or the performance of duties imposed under the provincial legislation by the Minister on behalf of the province (Section 120(2)(b))
* The exercise of powers conferred or the performance of duties imposed under the provincial legislation by the members of the Board or officers and employees employed in the federal public administration (Section 120(2)(c))
* The payment by the government of the province to the Government of Canada for expenses incurred by the Government of Canada in the administration of the provincial legislation (Section 120(2)(d))

**Scope of Powers and Duties**

The agreement can also provide for the exercise of powers and the performance of duties specified in the provincial legislation or agreement, subject to the provisions of the legislation and the approval of the Governor in Council (Section 120(3)).

question: Under what circumstances can the Governor in Council direct that a part of the Canada Labour Code (PART I - Industrial Relations) applies to certain employment?
answer:
**Application of the Canada Labour Code**

The Governor in Council can direct that a part of the Canada Labour Code (PART I - Industrial Relations) applies to certain employment under the following circumstances:

**Federal Work, Undertaking, or Business**

The Governor in Council may direct that a part of the Canada Labour Code applies in respect of any employment, or any class or classes of employment, on or in connection with a federal work, undertaking or business set out in the regulation that is, or is part of, a corporation that is an agent of Her Majesty in right of a province. This includes a corporation whose activities are regulated, in whole or in part, under the Nuclear Safety and Control Act.

**Source:** CLC-158, "Regulations: Provincial Crown corporations"

**Exclusion from Application**

The Governor in Council may also exclude, in whole or in part, from the application of the Canada Labour Code, any employment, or any class or classes of employment, on or in connection with a work or undertaking set out in the regulation whose activities are regulated, in whole or in part, pursuant to the Nuclear Safety and Control Act.

**Source:** CLC-266, "Application of Provincial Laws: Exclusion from application"

**Application to Provincial Crown Corporations**

The Governor in Council may direct that the Canada Labour Code applies in respect of any employment, or any class or classes of employment, on or in connection with a work or undertaking set out in the regulation that is, or is part of, a corporation that is an agent of Her Majesty in right of a province and whose activities are regulated, in whole or in part, pursuant to the Nuclear Safety and Control Act.

**Source:** CLC-121.1, "Application of Provincial Laws: Provincial Crown corporations"

question: What is the purpose of the Governor in Council's regulatory power under section 121.2 of the Canada Labour Code, and how does it relate to employment in the nuclear sector?
answer:
**Purpose of the Governor in Council's Regulatory Power**

The Governor in Council's regulatory power under section 121.2 of the Canada Labour Code is to
"...exclude, in whole or in part, from the application of any of the provisions of this Part any employment, or any class or classes of employment, on or in connection with a work or undertaking set out in the regulation whose activities are regulated, in whole or in part, pursuant to the Nuclear Safety and Control Act..."

This power allows the Governor in Council to create regulations that exempt certain employment in the nuclear sector from the provisions of the Canada Labour Code.

**Relation to Employment in the Nuclear Sector**

The Governor in Council may make regulations
"...relating to occupational safety and health in relation to employment that is subject to a regulation made pursuant to subsection (1)." This suggests that the regulatory power under section 121.2 is intended to address specific occupational health and safety concerns in the nuclear sector.

The regulations may also
"...by reference, in whole or in part, an Act of the legislature of a province or an instrument made under such an Act...", which could include provincial laws and regulations related to the nuclear sector.

**Administration and Enforcement**

The regulations made under section 121.2 may be administered and enforced by the person or authority responsible for the administration and enforcement of the incorporated Act or instrument (CLC-121.2(5)). This suggests that the regulatory power under section 121.2 is intended to work in conjunction with existing regulatory frameworks in the nuclear sector.

**Offence and Penalty**

Contravention of a regulation made under section 121.2 may be considered an offence against the Canada Labour Code, and the person responsible may be liable to the same punishment as is imposed by or under an Act of the legislature of the province for the contravention of the incorporated Act or instrument (CLC-121.2(6)).

question: What happens to a collective agreement and a bargaining agent when a new regulation is made under the Canada Labour Code that applies to the employees represented by the bargaining agent?
answer:
**Effect of New Regulation on Collective Agreement and Bargaining Agent**

When a new regulation is made under the Canada Labour Code that applies to the employees represented by the bargaining agent, the following occurs:

**Continuation of Collective Agreement**

A collective agreement that is in force immediately before the time when the regulation is made continues in force, at that time, under the regulation until its term expires. (
"Every collective agreement that is in force immediately before the time when a regulation is made that applies to employees who are subject to the collective agreement continues in force, at that time, under the regulation until its term expires.")

**Notice to Bargain
"A notice to bargain given under this Part is deemed, at the time when a regulation is made to which the employees who are affected by the notice to bargain are subject, to have been given pursuant to the regulation on the day on which it was given."

**Acquired Rights
"Any rights, privileges or duties acquired under this Part by the bargaining unit, bargaining agent, employer or employees before the time when a regulation is made are deemed to have been acquired pursuant to the regulation on the day on which they were acquired."

**Decisions
"A person or authority that, under an Act of the legislature of a province, is competent to decide a matter that is contemplated by this section in relation to a provision of an Act of the legislature of a province or an instrument made under such an Act may, on application by the employer or bargaining agent or, where the person or authority considers it appropriate, an employee, decide any matter that is contemplated by this section in relation to a regulation incorporating that provision."

**Source:** Canada Labour Code, Section 121.4

Subsection 122(1) of the Code defines "danger" as:  "any hazard, condition or activity that could reasonably be expected to be an imminent or serious threat to the life or health of a person exposed to it before the hazard or condition can be corrected or the activity altered."  3.1 HAZARD/CONDITION/ACTIVITY  "Hazard" means a source of harm or risk to an  employee. "Activity" means the tasks directly related to the  employee's duties.  3.2 ADDITIONAL DEFINITIONS  "Reasonably expected" means:             Does not require that the threat materialize every time the hazard, condition or activity occurs;             It is not necessary to establish precisely the time when the threat will materialize nor does the threat need to materialize frequently;             Only requires that a person determines in what circumstances the threat could reasonably be expected to materialize;             There is more than one way to establish that a condition, hazard, or activity can reasonably be expected to be a threat. "Imminent threat" means a threat on the point of happening.  "Serious threat" means a substantial threat to health or life and includes potential substantial threat. question: What is the definition of 'danger' in the context of occupational health and safety under the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
**Definition of 'Danger' under the Canada Labour Code**

The definition of 'danger' under the Canada Labour Code is as follows:
"...any hazard, condition or activity that could reasonably be expected to be an imminent or serious threat to the life or health of a person exposed to it before the hazard or condition can be corrected or the activity altered."

This definition is set out in subsection 122(1) of the Canada Labour Code.

**Breaking Down the Definition**

The definition of 'danger' is composed of three key components:

*   **Hazard**: A source of harm or risk to an employee.
*   **Condition**: Circumstances, including those affecting the functioning or existence of something.
*   **Activity**: The tasks directly related to the employee's duties.

**Key Concepts**

The definition also includes several key concepts:

*   **Reasonably expected**: This means that the threat does not need to materialize every time the hazard, condition, or activity occurs. It is not necessary to establish precisely the time when the threat will materialize, nor does the threat need to materialize frequently. Instead, it is sufficient to determine in what circumstances the threat could reasonably be expected to materialize.
*   **Imminent threat**: A threat on the point of happening.
*   **Serious threat**: A substantial threat to health or life, including potential substantial threat.
*   **Life or health**: Includes injury and illness.

**Application in the Workplace**

The definition of 'danger' is applied in the workplace to identify hazards, conditions, and activities that could pose a threat to an employee's life or health. Employers must assess these factors and take corrective action to prevent harm to employees.

question: What is the primary goal of preventive measures in the workplace according to the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
**Purpose of Preventive Measures**

The primary goal of preventive measures in the workplace according to the Canada Labour Code is to "ensure the health and safety of employees" (CLC-122.1).

**Elimination of Hazards**

The Code states that preventive measures should consist first of the elimination of hazards, then the reduction of hazards, and finally, the provision of personal protective equipment, clothing, devices or materials (CLC-122.2).

**Head of Compliance and Enforcement**

The Minister may designate a person as Head of Compliance and Enforcement, who is responsible for ensuring that preventive measures are implemented in the workplace (CLC-122.21(1)).

**Minister's Responsibility**

If no Head of Compliance and Enforcement is designated, the Minister shall exercise the powers and perform the duties and functions of the Head (CLC-122.21(2)).

question: How must employers provide direction, notice, information, instruction, or training to employees who have a condition that impairs their ability to receive information through standard communication methods?
answer:
**Canada Labour Code: Section 122.3**

**Providing Direction, Notice, Information, Instruction, or Training to Employees with Special Needs**

According to Section 122.3 of the Canada Labour Code, employers must provide direction, notice, information, instruction, or training to employees with special needs
"...by any method of communication that readily permits the employee to receive it..."

This means that employers must adapt their communication methods to accommodate employees with special needs, such as those who are deaf or hard of hearing, have a visual impairment, or have a learning disability.

**Examples of Adaptable Communication Methods**

The Code specifies that adaptable communication methods include:

* Braille
* Large print
* Audio tape
* Computer disk
* Sign language
* Verbal communication

These methods are designed to ensure that employees with special needs can receive the information they need to perform their jobs safely and effectively (CLC-122.3(2)).

**Implications for Employers**

By providing direction, notice, information, instruction, or training through adaptable communication methods, employers can help ensure that employees with special needs are able to participate fully in the workplace and contribute to the organization's success.

This requirement also highlights the importance of creating an inclusive and accessible work environment, where all employees feel valued and supported.

**Source:**
CLC-122.3, Canada Labour Code

question: What types of employment and entities are subject to the provisions of this Part of the Canada Labour Code (PART II - Occupational Health and Safety)?
answer:
**Employment Covered by Part II**

The Canada Labour Code (PART II - Occupational Health and Safety) applies to employment on or in connection with the operation of any federal work, undertaking, or business other than a work, undertaking, or business of a local or private nature in Yukon, the Northwest Territories, or Nunavut.

**Federal Work, Undertakings, or Businesses**

This includes federal work, undertakings, or businesses established to perform any function or duty on behalf of the Government of Canada.

**Canadian Carriers**

It also applies to Canadian carriers, as defined in section 2 of the Telecommunications Act, that are agents of Her Majesty in right of a province.

**Federal Public Administration**

The Part applies to the federal public administration and to persons employed in the federal public administration to the extent provided for under Part 3 of the Federal Public Sector Labour Relations Act.

**Applicability to Persons Appointed Under the Public Service Employment Act**

This includes persons appointed under subsection 128(1) of the Public Service Employment Act, other than persons appointed by a person holding the recognized position of Leader of the Opposition in the Senate or Leader of the Opposition in the House of Commons, and to their employer.

**Applicability to Other Persons**

The Part also applies to any person who is not an employee but who performs for an employer to which this Part applies activities whose primary purpose is to enable the person to acquire knowledge or experience, and to the employer, as if that person were an employee of the employer.

question: Who bears the burden of proof in a proceeding to determine if a person is an employee of an employer under the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
**Determining the Employer/Employee Relationship**

**Burden of Proof**

In a proceeding to determine if a person is an employee of an employer under the Canada Labour Code, the burden of proof lies with the employer.

**CLC-167.01
"A person who is paid remuneration by an employer is presumed to be their employee unless the contrary is proved by the employer."

This section of the Canada Labour Code states that a person who is paid remuneration by an employer is presumed to be their employee, and the burden of proof lies with the employer to prove otherwise.

**CLC-6
"If, in any proceeding under this Part other than a prosecution, an employer alleges that a person is not their employee, the burden of proof is on the employer."

This section of the Canada Labour Code explicitly states that in any proceeding under the Canada Labour Code, other than a prosecution, the burden of proof lies with the employer to prove that a person is not their employee.

**CLC-123.1
"If, in any proceeding under this Part other than a prosecution, or in any proceeding under Part IV in respect of a violation that is related to this Part, an employer alleges that a person is not their employee, the burden of proof is on the employer."

This section of the Canada Labour Code also states that in any proceeding under the Canada Labour Code, other than a prosecution, or in any proceeding under Part IV, the burden of proof lies with the employer to prove that a person is not their employee.

question: What is the general responsibility of an employer in relation to the health and safety of their employees at work?
answer:
**General Responsibility of an Employer**

The general responsibility of an employer in relation to the health and safety of their employees at work is outlined in Section 124 of the Canada Labour Code.


"Every employer shall ensure that the health and safety at work of every person employed by the employer is protected."

This section emphasizes the employer's duty to protect the health and safety of their employees, without restricting the generality of this duty.

**Scope of the Duty**

The duty of the employer extends to every work place controlled by the employer and to every work activity carried out by an employee in a work place that is not controlled by the employer, to the extent that the employer controls the activity.

**Employer's Obligations**

The employer's obligations under this section are not limited to the specific duties outlined in Section 125, but rather are a broader duty to ensure the health and safety of their employees.

**Source**

Source: Canada Labour Code, Section 124.

{"id": "CLC-125", "type": "Canada Labour Code", "title": "Duties of Employers: Specific duties of employer", "section": "125"}, "text": "Section 125 (1) Without restricting the generality of section 124, every employer shall, in respect of every work place controlled by the employer and, in respect of every work activity carried out by an employee in a work place that is not controlled by the employer, to the extent that the employer controls the activity, (a) ensure that all permanent and temporary buildings and structures meet the prescribed standards; (b) install guards, guard-rails, barricades and fences in accordance with prescribed standards; (c) except as provided for in the regulations, investigate, record and report, in accordance with the regulations, all accidents, occurrences of harassment and violence, occupational illnesses and other hazardous occurrences known to the employer; (d) make readily available to employees, in printed and electronic form, (i) a copy of this Part and a copy of the regulations made under this Part that apply to the work place, (ii) a statement of the employer’s general policy concerning the health and safety at work of employees, and (iii) any other information related to health and safety that is prescribed or that may be specified by the Head; (e) [Repealed, 2018, c. 22, s. 3] (f) if the information referred to in any of subparagraphs (d)(i) to (iii) is made available in electronic form, ensure that employees receive appropriate training to enable them to have access to the information and, on the request of an employee, make a printed copy of the information available; (g) keep and maintain in prescribed form and manner prescribed health and safety records; (h) provide prescribed first-aid facilities and health services; (i) provide prescribed sanitary and personal facilities; (j) provide, in accordance with prescribed standards, potable water; (k) ensure that the vehicles and mobile equipment used by the employees in the course of their employment meet prescribed standards; (l) provide every person granted access to the work place by the employer with prescribed safety materials, equipment, devices and clothing; (m) ensure that the use, operation and maintenance of the following are in accordance with prescribed standards: (i) boilers and pressure vessels, (ii) escalators, elevators and other devices for moving persons or freight, (iii) all equipment for the generation, distribution or use of electricity, (iv) gas or oil burning equipment or other heat generating equipment, and (v) heating, ventilation and air-conditioning systems; (n) ensure that the levels of ventilation, lighting, temperature, humidity, sound and vibration are in accordance with prescribed standards; (o) comply with prescribed standards relating to fire safety and emergency measures; (p) ensure, in the prescribed manner, that employees have safe entry to, exit from and occupancy of the work place; (q) provide, in the prescribed manner, each employee with the information, instruction, training and supervision necessary to ensure their health and safety at work; (r) maintain all installed guards, guard-rails, barricades and fences in accordance with prescribed standards; (s) ensure that each employee is made aware of every known or foreseeable health or safety hazard in the area where the employee works; (t) ensure that the machinery, equipment and tools used by the employees in the course of their employment meet prescribed health, safety and ergonomic standards and are safe under all conditions of their intended use; (u) ensure that the work place, work spaces and procedures meet prescribed ergonomic standards; (v) adopt and implement prescribed safety codes and safety standards; (w) ensure that every person granted access to the work place by the employer is familiar with and uses in the prescribed circumstances and manner all prescribed safety materials, equipment, devices and clothing; (x) comply with every oral or written direction given to the employer by the Head or the Board concerning the health and safety of employees; (y) ensure that the activities of every person granted access to the work place do not endanger the health and safety of employees; (z) ensure that employees who have supervisory or managerial responsibilities are adequately trained in health and safety and are informed of the responsibilities they have under this Part where they act on behalf of their employer; (z.01) ensure that members of policy and work place committees and health and safety representatives receive the prescribed training in health and safety and are informed of their responsibilities under this Part; (z.02) respond as soon as possible to reports made by employees under paragraph 126(1)(g); (z.03) develop, implement and monitor, in consultation with the policy committee or, if there is no policy committee, with the work place committee or the health and safety representative, a prescribed program for the prevention of hazards in the work place appropriate to its size and the nature of the hazards in it that also provides for the education of employees in health and safety matters; (z.06) consult the work place committee or the health and safety representative in the implementation of changes that might affect occupational health and safety, including work processes and procedures; (z.07) ensure the availability in the work place of premises, equipment and personnel necessary for the operation of the policy and work place committees; (z.08) cooperate with the policy and work place committees or the health and safety representative in the execution of their duties under this Part; (z.09) develop health and safety policies and programs in consultation with the policy committee or, if there is no policy committee, with the work place committee or the health and safety representative; (z.10) respond in writing to recommendations made by the policy and work place committees or the health and safety representative within thirty days after receiving them, indicating what, if any, action will be taken and when it will be taken; (z.11) provide to the policy committee, if any, and to the work place committee or the health and safety representative, a copy of any report on hazards in the work place, including an assessment of those hazards; (z.12) ensure that the work place committee or the health and safety representative inspects each month all or part of the work place, so that every part of the work place is inspected at least once each year; (z.13) when necessary, develop, implement and monitor a program for the provision of personal protective equipment, clothing, devices or materials, in consultation, except in emergencies, with the policy committee or, if there is no policy committee, with the work place committee or the health and safety representative; (z.14) take all reasonable care to ensure that all of the persons granted access to the work place, other than the employer’s employees, are informed of every known or foreseeable health or safety hazard to which they are likely to be exposed in the work place; (z.15) meet with the health and safety representative as necessary to address health and safety matters; (z.16) take the prescribed measures to prevent and protect against harassment and violence in the work place, respond to occurrences of harassment and violence in the work place and offer support to employees affected by harassment and violence in the work place; (z.161) ensure that employees, including those who have supervisory or managerial responsibilities, receive training in the prevention of harassment and violence in the work place and are informed of their rights and obligations under this Part in relation to harassment and violence; (z.162) undergo training in the prevention of harassment and violence in the work place; (z.163) ensure that the person designated by the employer to receive complaints relating to occurrences of harassment and violence has knowledge, training and experience in issues relating to harassment and violence and has knowledge of relevant legislation; (z.17) post and keep posted, in a conspicuous place or places where they are likely to come to the attention of employees, the names, work place telephone numbers and work locations of all of the members of work place committees or of the health and safety representative; (z.18) provide, within thirty days after receiving a request, or as soon as possible after that, the information requested from the employer by a policy committee under subsection 134.1(5) or (6), by a work place committee under subsection 135(8) or (9) or by a health and safety representative under subsection 136(6) or (7); and (z.19) consult with the work place committee or the health and safety representative on the implementation and monitoring of programs developed in consultation with the policy committee.
