question: What are the general responsibilities of an employer in ensuring a safe and healthy work environment for their employees under the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
**General Responsibilities of an Employer**

The Canada Labour Code sets out the general responsibilities of an employer in ensuring a safe and healthy work environment for their employees. According to Section 125 of the Code, an employer is required to
"...ensure that all permanent and temporary buildings and structures meet the prescribed standards..."

This responsibility is further emphasized in Section 125.1, which states that an employer must
"...install guards, guard-rails, barricades and fences in accordance with prescribed standards..." This highlights the employer's duty to ensure that the physical work environment is safe and free from hazards.

**Investigating and Reporting Accidents and Hazards**

An employer is also required to investigate and report all accidents, occurrences of harassment and violence, occupational illnesses, and other hazardous occurrences known to the employer (CLC-125.1). This demonstrates the employer's commitment to identifying and addressing potential hazards in the workplace.

**Providing Information and Training**

An employer must provide employees with information and training on health and safety matters, including the identification of hazards, the use of personal protective equipment, and emergency procedures (CLC-125.1). This responsibility is essential in ensuring that employees are aware of the potential risks in the workplace and can take steps to mitigate them.

**Consulting with Employees and Committees**

An employer must consult with employees and committees, such as the work place committee or the health and safety representative, to develop and implement health and safety programs (CLC-125.1). This demonstrates the employer's commitment to involving employees in the decision-making process and ensuring that their concerns are addressed.

**Compliance with Regulations**

An employer must comply with all regulations made under the Canada Labour Code, including those related to health and safety (CLC-125.1). This includes ensuring that employees receive training on the use of personal protective equipment, the proper handling of hazardous materials, and emergency procedures.

**Overall Responsibility**

In summary, an employer's general responsibilities under the Canada Labour Code include ensuring a safe and healthy work environment, investigating and reporting accidents and hazards, providing information and training, consulting with employees and committees, and complying with regulations. By fulfilling these responsibilities, an employer can help prevent injuries and illnesses in the workplace and promote a positive and healthy work environment for their employees.

question: What are the primary responsibilities of an employer in relation to managing and controlling hazardous substances in the workplace?
answer:
**Employer Responsibilities: Hazardous Substances**

The primary responsibilities of an employer in relation to managing and controlling hazardous substances in the workplace are outlined in Section 125.1 of the Canada Labour Code.

**Ensuring Control of Concentrations of Hazardous Substances**

The employer must ensure that concentrations of hazardous substances in the workplace are controlled in accordance with prescribed standards.
"...every employer shall, in respect of every work place controlled by the employer and, in respect of every work activity carried out by an employee in a work place that is not controlled by the employer, to the extent that the employer controls the activity, (a) ensure that concentrations of hazardous substances in the work place are controlled in accordance with prescribed standards..."

**Storing and Handling Hazardous Substances**

The employer must ensure that all hazardous substances in the workplace are stored and handled in the manner prescribed.
"...ensure that all hazardous substances in the work place are stored and handled in the manner prescribed..."

**Identifying Hazardous Substances**

The employer must ensure that all hazardous substances in the workplace, other than hazardous products, are identified in the manner prescribed.
"...ensure that all hazardous substances in the work place, other than hazardous products, are identified in the manner prescribed..."

**Labeling Hazardous Products**

The employer must ensure that each hazardous product in the workplace or each container in the workplace in which a hazardous product is contained has affixed to it, printed on it, attached to it or otherwise applied to it a label that meets the prescribed requirements.
"...subject to the Hazardous Materials Information Review Act , ensure that each hazardous product in the work place or each container in the work place in which a hazardous product is contained has affixed to it, printed on it, attached to it or otherwise applied to it a label that meets the prescribed requirements..."

**Providing Safety Data Sheets**

The employer must make available to every employee, in the prescribed manner, a safety data sheet for each hazardous product to which the employee may be exposed that meets the requirements set out in the regulations made under subsection 15(1) of the Hazardous Products Act.
"...make available to every employee, in the prescribed manner, a safety data sheet for each hazardous product to which the employee may be exposed that meets the requirements set out in the regulations made under subsection 15(1) of the Hazardous Products Act..."

**Investigating and Assessing Exposure**

The employer must investigate and assess the exposure of employees to hazardous substances in the manner prescribed, with the assistance of the workplace committee or the health and safety representative.
"...where employees may be exposed to hazardous substances, investigate and assess the exposure in the manner prescribed, with the assistance of the work place committee or the health and safety representative..."

**Keeping Records**

The employer must keep and maintain all records of exposure to hazardous substances in the prescribed manner and that personal records of exposure are made available to the affected employees.
"...ensure that all records of exposure to hazardous substances are kept and maintained in the prescribed manner and that personal records of exposure are made available to the affected employees."

question: What are the responsibilities of an employer and a medical professional regarding the disclosure and confidentiality of information about hazardous products in emergency situations?
answer:
**Employer Responsibilities**

According to the Canada Labour Code, Section 125.2, an employer shall provide, in respect of any hazardous product to which an employee may be exposed, as soon as is practicable in the circumstances, any information that is included in the safety data sheet that is in the employer’s possession for the hazardous product to any physician or other prescribed medical professional who requests that information for the purpose of making a medical diagnosis of, or rendering medical treatment to, an employee in an emergency.
"Any physician or other prescribed medical professional to whom information is provided by an employer pursuant to subsection (1) shall keep confidential any information specified by the employer as being confidential, except for the purpose for which it is provided."

Source: Canada Labour Code, Section 125.2

**Confidentiality of Information**

The employer shall specify which information is confidential and the medical professional shall keep it confidential, except for the purpose for which it is provided.

**Medical Professional Responsibilities**

The medical professional shall keep confidential any information specified by the employer as being confidential, except for the purpose for which it is provided.

**Disclosure of Information**

In emergency situations, the employer shall provide any information that is included in the safety data sheet that is in the employer’s possession for the hazardous product to any physician or other prescribed medical professional who requests that information.

**Hazardous Products Act**

The Hazardous Materials Information Review Act requires that employers make available to every employee, in the prescribed manner, a safety data sheet for each hazardous product to which the employee may be exposed that meets the requirements set out in the regulations made under subsection 15(1) of the Hazardous Products Act.

The Workplace Hazardous Material Information System (WHMIS) 2015 requires that employers ensure that each hazardous product in the work place or each container in the work place in which a hazardous product is contained has affixed to it, printed on it, attached to it or otherwise applied to it a label that meets the prescribed requirements.

The supplier shall affix a label to the container of the hazardous product that meets the prescribed requirements.

The employer shall review and revise the SDS as necessary to ensure that it is current and accurate.

{"id": "CLC-125.3", "type": "Canada Labour Code", "title": "Duties of Employers: Coal mines", "section": "125.3"}, "text": "Section 125.3 (1) Every employer of employees employed in a coal mine shall (a) comply with every condition imposed on the employer pursuant to paragraph 137.2(2)(b) or (3)(a); (b) comply with every provision substituted for a provision of the regulations, in respect of the employer, pursuant to paragraph 137.2(3)(b); (c) permit inspections and tests to be carried out on behalf of the employees, in any part of the mine and on any machinery or equipment therein, in the prescribed manner and at intervals not greater than the prescribed interval; and (d) as a condition of carrying out any activity for which the submission of plans and procedures is prescribed, submit to the Coal Mining Safety Commission for approval, in the form and manner and at the time prescribed, plans and procedures relating to that activity and carry out the activity in conformity with plans and procedures as approved. Marginal note: Methods, machinery and equipment (2) No employer shall require or permit the use in a coal mine of any mining method, machinery or equipment in respect of which no prescribed safety standards are applicable unless the use thereof has been approved pursuant to paragraph 137.2(2)(a). Marginal note: Searches (3) Every employer of employees employed in a coal mine shall, at intervals not greater than the prescribed interval, for the purpose of preventing alcohol, articles for use in smoking and drugs, other than drugs exempted by the regulations, from being brought into the mine, (a) require every person entering an underground portion of the mine who is not employed there to submit to a personal search conducted in the prescribed manner; and (b) require a proportion, not less than the prescribed proportion, of employees employed in the underground portions of the mine to submit to personal searches conducted in the prescribed manner. Definition of (4) For the purposes of this section and section 137.2, coal mine includes any work place above ground that is used in the operation of the mine and is under the control of the employer of employees employed in the mine. question: What are the key responsibilities of employers of employees employed in a coal mine to ensure a safe working environment?
answer:
**Key Responsibilities of Employers in Coal Mines**

The Canada Labour Code outlines the key responsibilities of employers in coal mines to ensure a safe working environment. According to Section 125.3, employers must:

* **Comply with prescribed conditions and provisions**:
"Every employer of employees employed in a coal mine shall (a) comply with every condition imposed on the employer pursuant to paragraph 137.2(2)(b) or (3)(a)..."
* **Permit inspections and tests**:
"...permit inspections and tests to be carried out on behalf of the employees, in any part of the mine and on any machinery or equipment therein, in the prescribed manner and at intervals not greater than the prescribed interval..."
* **Submit plans and procedures for approval**:
"...as a condition of carrying out any activity for which the submission of plans and procedures is prescribed, submit to the Coal Mining Safety Commission for approval, in the form and manner and at the time prescribed, plans and procedures relating to that activity and carry out the activity in conformity with plans and procedures as approved."
* **Conduct personal searches of employees**:
"Every employer of employees employed in a coal mine shall, at intervals not greater than the prescribed interval, for the purpose of preventing alcohol, articles for use in smoking and drugs, other than drugs exempted by the regulations, from being brought into the mine, (a) require every person entering an underground portion of the mine who is not employed there to submit to a personal search conducted in the prescribed manner..."

These responsibilities are crucial in ensuring the health and safety of employees working in coal mines. By complying with prescribed conditions and provisions, permitting inspections and tests, submitting plans and procedures for approval, and conducting personal searches of employees, employers can help prevent accidents and injuries in the workplace.

question: What is an employer prohibited from doing to an employee in terms of their employment status?
answer:
**Employer Prohibited Actions**

An employer is prohibited from treating an employee as if they were not their employee.

**Misclassification of Employees**

According to the Labour Standards Regulations,
"A person who is paid remuneration by an employer is presumed to be their employee unless the contrary is proved by the employer."

**Examples of Misclassification**

The regulations list examples of situations in which an employee may be misclassified, including:

* An incorporated driver who meets the criteria to be an employee is misclassified as a self-employed/independent worker
* An intern or employee is misclassified as a student intern
* Employees who have shares in a business are misclassified as an associate if they do not have any control over ownership or business operations

**Consequences of Misclassification**

Any employer who misclassifies an employee is contravening the Code and may be subject to enforcement action by the Labour Program, up to and including an administrative monetary penalty (AMP) or prosecution. (LABOUR-STANDARDS-8_3)

**Employer's Obligations**

An employer must provide an employee with a written employment statement within the first 30 days of employment, which must include the information listed in section 3.1 of the Canada Labour Standards Regulations. (LABOUR-STANDARDS-8_3)

question: What are the general responsibilities of an employee in ensuring health and safety in the workplace according to the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
**Duties of Employees: Health and Safety Matters**

According to the Canada Labour Code, Section 126, employees have several general responsibilities in ensuring health and safety in the workplace.

**Use of Safety Materials and Equipment
"...every employee shall (a) use any safety materials, equipment, devices and clothing that are intended for the employee’s protection and furnished to the employee by the employer or that are prescribed..."(a))

This subsection emphasizes the importance of employees using the safety materials and equipment provided by their employer to protect themselves and others from harm.

**Following Procedures and Instructions
"...follow prescribed procedures with respect to the health and safety of employees..."(b))

This subsection highlights the need for employees to follow established procedures to ensure health and safety in the workplace.

**Cooperation and Reporting
"...cooperate with any person carrying out a duty imposed under this Part; (f) cooperate with the policy and work place committees or the health and safety representative; (g) report to the employer any thing or circumstance in a work place that is likely to be hazardous to the health or safety of the employee, or that of the other employees or other persons granted access to the work place by the employer..."(e) and (g))

These subsections emphasize the importance of employees cooperating with their employer and other individuals in carrying out health and safety duties, as well as reporting any hazards or incidents that may affect their health and safety or that of others.

**Compliance with Instructions and Reporting Incidents
"...comply with every oral or written direction of the Head or the Board concerning the health and safety of employees; and (j) report to the employer any situation that the employee believes to be a contravention of this Part by the employer, another employee or any other person."(i) and (j))

**Limitation of Liability
"No employee is personally liable for anything done or omitted to be done in good faith by the employee when the employee is assisting the employer, as requested by the employer, in providing first-aid or in carrying out any other emergency measures."

This subsection provides a limitation of liability for employees who act in good faith when providing first-aid or carrying out emergency measures at the request of their employer.

answer:
**Workplace Incident Handling**

**Section 127 of the Canada Labour Code**

The rules regarding the handling of wreckage, articles, or things related to a workplace incident where an employee is killed or seriously injured are outlined in Section 127 of the Canada Labour Code.

**Authorized Interference
"...no person shall, unless authorized to do so by the Head, remove or in any way interfere with or disturb any wreckage, article or thing related to the incident except to the extent necessary to (a) save a life, prevent injury or relieve human suffering in the vicinity; (b) maintain an essential public service; or (c) prevent unnecessary damage to or loss of property."

question: What steps should an employee take if they believe there has been a contravention of the Part of the Canada Labour Code related to workplace safety and health, or if they believe there is likely to be an accident, injury or illness arising out of their employment?
answer:
**Employee Responsibilities**

According to Section 127.1 of the Canada Labour Code,
"An employee who believes on reasonable grounds that there has been a contravention of this Part or that there is likely to be an accident, injury or illness arising out of, linked with or occurring in the course of employment shall, before exercising any other recourse available under this Part, except the rights conferred by subsection (8.1) and sections 128, 129 and 132, make a complaint to the employee’s supervisor."

This means that employees should first report their concerns to their supervisor, who may be able to resolve the issue internally. If the issue cannot be resolved with the supervisor, the employee may refer the complaint to a chairperson of the workplace committee or a health and safety representative for investigation.

**Internal Complaint Resolution Process**

The Internal Complaint Resolution Process is a formal process that allows employees to report concerns about workplace safety and health. According to Section 127.1 of the Canada Labour Code,
"The employee and the supervisor or designated person, as the case may be, shall try to resolve the complaint between themselves as soon as possible."

If the issue cannot be resolved through internal channels, the employee may refer the complaint to a chairperson of the workplace committee or a health and safety representative for investigation. The investigation will be conducted jointly by an employee member and an employer member of the workplace committee, or by the health and safety representative and a person designated by the employer.

**Reporting to the Head**

If the issue is not resolved through internal channels, the employee may refer the complaint to the Head of the workplace. According to Section 127.1 of the Canada Labour Code,
"The employee or employer may refer a complaint that there has been a contravention of this Part to the Head in the following circumstances: (a) where the employer does not agree with the results of the investigation; (b) where the employer has failed to inform the persons who investigated the complaint of how and when the employer intends to resolve the matter or has failed to take action to resolve the matter; (c) where the persons who investigated the complaint do not agree between themselves as to whether the complaint is justified; or (d) in the case of a complaint relating to an occurrence of harassment and violence, the employee and the supervisor or designated person, as the case may be, failed to resolve the complaint between themselves."

The Head will investigate the complaint and may issue directions to the employer or employee, recommend that the employee and employer resolve the matter between themselves, or issue directions under subsection 145(2) if a danger exists.

{"id": "920-1-IPG-070_1", "type": "canada.ca", "title": "Danger as a Normal Condition of Employment - 920-1-IPG-070", "section": "N/A"}, "text": "DANGER AS A NORMAL CONDITION OF EMPLOYMENT –905-1-IPG-070       OHS IPGs   Disclaimer    Effective Date: October, 2014  1. SUBJECT Clarification of the  interpretation of danger as a “normal condition of employment” as found in  paragraph 128(2)(b) of the  Canada  Labour Code , Part II (Code).  2. ISSUE The Labour Program of Employment and Social Development Canada (ESDC) has been asked on several occasions to provide guidance on and clarification of what danger is a “normal condition of employment”. Subsection 128(1) of the Code states:  “Subject to this section, an employee may refuse to use or operate a machine or thing, to work in a place or to perform an activity, if the employee while at work has reasonable cause to believe that:  the use or operation of the machine or thing constitutes a danger to the employee or to another employee, or a condition exists in the place that constitutes a danger to the employee, or the performance of the activity by the employee constitutes a danger to the employee or to another employee.”   Paragraph 128(2)(b) of the Code states:  “An employee may not, under this section, refuse to use or operate a machine or thing, to work in a place or to perform an activity if […] (b) the danger referred to in subsection (1) is a normal condition of employment.”  WHAT IT IS  After the employer has:        identified every hazard; and  eliminated it, reduced and controlled it or provided  protective clothing, equipment, devices or materials to employees to protect  them against it; then, any danger that remains constitutes a normal condition  of employment.   The existence of any danger that is a normal  condition of employment is not a grounds for a refusal to work. Normal refers  to something that is regular, to a typical state or level of affairs, something  that is not out of the ordinary."

question: What are the steps an employee can take if they have reasonable cause to believe that using a machine or working in a place poses a danger to themselves or another employee?
answer:
**Refusal to Work Due to Danger**

If an employee has reasonable cause to believe that using a machine or working in a place poses a danger to themselves or another employee, they may refuse to use or operate the machine, work in the place, or perform the activity.

**Section 128(1) of the Canada Labour Code
"...to this section, an employee may refuse to use or operate a machine or thing, to work in a place or to perform an activity, if the employee while at work has reasonable cause to believe that:  the use or operation of the machine or thing constitutes a danger to the employee or to another employee, or a condition exists in the place that constitutes a danger to the employee, or the performance of the activity by the employee constitutes a danger to the employee or to another..."

**Reporting the Refusal**

The employee must report the refusal to their employer without delay.

**Section 128(6) of the Canada Labour Code
"An employee who refuses to use or operate a machine or thing, work in a place or perform an activity under subsection (1), or who is prevented from acting in accordance with that subsection by subsection (4), shall report the circumstances of the matter to the employer without delay."

**Investigation and Resolution**

The employer must investigate the matter immediately after being informed of the refusal. If the employer agrees that a danger exists, they must take immediate action to protect employees from the danger.

**Section 128(8) of the Canada Labour Code
"If, following its investigation, the employer agrees that a danger exists, the employer shall take immediate action to protect employees from the danger. The employer shall inform the work place committee or the health and safety representative of the matter and the action taken to resolve it."

**Continuing the Refusal**

If the employer does not agree that a danger exists, the employee may continue the refusal. In this case, the employee must report the circumstances of the matter to the employer and to the work place committee or the health and safety representative.

**Section 128(9) of the Canada Labour Code
"If the employee continues the refusal under subsection (15), the employer shall immediately inform the Head and the work place committee or the health and safety representative of its decision and the continued refusal. The employer shall also provide a copy of the report on the matter prepared under subsection (7.1) to the Head along with a copy of any report referred to in subsection (10.1) or (10.2)."

question: What happens to an employee's pay and benefits during a work stoppage due to certain provisions of the Canada Labour Code, and under what conditions might they have to repay those wages or benefits?
answer:
**Work Stoppage and Pay**

During a work stoppage due to certain provisions of the Canada Labour Code, employees are deemed to be at work until work resumes or until the end of the scheduled work period or shift, whichever period is shorter.
"...employees who are affected by a stoppage of work arising from the application of section 127.1, 128 or 129 or subsection 145(2) are deemed, for the purpose of calculating wages and benefits, to be at work during the stoppage until work resumes or until the end of the scheduled work period or shift, whichever period is shorter."

This means that employees will continue to receive pay and benefits during the work stoppage, even if they are not physically working.

**Repayment of Wages and Benefits**

However, employees who are paid wages or benefits during a work stoppage may be required to repay those wages and benefits if it is determined that they exercised their rights under section 128 or 129 knowing that no circumstances existed that would warrant it.
"Unless otherwise provided in a collective agreement or other agreement, employees who are paid wages or benefits under subsection (1) or (2) may be required by the employer to repay those wages and benefits if it is determined, after all avenues of redress have been exhausted by the employee who exercised rights under section 128 or 129, that the employee exercised those rights knowing that no circumstances existed that would warrant it."

This repayment requirement is subject to certain conditions, including that the employee has exercised their rights under section 128 or 129 and that there are no other avenues of redress available to them.

question: What are the circumstances under which the Head may decide not to investigate an employee's refusal to work due to a potential danger, and what happens to the employee's refusal in such cases?
answer:
**Circumstances for Non-Investigation**

The Head may decide not to investigate an employee's refusal to work due to a potential danger under the following circumstances:

*   The matter is one that could more appropriately be dealt with, initially or completely, by means of a procedure provided for under Part I or III or under another Act of Parliament.
*   The matter is trivial, frivolous, or vexatious.
*   The continued refusal by the employee under subsection 128(15) is in bad faith.

**Consequences of Non-Investigation**

If the Head decides not to investigate an employee's refusal to work due to a potential danger, the employee's refusal is no longer entitled to continue under subsection 128(15).

question: Under what circumstances can employees be excluded from the application of certain health and safety provisions in the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
**Exclusion from Application of Health and Safety Provisions**

**Section 159 of the Canada Labour Code**

The Governor in Council may exclude, in whole or in part, from the application of any of the provisions of this Part any employment, or any class or classes of employment, on or in connection with a work or undertaking set out in the regulation whose activities are regulated, in whole or in part, pursuant to the Nuclear Safety and Control Act.

**Source:** CLC-159, Section 159(1)

**Section 266 of the Canada Labour Code**

The Governor in Council may by regulation exclude, in whole or in part, from the application of any of the provisions of this Part any employment, or any class or classes of employment, on or in connection with a work or undertaking set out in the regulation whose activities are regulated, in whole or in part, pursuant to the Nuclear Safety and Control Act.

**Source:** CLC-266, Section 266(1)

**Section 130 of the Canada Labour Code**

The Head may, on the joint application of the parties to a collective agreement, if the Head is satisfied that the agreement contains provisions that are at least as effective as those under sections 128 and 129 in protecting the employees to whom the agreement relates from danger to their health or safety, exclude the employees from the application of those sections for the period during which the agreement remains in force.

**Source:** CLC-130, Section 130

**General Provisions**

The Canada Labour Code provides that nothing in Section 126 relieves an employer from any duty imposed on the employer under this Part. This means that even if employees are excluded from certain health and safety provisions, employers are still responsible for complying with the remaining provisions.

**Source:** CLC-126, Section 126(2)

The question is answered in Section 131 of the Canada Labour Code, which states:
"The fact that an employer or employee has complied with or failed to comply with any of the provisions of this Part may not be construed as affecting any right of an employee to compensation under any statute relating to compensation for employment injury or illness, or as affecting any liability or obligation of any employer or employee under any such statute."

question: What are the steps an employee who is pregnant or nursing must take if they believe continuing their current job functions may pose a risk to their health or to that of the fetus or child?
answer:
**Maternity-Related Reassignment and Leave**

According to the Canada Labour Code, Section 132, an employee who is pregnant or nursing must take the following steps if they believe continuing their current job functions may pose a risk to their health or to that of the fetus or child:
"...as defined in section 166, of her choice as soon as possible to establish whether continuing any of her current job functions poses a risk to her health or to that of the foetus or child."

This means that the employee must seek medical advice from a healthcare practitioner of their choice to determine whether their current job functions pose a risk to their health or the health of their fetus or child.

**Cease to Perform Job**

If the employee believes that continuing their current job functions poses a risk to their health or to that of the fetus or child, they may cease to perform their job. (CLC-132(1))
"...the employer, with the consent of the employee, shall notify the work place committee or the health and safety representative."

This means that the employee must inform their employer and, if possible, the workplace committee or health and safety representative about their decision to cease performing their job.

**Reassignment**

If the employee ceases to perform their job, the employer may reassign them to another job that would not pose a risk to their health or to that of the fetus or child. (CLC-132(4))
"For the period during which the employee does not perform her job under subsection (1), the employer may, in consultation with the employee, reassign her to another job that would not pose a risk to her health or to that of the foetus or child."

This means that the employer may offer the employee a new job that is safer for their health and the health of their fetus or child.

**Status of Employee**

The employee's status remains the same, and they continue to hold their original job and receive their wages and benefits. (CLC-132(5))
"The employee, whether or not she has been reassigned to another job, is deemed to continue to hold the job that she held at the time she ceased to perform her job functions and shall continue to receive the wages and benefits that are attached to that job for the period during which she does not perform the job."

This means that the employee's employment status remains unchanged, and they continue to receive their wages and benefits as if they had not ceased performing their job.

question: What is the process for an employee to make a complaint if they believe their employer has taken action against them in contravention of section 147, and what is the role of the Board in handling such complaints?
answer:
**Process for an Employee to Make a Complaint**

To make a complaint, an employee must follow the process outlined in Section 133 of the Canada Labour Code.

According to Section 133(1),
"An employee, or a person designated by the employee for the purpose, who alleges that an employer has taken action against the employee in contravention of section 147 may, subject to subsection (3), make a complaint in writing to the Board of the alleged contravention."

This means that the employee must submit a written complaint to the Board, detailing the alleged contravention of section 147.

**Role of the Board in Handling Complaints**

The Board plays a crucial role in handling complaints under Section 133. According to Section 133(5),
"On receipt of a complaint made under this section, the Board may assist the parties to the complaint to settle the complaint and shall, if it decides not to so assist the parties or the complaint is not settled within a period considered by the Board to be reasonable in the circumstances, hear and determine the complaint."

This means that the Board will review the complaint and may attempt to settle the matter between the parties. If the complaint is not settled, the Board will hear and determine the complaint.

**Time Limit for Making a Complaint**

According to Section 133(2),
"The complaint shall be made to the Board not later than ninety days after the date on which the complainant knew, or in the Board’s opinion ought to have known, of the action or circumstances giving rise to the complaint."

This means that the employee must submit the complaint to the Board within 90 days of becoming aware of the alleged contravention.

**Exclusion of Arbitration**

According to Section 133(4),
"Notwithstanding any law or agreement to the contrary, a complaint made under this section may not be referred by an employee to arbitration or adjudication."

This means that the employee cannot refer the complaint to arbitration or adjudication, and must instead follow the process outlined in Section 133.

**Burden of Proof**

According to Section 133(6),
"A complaint made under this section in respect of the exercise of a right under section 128 or 129 is itself evidence that the contravention actually occurred and, if a party to the complaint proceedings alleges that the contravention did not occur, the burden of proof is on that party."

This means that the employee's complaint is considered evidence that the contravention occurred, and the burden of proof lies with the employer to disprove the allegations.

question: What actions can the Board require an employer to take if it determines that the employer has contravened section 147 of the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
**Actions the Board Can Require an Employer to Take**

If the Board determines that an employer has contravened section 147 of the Canada Labour Code, the Board may require the employer to take certain actions.

**Cease Contravening Section 147**

The Board may, by order, require the employer to cease contravening section 147. This means that the employer must stop taking disciplinary action against employees for exercising their rights under the Canada Labour Code.

**Permit Affected Employees to Return to Work**

The Board may also require the employer to permit any employee who has been affected by the contravention to return to the duties of their employment. This means that the employer must allow the affected employee to resume their job and continue to receive their regular remuneration.

**Reinstate Former Employees**

In addition, the Board may require the employer to reinstate any former employee affected by the contravention. This means that the employer must rehire the former employee and provide them with their regular remuneration.

**Pay Compensation to Affected Employees**

The Board may also require the employer to pay to any employee or former employee affected by the contravention compensation not exceeding the sum that, in the Board's opinion, is equivalent to the remuneration that would, but for the contravention, have been paid by the employer to the employee or former employee.

**Rescind Disciplinary Action**

Finally, the Board may require the employer to rescind any disciplinary action taken in respect of, and pay compensation to any employee affected by, the contravention. This means that the employer must remove any penalties or fines imposed on the employee and provide them with compensation for any financial or other losses they suffered as a result of the contravention.

**Source:**
CLC-134, Section 134(1)

question: What are the responsibilities of a workplace health and safety committee in a workplace with 20 or more employees, according to the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
**Workplace Health and Safety Committees: Responsibilities**

According to the Canada Labour Code, a workplace health and safety committee is responsible for several key functions in a workplace with 20 or more employees.

**Establishment and Selection of Members**

The Code requires that every employer establish a workplace health and safety committee and select its members (CLC-135, subsection 135(1)). The committee's members are responsible for carrying out the functions and duties of the committee.

**Responsibilities of the Committee**

The committee is responsible for considering and expeditiously disposing of complaints relating to the health and safety of employees (CLC-135, subsection 135(7)(a)). The committee must also participate in the implementation and monitoring of the program referred to in paragraph 134.1(4)(c) of the Code, and develop, implement, and monitor a program for the prevention of hazards in the workplace that also provides for the education of employees in health and safety matters (CLC-135, subsection 135(7)(c) and (d)).

**Investigations and Inspections**

The committee must participate in all inquiries, investigations, studies, and inspections pertaining to the health and safety of employees (CLC-135, subsection 135(7)(e)). The committee must also inspect each month all or part of the workplace, so that every part of the workplace is inspected at least once each year (CLC-135, subsection 135(7)(k)).

**Access to Information**

The committee has full access to all government and employer reports, studies, and tests relating to the health and safety of employees, or to the parts of those reports, studies, and tests that relate to the health and safety of employees (CLC-135, subsection 135(9)).

**Meetings**

The committee must meet during regular working hours at least nine times a year at regular intervals, and may meet as required during regular working hours or outside those hours in exceptional circumstances (CLC-135, subsection 135(10)).

**Exceptions and Exemptions**

The Code also provides for exceptions and exemptions, such as for workplaces with fewer than 20 employees, or for workplaces that have a collective agreement or other agreement that provides for a committee of persons with health and safety responsibilities (CLC-135, subsection 135(6)).

question: What are the requirements for the composition of a policy committee or a work place committee in terms of employee representation and selection?
answer:
**Composition Requirements**

The Canada Labour Code sets out the requirements for the composition of policy committees and work place committees.

**Employee Representation**

According to section 135.1(1), a policy committee or a work place committee shall consist of at least two persons, and at least half of the members shall be employees who "do not exercise managerial functions" (CLC-135.1(1)).

**Selection of Employee Members**

The employee members shall be selected by the employees, if they are not represented by a trade union, or by the trade union representing employees, in consultation with any employees who are not so represented (CLC-135.1(1)). This means that employee members must be chosen through a process that involves the employees themselves, rather than being appointed by the employer.

**Exception for Policy Committees**

Despite the general requirement, the members of a policy committee may include persons who are not employees, as long as the employer has provided for this in a collective agreement or other agreement (CLC-135.1(2)).

**Exception for Work Place Committees**

If there is no policy committee, a work place committee may select two additional members, one of whom must be an employee who meets the criteria set out in paragraphs (1)(a) and (b) (CLC-135.1(3)).

**Alternate Members**

The employer and employees may select alternate members to serve as replacements for members selected by them who are unable to perform their functions (CLC-135.1(6)).

**Chairpersons**

A committee shall have two chairpersons selected from among the committee members, one of whom shall be selected by the employee members and the other by the employer members (CLC-135.1(7)).

**Selection of Members**

The selection of members shall be made in accordance with the regulations made under subsection 135.2(1), which may specify the qualifications and terms of office of members, the method of selecting employee members, and other matters (CLC-135.2(1)).

question: What are the rules surrounding the provision of information that could reveal the identity of a person involved in workplace harassment and violence to a policy committee or a workplace committee?
answer:
**Canada Labour Code: Provisions for Policy Committees and Workplace Committees**

The Canada Labour Code outlines the rules surrounding the provision of information that could reveal the identity of a person involved in workplace harassment and violence to a policy committee or a workplace committee.

**Section 135.11: Information Likely to Reveal Identity**

Neither the Head nor an employer shall, without the person’s consent, provide, under this Part, a policy committee or a work place committee with any information that is likely to reveal the identity of a person who was involved in an occurrence of harassment and violence in the work place.
"Neither a policy committee nor a work place committee shall have access to that information without the person’s consent."

This section emphasizes the importance of obtaining consent from the individual involved before providing information that could reveal their identity to a policy committee or a workplace committee.

**Section 135.11(2): Exceptions**

Subsection (1) does not apply with respect to (a) information provided under section 128 or 129 or a direction or report relating to the application of those sections; or (b) a decision, reasons or a direction referred to in subsection 146.1(2).

This exception highlights that certain types of information, such as reports and decisions related to sections 128 and 129, are exempt from the requirement for consent.

**Section 136.1: Health and Safety Representatives**

Section 136.1 of the Canada Labour Code addresses the provision of information to health and safety representatives, which is similar to the rules for policy committees and workplace committees.
"Neither the Head nor an employer shall, without the person’s consent, provide, under this Part, a health and safety representative with any information that is likely to reveal the identity of a person who was involved in an occurrence of harassment and violence in the work place."

This section reiterates the importance of obtaining consent from the individual involved before providing information that could reveal their identity to a health and safety representative.

**General Guidelines**

In general, employers must obtain consent from the individual involved before providing information that could reveal their identity to a policy committee or a workplace committee. This consent can be obtained in writing, and employers should ensure that the individual is fully informed about the regulatory requirements and the consequences of giving consent or not.

(l) shall assist the employer in investigating and assessing the exposure of employees to hazardous substances; and (m) shall participate in the implementation and monitoring of a program for the provision of personal protective equipment, clothing, devices or materials and, where there is no policy committee, shall participate in the development of the program. question: What are the primary responsibilities of a health and safety representative in a workplace with fewer than 20 employees, and how are they selected?
answer:
**Primary Responsibilities of a Health and Safety Representative**

According to the Canada Labour Code, a health and safety representative is responsible for considering and expeditiously disposing of complaints relating to the health and safety of employees (
"...shall consider and expeditiously dispose of complaints relating to the health and safety of employees..." CLC-136.5).

They are also responsible for ensuring that adequate records are maintained pertaining to work accidents, injuries, health hazards, and the disposition of complaints related to the health and safety of employees (
"...shall ensure that adequate records are maintained pertaining to work accidents, injuries, health hazards and the disposition of complaints related to the health and safety of employees..." CLC-136.5).

Furthermore, they must participate in the implementation and monitoring of a program for the prevention of hazards in the workplace that also provides for the education of employees in health and safety matters (
"...shall participate in the development, implementation and monitoring of a program for the prevention..." CLC-136.5).

**Selection of a Health and Safety Representative**

The selection of a health and safety representative is governed by section 136 of the Canada Labour Code. According to this section, if employees do not exercise managerial functions, they must select a person from among their colleagues to be the health and safety representative (
"...the employees at the work place who do not exercise managerial functions shall select from among those employees the person to be appointed..." CLC-136.2).

If employees are represented by a trade union, the trade union must select the person to be appointed, in consultation with any employees who are not so represented, and subject to any regulations made under subsection (11) (
"...the trade union shall select the person to be appointed, in consultation with any employees who are not so represented, and subject to any regulations made under subsection (11)." CLC-136.2).

In either case, the employees or the trade union must advise the employer in writing of the name of the person selected (
"The employees or the trade union shall advise the employer in writing of the name of the person so selected." CLC-136.3).

question: Under what circumstances may an employer need to establish multiple workplace health and safety committees or appoint multiple health and safety representatives?
answer:
**Section 137: Health and Safety Representatives: Committees or Representatives — specified work places**

**Single Workplace with Ineffective Committee/Representative**

According to Section 137 of the Canada Labour Code,
"...if an employer controls more than one work place or the size or nature of the operations of the employer or those of the work place precludes the effective functioning of a single work place committee or health and safety representative, as the case may be, for those work places, the employer shall, subject to the approval or in accordance with the direction of the Head, establish or appoint in accordance with section 135 or 136, as the case may be, a work place committee or health and safety representative for the work places that are specified in the approval or direction."

This section implies that if a single workplace health and safety committee or representative is not functioning effectively due to the size or nature of the operations, the employer may need to establish multiple committees or appoint multiple representatives.

**Multiple Workplaces**

In addition, Section 137 also addresses the scenario where an employer controls more than one workplace. In this case, the employer may establish a single workplace health and safety committee or representative for all workplaces, subject to the approval of the Head. However, this is not a requirement, and the employer may choose to establish multiple committees or appoint multiple representatives for each workplace.

**Approval Required**

It is worth noting that the establishment of multiple workplace health and safety committees or the appointment of multiple health and safety representatives may require the approval of the Head or a Health and Safety Officer. (CLC-137)

**Source:** CLC-137, Section 137 of the Canada Labour Code

question: What is the purpose of the Coal Mining Safety Commission and how is it structured?
answer:
**Purpose of the Coal Mining Safety Commission**

The purpose of the Coal Mining Safety Commission is to ensure the health and safety of employees in coal mines. According to the Canada Labour Code, the Commission "shall endeavour to carry out its terms of reference" and make its report and recommendations to the Minister within fourteen days after its appointment or within such longer period as the Minister may allow (CLC-137.1(4)).

**Structure of the Coal Mining Safety Commission**

The Coal Mining Safety Commission is established by the Minister and consists of not more than five members appointed by the Minister to hold office during pleasure (CLC-137.1(1)). One member of the Commission is designated as the chairperson by the Minister, and the others are equally representative of non-supervisory employees employed in coal mines and of employers of those employees (CLC-137.1(2)).

The Commission has a quorum of three members, consisting of the chairperson or alternate chairperson, one member representative of non-supervisory employees, and one member representative of employers (CLC-137.1(4)).

**Alternate Chairperson**

The Minister may appoint an alternate chairperson to act in the absence or incapacity of the chairperson, who has all the powers, duties, and immunity of the chairperson (CLC-137.1(2.1)).

**Remuneration and By-laws**

The members of the Commission, including the alternate chairperson, are paid the remuneration that may be fixed by the Governor in Council and are entitled to reasonable travel and living expenses incurred while performing their functions away from their ordinary place of residence (CLC-137.1(6)). The Commission may also make by-laws for the conduct of its activities, subject to the approval of the Minister (CLC-137.1(7)).

question: What is the primary goal that the Commission considers when approving plans, procedures, methods, machinery, and equipment in coal mines, or when granting exemptions and substitutions for regulatory provisions?
answer:
**Primary Goal of Commission's Approval and Exemptions**

The primary goal that the Commission considers when approving plans, procedures, methods, machinery, and equipment in coal mines, or when granting exemptions and substitutions for regulatory provisions is to "protect the health and safety of employees".

This is evident in Section 137.2(2) of the Canada Labour Code, which states:
"On the application of an employer, the Commission or persons designated by the Commission for the purposes of this subsection may, if, in the opinion of the Commission or those persons, protection of the health and safety of employees would not thereby be diminished, (a) approve in writing the use by the employer in coal mines of mining methods, machinery or equipment in respect of which no prescribed safety standards are applicable; or (b) approve in writing, notwithstanding anything in this Part, the use by the employer in coal mines, for a specified time and subject to specified conditions, of any mining method, machinery or equipment that does not meet prescribed safety standards applicable in respect of it."

This quote highlights the Commission's primary consideration when making decisions regarding the approval and exemptions of plans, procedures, methods, machinery, and equipment in coal mines. The Commission's goal is to ensure that the use of these items does not compromise the health and safety of employees.

question: What actions can the Minister take to promote and ensure occupational health and safety in employment to which the Part applies?
answer:
**Minister's Powers and Responsibilities**

The Minister has several powers and responsibilities to promote and ensure occupational health and safety in employment to which the Part applies.

**Designating a Head of Compliance and Enforcement**

The Minister may designate a person as Head of Compliance and Enforcement, as stated in Section 122.21(1) of the Canada Labour Code:
"The Minister may designate a person as Head of Compliance and Enforcement."

**Undertaking Research and Programs**

The Minister may undertake research into the cause of and the means of preventing employment injury and occupational illness, as stated in Section 138(4) of the Canada Labour Code:
"The Minister may undertake research into the cause of and the means of preventing employment injury and occupational illness and may, where the Minister deems it appropriate, undertake such research in cooperation with any department or agency of the Government of Canada or with any or all provinces or with any organization undertaking similar research."

The Minister may also undertake programs to reduce or prevent employment injury and occupational illness, as stated in Section 138(6) of the Canada Labour Code:
"The Minister may undertake programs to reduce or prevent employment injury and occupational illness and may, where the Minister deems it appropriate, undertake those programs in cooperation with any department or agency of the Government of Canada or with any or all provinces or any organization undertaking similar programs."

**Publishing Information and Data**

The Minister may publish the results of any research undertaken under Section 138(5) of the Canada Labour Code:
"The Minister may publish the results of any research undertaken under subsection (4) and compile, prepare and disseminate data or information bearing on health or safety of employees obtained from that research or otherwise."

**Appointing Committees and Holding Inquiries**

The Minister may appoint committees of persons to assist or advise the Minister on any matter that the Minister considers advisable concerning occupational health and safety, as stated in Section 138(1) of the Canada Labour Code:
"The Minister may appoint committees of persons to assist or advise the Minister on any matter that the Minister considers advisable concerning occupational health and safety related to employment to which this Part applies."

The Minister may also cause an inquiry to be made into and concerning occupational health and safety in any employment to which the Part applies, as stated in Section 138(2) of the Canada Labour Code:
"The Minister may cause an inquiry to be made into and concerning occupational health and safety in any employment to which this Part applies and may appoint one or more persons to hold the inquiry."

**Investigating Complaints and Reporting**

The Minister is required to protect the health and safety of employees at work, by ensuring that employee complaints, including refusals to work, and accidents and injuries are properly investigated, as stated in Section 122.1 of the Canada Labour Code:
"Section 122.1 The purpose of this Part is to prevent accidents, occurrences of harassment and violence and physical or psychological injuries and illnesses arising out of, linked with or occurring in the course of employment to which this Part applies."

Overall, the Minister has a range of powers and responsibilities to promote and ensure occupational health and safety in employment to which the Part applies.

question: What is the role of the Minister in relation to medical surveillance, examination programs, and reporting on harassment and violence in workplaces under the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
**Medical Surveillance and Examination Programs**

The Minister plays a significant role in medical surveillance and examination programs under the Canada Labour Code. According to Section 139 of the Code, the Minister
"...may undertake medical surveillance and examination programs with respect to occupational health and safety..."

The Minister may also appoint medical officers qualified in occupational medicine to undertake these programs (CLC-139). This suggests that the Minister has the authority to oversee and regulate medical surveillance and examination programs in workplaces.

**Annual Report on Harassment and Violence**

The Minister is also responsible for preparing and publishing an annual report on harassment and violence in workplaces. According to Section 139.1 of the Code, the report must contain
"...statistical data relating to harassment and violence in work places to which this Part applies."

The report must include information categorized according to prohibited grounds of discrimination under the Canadian Human Rights Act (CLC-139.1). This suggests that the Minister's report will provide a comprehensive overview of harassment and violence in workplaces, including data on the types of incidents and the individuals affected.

**Five-Year Review**

The Minister is also required to conduct a five-year review of the provisions of the Canada Labour Code relating to harassment and violence. According to Section 139.2 of the Code, the Minister must
"...commence a review of the provisions of this Part relating to harassment and violence."

At the conclusion of the review, the Minister must prepare a report on the review, which must be tabled in each House of Parliament (CLC-139.2). This suggests that the Minister's review will provide an opportunity for stakeholders to provide input and feedback on the Code's provisions related to harassment and violence.

**Minister's Consent Required**

It is worth noting that the Minister's role in relation to medical surveillance, examination programs, and reporting on harassment and violence is subject to the requirement that no proceeding in respect of an offence under the Canada Labour Code may be instituted except with the consent of the Minister or a person designated by the Minister (CLC-149). This suggests that the Minister's authority is not absolute and is subject to certain limitations and requirements.

question: Who can the Minister and the Head delegate their powers, duties, or functions to, and under what conditions?
answer:
**Delegation of Powers, Duties, or Functions**

The Minister and the Head can delegate their powers, duties, or functions to "any qualified person or class of persons" (CLC-272).

**Qualified Person or Class of Persons**

The text does not specify what constitutes a "qualified person or class of persons". However, it is implied that the person or class must have the necessary authority, expertise, and capacity to exercise the delegated powers, duties, or functions.

**Terms and Conditions**

The delegation of powers, duties, or functions is subject to "any terms and conditions specified by the Minister" (CLC-272). This means that the Minister has the authority to impose conditions on the delegation, such as requirements for the delegate's qualifications, experience, or performance.

**Minister's Delegation**

The Minister can delegate their powers, duties, or functions to "any qualified person or class of persons" (CLC-111.1). This delegation is also subject to "any terms and conditions specified by the Minister".

**Head's Delegation**

The Head can delegate their powers, duties, or functions to "any qualified person or class of persons" (CLC-272). The Head may also make the delegation
"...subject to any terms and conditions that the Head considers appropriate."

**Agreements**

The Minister can enter into an agreement with a province or provincial body to delegate powers, duties, or functions to a person employed by that province or provincial body (CLC-140). However, certain powers, duties, or functions are excluded from such agreements.

**Certificate of Authority**

The Minister or the Head may provide a delegate with a certificate of authority, which must be shown when exercising the delegated powers, duties, or functions (CLC-140).

**Limitation of Liability**

A person to whom powers, duties, or functions have been delegated is not personally liable for anything done or omitted to be done in good faith (CLC-140). However, Her Majesty in right of Canada is not relieved of any civil liability to which Her Majesty in right of Canada may otherwise be subject.

question: What are the powers and responsibilities of the Head in carrying out duties related to workplace health and safety, particularly in terms of entering workplaces, conducting examinations, and issuing directions?
answer:
**Powers and Responsibilities of the Head**

The Head has the power to enter any work place controlled by an employer and conduct examinations, tests, inquiries, investigations, and inspections, or direct the employer to conduct them. This power is outlined in Section 141 of the Canada Labour Code.

**Entering Workplaces**

The Head may enter the workplace at any reasonable time, as stated in Section 141(1)(a):
"...the Head may, in carrying out the Head’s duties and at any reasonable time, enter any work place controlled by an employer..."

**Conducting Examinations and Issuing Directions**

The Head may conduct examinations, tests, inquiries, investigations, and inspections, or direct the employer to conduct them, as stated in Section 141(1)(b):
"...conduct examinations, tests, inquiries, investigations and inspections or direct the employer to conduct them..."

The Head may also issue directions to the employer or employees, as stated in Section 141(1)(i):
"...direct the employer or an employee to make or provide statements, in the form and manner that the Head may specify, respecting working conditions and material and equipment that affect the health or safety of employees..."

**Authority to Direct**

The Head has the authority to direct the employer or employees to take specific actions, such as ensuring that a place or thing is not disturbed for a reasonable period pending an examination or inspection, as stated in Section 141(1)(f):
"...direct the employer to ensure that any place or thing specified by the Head not be disturbed for a reasonable period pending an examination, test, inquiry, investigation or inspection in relation to the place or thing..."

**Investigations and Reports**

The Head is also responsible for investigating deaths and injuries in the workplace, as stated in Section 141(4):
"The Head shall investigate every death of an employee that occurred in the work place or while the employee was working, or that was the result of an injury that occurred in the work place or while the employee was working."

The Head must provide a written report on the findings of an inquiry or investigation within 10 days, as stated in Section 141(6):
"Within 10 days after completing a written report on the findings of an inquiry or investigation, the Head shall provide the employer and the work place committee or the health and safety representative with a copy of the report."

question: What are the consequences and prohibitions related to interfering with the exercise of powers and duties under Part of the Canada Labour Code (PART II - Occupational Health and Safety), and providing information to authorities?
answer:
**Consequences of Interfering with the Exercise of Powers and Duties**

Interfering with the exercise of powers and duties under Part II of the Canada Labour Code can have severe consequences. According to Section 143 of the Canada Labour Code,
"No person shall obstruct or hinder, or make a false or misleading statement either orally or in writing to (a) the Head in the exercise of his or her powers, or in the performance of his or her duties or functions, under this Part..."

This prohibition applies to anyone who attempts to hinder or obstruct the exercise of powers and duties under Part II, including the Head, external adjudicators, and members of the Board. The consequences of violating this provision can be severe, as it can lead to disciplinary action, fines, or even prosecution.

**Prohibition on Providing False Information**

Providing false or misleading information to authorities is also strictly prohibited under Section 143 of the Canada Labour Code. The provision states,
"(b) any person to whom powers, duties or functions have been delegated under subsection 140(1) or (1.1), or under an agreement entered into under subsection 140(2), who is exercising those powers or performing those duties or functions."

This prohibition applies to anyone who provides false or misleading information to delegated authorities, including those who exercise powers and duties under Part II. Providing false information can lead to serious consequences, including disciplinary action, fines, or even prosecution.

**Protection of Employees' Rights**

Section 143.1 of the Canada Labour Code also provides protection for employees who wish to provide information to authorities. The provision states,
"No person shall prevent an employee from providing information to (a) the Head in the exercise of his or her powers, or in the performance of his or her duties or functions under this Part..."

This provision ensures that employees have the right to provide information to authorities without fear of obstruction or hindrance. This protection is essential for ensuring that employees can report hazards, injuries, and illnesses without fear of reprisal.

**Consequences of Violating Section 143.1**

Violating Section 143.1 can have serious consequences, including disciplinary action, fines, or even prosecution. The provision states,
"(b) any person to whom powers, duties or functions have been delegated under subsection 140(1) or (1.1), or under an agreement entered into under subsection 140(2), who is exercising those powers or performing those duties or functions."

This provision ensures that employees who wish to provide information to authorities are protected from obstruction or hindrance. Violating this provision can lead to serious consequences, including disciplinary action, fines, or even prosecution.

question: What are the general rules regarding the disclosure of information obtained by certain individuals, such as the Head, external adjudicators, members of the Board, and others, in the exercise of their powers or performance of their duties under the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
**Disclosure of Information Under the Canada Labour Code**

The Canada Labour Code has specific rules regarding the disclosure of information obtained by certain individuals in the exercise of their powers or performance of their duties under the Code.

**General Rule**

The general rule is that
"No person to whom powers, duties or functions have been delegated under subsection 140(1) or (1.1), or under an agreement entered into under subsection 140(2), and no person who has accompanied or assisted that person in exercising those powers or performing those duties or functions may be required to give testimony in civil or administrative proceedings, other than proceedings under this Part, with regard to information obtained in exercising those powers or performing those duties or functions, except with the written permission of the Head, in which case subsection (5) does not apply to restrict the disclosure of the information."

**Head's Discretion**

The Head has discretion to grant or deny permission for disclosure of information obtained by the Head or others in the exercise of their powers or performance of their duties. The Head may consider factors such as the publication or disclosure being in the interest of occupational health and safety or the public interest.

**Exceptions**

There are exceptions to the general rule, including situations where the publication or disclosure is for the purposes of a coroner's inquiry, the administration or enforcement of a federal or provincial law, or the administration of a foreign law or international agreement.

**Confidential Communication
"No person to whom information obtained under section 141 is communicated in confidence shall divulge the name of the informant to any person except for the purposes of this Part, and no such person is competent or compellable to divulge the name of the informant before any court or other tribunal."

**Source**

The rules regarding the disclosure of information under the Canada Labour Code are outlined in section 144 of the Canada Labour Code.

question: What actions can the Head take if they believe a provision of the Part is being or has been contravened, and what are the requirements for documenting and communicating these actions?
answer:
**Subrogation and Contravention**

According to the Government Employees Compensation Act (GECA), the Head may take the following actions if they believe a provision of the Part is being or has been contravened:
"If the Head is of the opinion that a provision of this Part is being contravened or has recently been contravened, the Head may direct the employer or employee concerned, or both, to (a) terminate the contravention within the time that the officer may specify; and (b) take steps, as specified by the Head and within the time that the Head may specify, to ensure that the contravention does not continue or re-occur."

**Documentation and Communication Requirements**

The Head must provide a written version of the direction to the employer and the employee, if issued orally,
"...before the Head leaves the work place, if the Head was in the work place when the direction was issued; or (b) as soon as possible by mail, or by facsimile or other electronic means, in any other case."

Additionally, the Head must ensure that the employer posts a notice of the direction in a conspicuous place accessible to every employee, and provide a copy of the direction to the policy committee and the work place committee or the health and safety representative.

**Direction to Terminate Contravention**

If the Head directs the employer or employee to terminate the contravention, the employer must cause the use of the place, the use or operation of the machine or thing, or the performance of the activity to be discontinued, and no person shall use or operate the machine or thing, work in that place, or perform the activity until the measures directed by the Head have been taken.

**Appeals and Investigations**

If the employee refuses to comply with the direction, the Head may proceed with an investigation, which may involve the employer, the employee, and one other person. The Head must verify if there are previous or ongoing investigations in relation to the same employer that involve substantially the same issues and may combine that investigation with the investigation being conducted.

The Head shall make a decision on completion of the investigation and immediately give written notification of the decision to the employer and the employee.

question: What are the powers, duties, and functions of the Board in relation to certain sections of the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
**Powers, Duties, and Functions of the Board**

The Canada Labour Code outlines the powers, duties, and functions of the Board in various sections.

**Section 15: Powers and Duties - Regulations**

The Board has the power to make regulations of general application respecting various matters, including:

* The establishment of rules of procedure for its pre-hearing proceedings and hearings
* The use of means of telecommunication for communication among parties and the Board
* The determination of units appropriate for collective bargaining
* The certification of trade unions as bargaining agents for bargaining units
* The conduct of representation votes
* The specification of periods for receiving applications for certification or revocation of certification
* The hearing or determination of applications, complaints, questions, disputes, differences, or appeals
* The forms to be used in proceedings
* The time within which and circumstances under which the Board may exercise its powers under section 18
* The inquiry that the Board may make under subsection 34(2)
* The form in which and period during which evidence and information may be presented to the Board
* The determination of the form in which and period during which evidence as to membership, objections, or signification of employees' wishes to be represented by a trade union shall be presented
* The criteria for determining whether an employee is a member of a trade union
* The circumstances in which evidence may be received by the Board as evidence that employees wish or do not wish to have a particular trade union represent them
* The conditions for valid strike or lockout votes
* The authority of persons to act on behalf of the Board
* The manner and criteria for selecting external adjudicators
* Any other matters and things that may be incidental or conducive to the proper performance of the duties of the Board under this Act.

**Section 16: Powers of the Board**

The Board has the power to:

* Summon and enforce the attendance of witnesses and compel them to give oral or written evidence on oath and to produce documents and things as the Board deems requisite
* Order pre-hearing procedures, including pre-hearing conferences that are held in private
* Order that a hearing or pre-hearing conference be conducted using a means of telecommunication that permits the parties and the Board to communicate with each other simultaneously
* Administer oaths and solemn affirmations
* Receive and accept evidence and information on oath, affidavit, or otherwise
* Examine evidence respecting the membership of employees in a trade union seeking certification
* Examine documents forming or relating to the constitution or articles of association of a trade union or council of trade unions seeking certification
* Make such examination of records and inquiries as it deems necessary
* Compel any person to provide information or produce documents and things that may be relevant to a matter before the Board
* Require an employer to post and keep posted in appropriate places, or to transmit by any electronic means that the Board deems appropriate, any notice that it considers necessary to bring to the attention of any employees any matter relating to the proceeding
* Enter any premises of an employer where work is being or has been done by employees and inspect and view any work, material, machinery, appliances, or articles therein and interrogate any person respecting any matter that is before the Board in the proceeding
* Order a representation vote or additional representation vote to be taken among employees affected by the proceeding
* Enter on the premises of an employer for the purpose of conducting representation votes during working hours
* Authorize any person to do anything that the Board may do under paragraphs (a) to (h), (j), or (m) and report to the Board thereon
* Adjourn or postpone the proceeding from time to time
* Deferring deciding any matter, where the Board considers that the matter could be resolved by arbitration or an alternate method of resolution
* Abridging or extending the time for doing any act, filing any document, or presenting any evidence in connection with a proceeding
* Extending the time limits set out in this Act for instituting a proceeding
* Amending or permitting the amendment of any document filed in connection with the proceeding
* Adding a party to the proceeding at any stage of the proceeding
* Deciding for all purposes of this Part any question that may arise in the proceeding

**Section 145.1: Appeal of Direction**

The Board has all of the powers, duties and functions of the Minister and the Head under this Part, except for those referred to in section 130, subsections 135(6), 137.1(1) to (2.1) and (7) to (9), 137.2(4), 138(1) to (2) and (4) to (6), section 139, subsections 140(1) to (2) and (4) and 144(1), section 146.01, subsection 149(1), sections 152 and 155 and subsections 156.1(1), 157(3) and 159(2).
