MATERNITY LEAVE (UNPAID) As a pregnant employee, you are entitled to up to 17 weeks of maternity leave. You must also give your employer written notice at least 4 weeks before starting your leave. This notice must advise your employer of the length of the leave. If your child was not born during the 17 weeks of your maternity leave, the maternity leave is extended until the date of the birth. question: What are the responsibilities of an employee who is pregnant or nursing in terms of notifying their employer and providing documentation regarding their leave of absence?
answer:
**Employee Responsibilities: Notification and Documentation**

According to the Canada Labour Code, an employee who is pregnant or nursing has specific responsibilities regarding notification and documentation of their leave of absence.

**Notification of Employer**

An employee who intends to interrupt their maternity or parental leave to return to work as a result of the hospitalization of their child must provide their employer with a notice in writing of the interruption as soon as possible. (
"Section 207.2 (1) An employee who intends to interrupt their maternity or parental leave in order to return to work as a result of the hospitalization of his or her child shall provide the employer with a notice in writing of the interruption as soon as possible.")

This notice must be provided at least 4 weeks before starting the leave, and it must advise the employer of the length of the leave. (
"You must provide your employer with a certificate from a health care practitioner confirming that you are pregnant. You must also give your employer written notice at least 4 weeks before starting your leave.")

**Providing Documentation**

An employee who is pregnant or nursing must provide their employer with a certificate issued by a health care practitioner of their choice indicating that they are unable to work by reason of the pregnancy or nursing and indicating the duration of that inability. (
"An employee who is pregnant or nursing is entitled to and shall be granted a leave of absence during the period from the beginning of the pregnancy to the end of the twenty-fourth week following the birth, if she provides the employer with a certificate issued by a health care practitioner of her choice indicating that she is unable to work by reason of the pregnancy or nursing and indicating the duration of that inability.")

Additionally, an employee who has been reassigned or has a modified job function must provide their employer with a new certificate if there is a change in the duration of the risk or in the inability as indicated in the original certificate. (
"Section 205.2 An employee whose job functions have been modified, who has been reassigned or who is on a leave of absence shall give at least two weeks’ notice in writing to the employer of any change in the duration of the risk or in the inability as indicated in the certificate issued by a health care practitioner, unless there is a valid reason why that notice cannot be given, and the notice must be accompanied by a new certificate.")

These responsibilities are outlined in the Canada Labour Code, specifically in sections 205.1, 205.2, 207.2, and 132.

"If, during the period of 17 weeks following the date of confinement, the child who was born is hospitalized, the period is extended by the number of weeks during which the child is hospitalized."

**Maximum Aggregate Leave Limits**

The Canada Labour Code sets out the maximum aggregate leave limits for multiple employees and for a single employee in respect of the same birth.

**Multiple Employees**

For multiple employees, the maximum aggregate leave limit is 86 weeks, as stated in section 206.2 of the Canada Labour Code:
"The aggregate amount of leave that may be taken by more than one employee under sections 206 and 206.1 in respect of the same birth shall not exceed 86 weeks..."

**Single Employee**

For a single employee, the maximum aggregate leave limit is 78 weeks, as stated in section 206.2 of the Canada Labour Code:
"...the aggregate amount of leave that may be taken by one employee under those sections in respect of the same birth shall not exceed 78 weeks."

**Combining Maternity and Parental Leave**

It's worth noting that the maximum aggregate leave limits apply to both maternity and parental leave. For example, if a single employee takes 17 weeks of maternity leave and 63 weeks of parental leave, the total leave taken would not exceed 78 weeks.

**Shared Parental Leave**

If both parents share the parental leave, the maximum aggregate leave limit increases to 86 weeks. However, the individual parental leave limits remain the same, with a maximum of 63 weeks for one employee and 71 weeks for two employees sharing the leave.

question: What is the purpose of the leave of absence provided for in the CLC, and under what conditions can an employee take this leave?
answer:
**Purpose of the Leave of Absence**

The purpose of the leave of absence provided for in the Canada Labour Code (CLC) is to allow employees to take time off from work to care for a family member who is critically ill or to take part in military operations or activities.

**Conditions for Taking the Leave**

According to Section 247.5 of the CLC, an employee who is a member of the reserve force and has completed at least three consecutive months of continuous employment with an employer is entitled to a leave of absence to take part in the following operations or activities:

* An operation in Canada or abroad, including preparation, training, rest or travel from or to the employee's residence, that is designated by the Minister of National Defence;
* An activity set out in the regulations;
* Canadian Armed Forces military skills training;
* Training that the employee is ordered to take under paragraph 33(2)(a) of the National Defence Act;
* Duties that the employee is called out on service to perform under paragraph 33(2)(b) of the National Defence Act;
* Service in aid of a civil power for which the employee is called out under section 275 of the National Defence Act; or
* Treatment, recovery or rehabilitation in respect of a physical or mental health problem that results from service in an operation or activity referred to in this subsection.

The leave can be taken under Section 206.3 of the CLC for employees who are caring for a critically ill family member, but the conditions for taking this leave are different.

**Caring for a Critically Ill Family Member**

According to Section 206.3 of the CLC, an employee who is a family member of a critically ill child is entitled to a leave of absence to care for or support that child if a health care practitioner has issued a certificate that states that the child is a critically ill child and requires the care or support of one or more of their family members. The leave can be taken for up to 37 weeks.

In contrast, an employee who is a family member of a critically ill adult is entitled to a leave of absence to care for or support that adult if a health care practitioner has issued a certificate that states that the adult is a critically ill adult and requires the care or support of one or more of their family members. The leave can be taken for up to 17 weeks.

**Notice Requirements**

Employees who take a leave of absence under the CLC are required to provide their employer with notice of the reasons for the leave and the length of the leave that they intend to take. The notice must be provided in writing and must be given as soon as possible.

**Prohibition on Discrimination**

The CLC prohibits employers from dismissing, suspending, laying off, demoting or disciplining an employee because the employee is pregnant or has applied for leave of absence in accordance with the CLC. This prohibition also applies to employees who have taken a leave of absence under any of sections 206.3 to 206.9.

answer:
**Section 206.4 of the Canada Labour Code**

**Entitlement to Leave**

An employee is entitled to take a leave of absence under section 206.4 of the Canada Labour Code if they are a family member of a critically ill child or adult. The leave is granted to care for or support the critically ill child or adult.
"Every employee who is a family member of a critically ill child is entitled to and shall be granted a leave of absence from employment of up to 37 weeks in order to care for or support that child if a health care practitioner has issued a certificate that (a) states that the child is a critically ill child and requires the care or support of one or more of their family members; and (b) sets out the period during which the child requires that care or support."

Alternatively, an employee is entitled to take a leave of absence under section 206.4 if they are a family member of a critically ill adult.

* Leave for work-related illness or injury (unpaid)

* Leave for critical illness (up to 17 weeks per year)

* Leave related to a critical illness or death/disappearance of a family member

* New Year's Day
* Good Friday

question: What are the circumstances under which an employee is entitled to a leave of absence from employment according to the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
**Types of Leaves Entitled to Under the Canada Labour Code**

The Canada Labour Code outlines various circumstances under which an employee is entitled to a leave of absence from employment. The following sections provide insight into these circumstances:

**Medical Leave (CLC-239)**

An employee is entitled to a medical leave of absence from employment for up to 27 weeks due to personal illness or injury, organ or tissue donation, medical appointments during working hours, or quarantine. (
"Every employee is entitled to and shall be granted a medical leave of absence from employment of up to 27 weeks...")

The employee earns pay for the first three days of the leave, and subsequent days are paid at their regular rate of wages for their normal hours of work. (
"If the employee has completed three consecutive months of continuous employment with the employer, the employee is entitled to the first three days of the leave with pay at their regular rate of wages...")

**Personal Leave (CLC-206.6)**

An employee is entitled to a leave of absence for up to five days in every calendar year for various reasons, including carrying out responsibilities related to the health or care of family members, education of family members under 18, addressing urgent matters, attending a citizenship ceremony, and other reasons prescribed by regulation. (
"Every employee is entitled to and shall be granted a leave of absence from employment of up to five days in every calendar year...")

**Leave for Court or Jury Duty (CLC-206.9)**

An employee is entitled to a leave of absence from employment to attend court as a witness, juror, or participate in a jury selection process. (
"Every employee is entitled to and shall be granted a leave of absence from employment to attend court to...")

**Leave for Military Service (CLC-247.5)**

An employee who is a member of the reserve force is entitled to a leave of absence from employment for up to 24 months for military service, including training, operations, and other activities. (
"An employee who is a member of the reserve force and has completed at least three consecutive months of continuous employment with an employer — or a shorter period that is prescribed for a class of employees to which the employee belongs — is entitled to and shall be granted a leave of absence from employment to take part in the following operations or activities...")

**Leave for Family Responsibilities (CLC-206.6)**

An employee is entitled to a leave of absence for up to five days in every calendar year for carrying out responsibilities related to the health or care of family members, education of family members under 18, addressing urgent matters, attending a citizenship ceremony, and other reasons prescribed by regulation. (
"Every employee is entitled to and shall be granted a leave of absence from employment of up to five days in every calendar year for...")

question: What are the general obligations of an employee who intends to take a leave of absence under section 206 or 206.1 of the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
**General Obligations of an Employee**

The Canada Labour Code outlines the general obligations of an employee who intends to take a leave of absence under section 206 or 206.1.

**Notice Requirements**

According to section 207 of the Canada Labour Code,
"Every employee who intends to take a leave of absence from employment under section 206 or 206.1 shall (a) unless there is a valid reason for not doing so, give at least four weeks notice in writing to the employer before the day on which the leave is to begin; and (b) inform the employer in writing of the length of leave intended to be taken."

This means that employees must provide their employer with at least four weeks' notice in writing before taking a leave of absence under section 206 or 206.1, unless there is a valid reason for not doing so.

**Change in Leave Length**

Additionally, employees must provide their employer with notice in writing of any change in the length of the leave they intend to take. According to section 207 of the Canada Labour Code,
"Every employee who intends to take or who is on a leave of absence from employment under section 206 or 206.1 shall provide the employer with notice in writing of at least four weeks of any change in the length of leave intended to be taken, unless there is a valid reason why that notice cannot be given, in which case the employee shall provide the employer with notice in writing as soon as possible."

This ensures that employees and employers are aware of any changes to the length of the leave, and that the employer can plan accordingly.

**Documentation and Return to Work**

In some cases, employers may require employees to provide documentation in support of the reasons for the leave taken under section 206.4, 206.5 or 206.9. According to section 207.3 of the Canada Labour Code,
"The employer may require the employee to provide documentation in support of the reasons for the leave taken under section 206.4, 206.5 or 206.9 and of any change in the length of leave that the employee intends to take."

Additionally, if an employee who takes a leave of more than four weeks under any of sections 206.3 to 206.5 wishes to shorten the length of the leave but does not provide the employer with four weeks' notice, the employer may postpone the employee's return to work for a period of up to four weeks after the day on which the employee informs the employer of the new end date of the leave. According to section 207.3 of the Canada Labour Code,
"If an employee who takes a leave of more than four weeks under any of sections 206.3 to 206.5 wishes to shorten the length of the leave but does not provide the employer with four weeks’ notice, the employer may postpone the employee’s return to work for a period of up to four weeks after the day on which the employee informs the employer of the new end date of the leave."

question: What are the requirements for an employee who needs to interrupt their leave of absence for certain reasons, such as a work-related illness or injury, or other specified reasons?
answer:
**Interrupting Leave of Absence**

**General Requirements**

An employee who needs to interrupt their leave of absence for certain reasons, such as a work-related illness or injury, or other specified reasons, must provide their employer with a written notice of the interruption before or as soon as possible after it begins.
"An employee who intends to interrupt their leave under subsection 206.1(2.4) or 207.02(1) shall provide the employer with a notice in writing of the interruption before or as soon as possible after it begins."

**Notice to Employer**

The employee must provide the employer with a written notice of the day on which they intend to resume their leave before or as soon as possible after that day.
"The employee shall provide the employer with a notice in writing of the day on which they resume their leave before or as soon as possible after that day."

**Resumption of Leave**

The interrupted leave resumes immediately after the interruption ends.

"The interrupted leave resumes immediately after the interruption ends." (CLC-207.02)

**Work-Related Illness or Injury**

For an employee who interrupted their leave in order to be absent due to a reason referred to in subsection 239.1(1), section 209.1 applies to the extent that it is not inconsistent with subsections 239.1(3) and (4).
"Except to the extent that it is inconsistent with subsections 239.1(3) and (4), section 209.1 applies to an employee who interrupted the leave in order to be absent due to a reason referred to in subsection 239.1(1)."

**Other Specified Reasons**

For an employee who interrupted their leave in order to be absent due to a reason referred to in subsection 239(1), section 209.1 applies to the extent that it is not inconsistent with subsection 239(7).
"Except to the extent that it is inconsistent with subsection 239(7), section 209.1 applies to an employee who interrupted the leave in order to be absent due to a reason referred to in subsection 239(1)."

If an employee needs to interrupt their maternity or parental leave to care for a hospitalized child, they must provide their employer with a written notice as soon as possible.

If the employer refuses the interruption or does not advise the employee within the week, the leave under section 206 or 206.1 is extended by the number of weeks during which the child is hospitalized.

**Resuming Maternity or Parental Leave**

"An employee who intends to return to their maternity or parental leave after an interruption shall, as soon as possible, advise the employer in writing of the date on which the maternity or parental leave is to resume."

This section indicates that employers may request documentation to support the employee's leave, including the reasons for the leave and any changes to the length of the leave.

**Change in Length of Leave**

Section 207.3 also states that
"If an employee who takes a leave of more than four weeks under any of sections 206.3 to 206.5 wishes to shorten the length of the leave but does not provide the employer with four weeks’ notice, the employer may postpone the employee’s return to work for a period of up to four weeks after the day on which the employee informs the employer of the new end date of the leave."

This section outlines the process for changing the length of a leave, including the requirement for four weeks' notice for leaves of more than four weeks.

question: What are the rights of an employee who takes a leave of absence from employment under the Canada Labour Code regarding their job and benefits when they return to work?
answer:
**Right to Reinstatement in the Same Position**

According to Section 209.1 of the Canada Labour Code,
"Every employee who takes or is required to take a leave of absence from employment under this Division is entitled to be reinstated in the position that the employee occupied when the leave of absence from employment commenced, and every employer of such an employee shall, on the expiration of any such leave, reinstate the employee in that position."

This means that employees who take a leave of absence under the Canada Labour Code have the right to be reinstated in their previous position when they return to work.

**Right to Comparable Position**

If an employer cannot reinstate an employee in the same position, the employer must offer a comparable position with the same wages and benefits and in the same location. (CLC-209.1(2))

**Right to Accrue Benefits**

The pension, health and disability benefits, and seniority of an employee who takes a leave of absence under the Canada Labour Code shall accumulate during the entire period of the leave. (CLC-209.2(1))

**Right to Continued Contributions**

An employer who pays contributions in respect of a benefit referred to in subsection (1) shall continue to pay those contributions during an employee's leave of absence under this Division in at least the same proportion as if the employee were not on leave. (CLC-209.2(2.1))

**Right to Deemed Continuous Employment**

For the purposes of calculating benefits of an employee who takes or is required to take a leave of absence from employment under this Division, other than benefits referred to in subsection (1), employment on the employee's return to work shall be deemed to be continuous with employment before the employee's absence. (CLC-209.2(4))

**Protection from Discrimination**

The Canada Labour Code also prohibits employers from discriminating against employees who take a leave of absence under the Code. (CLC-209.21(1))

question: What happens to an employee's pension, health and disability benefits, and seniority during a leave of absence under this Division of the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
**Pension, Health and Disability Benefits**

According to Section 209.2 of the Canada Labour Code,
"The pension, health and disability benefits and the seniority of any employee who takes or is required to take a leave of absence from employment under this Division shall accumulate during the entire period of the leave."

This means that an employee's pension, health and disability benefits, and seniority will continue to accrue during their leave of absence, and will not be affected by the leave.

**Seniority**

The same section also states that
"...employment on the employee’s return to work shall be deemed to be continuous with employment before the employee’s absence."

This implies that an employee's seniority will continue to accrue during their leave of absence, and will be taken into account when calculating their seniority upon their return to work.

**Contribution to Pension Plans and Other Employee Benefits**

It is worth noting that an employee's employer is not required to contribute to pension plans or other employee benefits during a leave of absence under this Division. (LABOUR-STANDARDS-5_20)

However, this does not affect the employee's pension, health and disability benefits, and seniority, which continue to accrue during the leave.

question: What protections are afforded to employees who are pregnant or taking a leave of absence under the Code, in terms of their employment status and benefits?
answer:
**Protection from Termination**

According to Section 208 of the Canada Labour Code,
"...no employer shall require an employee to take a leave of absence from employment because the employee is pregnant." This provision protects pregnant employees from being forced to take a leave of absence due to their pregnancy.

**Right to Reassignment or Leave**

Section 205.1 of the Code states that an employee who is pregnant or nursing is entitled to and shall be granted a leave of absence during the period from the beginning of the pregnancy to the end of the twenty-fourth week following the birth, if she provides the employer with a certificate issued by a health care practitioner of her choice (CLC-205.1).

**Protection from Discrimination**

Section 209.21 of the Code states that
"No employer shall dismiss, suspend, lay off, demote or discipline an employee because the employee is pregnant or has applied for leave of absence in accordance with this Division..." This provision protects pregnant employees from being discriminated against in the workplace.

**Continuation of Employment Status**

Section 132 of the Code states that
"The employee, whether or not she has been reassigned to another job, is deemed to continue to hold the job that she held at the time she ceased to perform her job functions and shall continue to receive the wages and benefits that are attached to that job for the period during which she does not perform the job."

**Benefits and Income-Replacement Schemes**

Section 209.21 of the Code states that
"...an employee who takes a leave of absence under this Division is entitled to benefits under the scheme or plan on the same terms as any employee who is absent from work for health-related reasons and is entitled to benefits under the scheme or plan." This provision ensures that pregnant employees continue to receive benefits and income replacement under their employment insurance plan.

**Conclusive Proof of Certificate**

Section 209.22 of the Code states that
"A certificate issued by a health care practitioner under this Division is conclusive proof of the statements contained in it." This provision ensures that the certificate issued by the health care practitioner is a reliable and binding document.

question: What are the conditions and entitlements for an employee to take a leave of absence in the event of the death of a member of their immediate family or a family member?
answer:
**Leave Entitlements**

According to the Canada Labour Code, Section 210, every employee is entitled to and shall be granted a leave of absence from employment of up to 10 days in the event of the death of a member of their immediate family or a family member.

**Conditions for Leave Entitlement**

The leave can be taken during the period that begins on the day on which the death occurs and ends six weeks after the latest of the days on which any funeral, burial, or memorial service of the deceased person occurs.

**Extension of Leave**

At the request of the employee, the employer may extend, in writing, the period during which the leave of absence from employment may be taken.

**Notice to Employer**

Every employee who takes the leave of absence shall, as soon as possible, provide the employer with written notice of the beginning of any period of leave of absence and of the length of that leave.

**Bereavement Leave with Pay**

If the employee has completed three consecutive months of continuous employment with the employer, the employee is entitled to the first three days of the leave with pay at their regular rate of wages for their normal hours of work.

**Source:**
CLC-210, Section 210

**Definitions**

Section 211 of the Canada Labour Code defines two key terms: "joint planning committee" and "redundant employee".

A redundant employee is defined as

answer:
**Obligations of an Employer Planning a Group Termination**

An employer who plans to terminate the employment of a group of 50 or more employees within a certain timeframe has several obligations.

**Notice Requirements**

The employer must give notice to the Labour Program's Head of Compliance and Enforcement in writing at least 16 weeks before the termination of employment is to take effect. This notice must be given to the Minister of Employment and Social Development Canada (ESDC), the Canada Employment Insurance Commission, and any union representing the affected employees, or to the employees if they are not represented by a union. The notice must also be posted in a visible place within the workplace in which the employees are employed. [CLC-212(1)]

**Information to be Provided**

The notice must include the following information:

*   The name of the employer location or establishment where the termination is to take place
*   The nature of the industry of the employer
*   The number of affected employees (both unionized and non-unionized)
*   The date or dates of termination of employment
*   Union information, if applicable
*   The reason(s) for the group termination of employment [CLC-212(3)]

**Additional Requirements**

The employer must also establish a joint planning committee consisting of at least four members, with at least half of the members appointed as representatives of the redundant employees and the rest appointed as representatives of the employer. [CLC-214(2)]

**Cooperation with the Commission**

The employer must cooperate with the Canada Employment Insurance Commission to facilitate the re-establishment in employment of redundant employees. [CLC-213(1)]

question: What are the key responsibilities of an employer who gives notice of termination to the Head under section 212 of the Canada Labour Code, particularly in relation to redundant employees and the Canada Employment Insurance Commission?
answer:
**Key Responsibilities of an Employer**

The employer has several key responsibilities when giving notice of termination to the Head under section 212 of the Canada Labour Code.

**Providing Information to the Canada Employment Insurance Commission**

The employer must give the Canada Employment Insurance Commission any information requested by it for the purpose of assisting any redundant employee. This is stated in section 213(1) of the Canada Labour Code:
"An employer who gives notice to the Head under section 212 and any trade union to which a copy of that notice is given must give the Canada Employment Insurance Commission any information requested by it for the purpose of assisting any redundant employee..."

**Cooperating with the Commission**

The employer must also cooperate with the Commission to facilitate the re-establishment in employment of the redundant employee. This is also stated in section 213(1) of the Canada Labour Code:
"An employer who gives notice to the Head under section 212 and any trade union to which a copy of that notice is given must give the Canada Employment Insurance Commission any information requested by it for the purpose of assisting any redundant employee and must cooperate with the Commission to facilitate the re-establishment in employment of that employee."

**Providing Information to the Redundant Employee**

The employer must give each redundant employee a statement in writing setting out, as at the date of the statement, their vacation benefits, wages, severance pay, and any other benefits and pay arising from their employment with the employer. This is stated in section 213(2) of the Canada Labour Code:
"An employer who gives notice to the Head under section 212 shall give each redundant employee, as soon as possible after the notice is so given but in any case not later than two weeks before the date of the termination of the employment of the employee, a statement in writing setting out, as at the date of the statement, his vacation benefits, wages, severance pay and any other benefits and pay arising from his employment with that employer."

**General Obligations**

The employer must also comply with the requirements of section 212 of the Canada Labour Code, which includes giving notice to the Head at least 16 weeks before the date of termination of the employment of the employee in the group whose employment is first to be terminated.

question: What are the requirements for the appointment and first sitting of the members of a joint planning committee under the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
**Appointment Requirements**

The Canada Labour Code sets out the requirements for the appointment of members of a joint planning committee. According to Section 215(1),
"Where all redundant employees are represented by a trade union or trade unions, each trade union is entitled to appoint at least one member of the joint planning committee as a representative of the redundant employees it represents."

This means that if all redundant employees are represented by a trade union, each trade union must appoint at least one member to the joint planning committee. This is a requirement for the appointment of employee representatives on the committee.

**Appointment of Employer Representatives**

In addition to employee representatives, the employer is also entitled to appoint representatives to the joint planning committee. According to Section 215(5),
"An employer is entitled to appoint, as his representatives on a joint planning committee, a number of members not exceeding the number of members to be appointed to the committee pursuant to subsections (1), (2) and (3)."

This means that the employer can appoint a number of representatives to the joint planning committee that is not more than the number of employee representatives appointed. The employer's representatives are also entitled to participate in the committee's decision-making process.

**First Sitting Requirements**

The Canada Labour Code also sets out the requirements for the first sitting of the joint planning committee. According to Section 216,
"The members of a joint planning committee must be appointed and must convene for their first sitting within two weeks after the date of the notice given to the Head under section 212."

This means that the joint planning committee must be appointed and hold its first sitting within two weeks of the date of the notice given to the Head under Section 212. This ensures that the committee is established and can begin its work as soon as possible after the notice is given.

question: What happens if a trade union or redundant employees fail to appoint a member to a joint planning committee as required, and how can the issue be resolved?
answer:
**Failure to Appoint a Member to a Joint Planning Committee**

If a trade union or redundant employees fail to appoint a member to a joint planning committee as required, the Head may take action to resolve the issue.

**Section 217 of the Canada Labour Code
"If a trade union fails, or redundant employees fail, to appoint a member to a joint planning committee as provided in sections 214 and 215, the Head may, on application of any redundant employee, appoint a member to the committee in lieu of that trade union or those employees, as the case may be, and that member is a representative of the redundant employees represented by the trade union or of the redundant employees who failed to appoint the member, as the case may be."

In this case, the Head has the authority to appoint a member to the joint planning committee in lieu of the trade union or redundant employees who failed to appoint a representative. This member will represent the interests of the redundant employees who failed to appoint a representative.

**Resolution of the Issue**

The issue can be resolved by the Head appointing a member to the joint planning committee in lieu of the trade union or redundant employees who failed to appoint a representative. This ensures that the joint planning committee has a representative from the redundant employees, even if the trade union or employees failed to appoint one.

question: What are the key aspects of how a joint planning committee is structured and operates according to the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
**Structure of a Joint Planning Committee**

A joint planning committee is established by an employer who gives notice to the Head under section 212 of the Canada Labour Code. The committee must consist of at least four members, with at least half of the members being appointed as representatives of the redundant employees and the rest being appointed as representatives of the employer.

**Membership of a Joint Planning Committee**

According to section 214 of the Canada Labour Code,
"At least half of the members of a joint planning committee shall be appointed, in accordance with subsections 215(1), (2) and (3), as representatives of the redundant employees and the rest of the members shall be appointed, in accordance with subsection 215(5), as representatives of the employer."

**Co-Chairpersons of a Joint Planning Committee**

The members of a joint planning committee elect two co-chairpersons, one being a representative of the redundant employees and the other being a representative of the employer. The co-chairpersons are responsible for fixing the time and place of the committee's sittings and notifying the members of the time and place so fixed.

**Procedure of a Joint Planning Committee**

A joint planning committee may determine its own procedure, subject to the requirements of the Canada Labour Code. The committee must elect co-chairpersons, fix the time and place of its sittings, and notify the members of the time and place so fixed. A majority of the members of the committee in office, at least half of which majority are representatives of the redundant employees, constitutes a quorum.

**Quorum and Decision-Making**

A decision or other act or thing taken or done by a majority of the members of a joint planning committee present at a sitting of the committee, if the members present constitute a quorum, shall be deemed to have been taken or done by the committee.

**Cooperation and Assistance**

The employer and any trade union or redundant employees who appointed the members of a joint planning committee must cooperate with and assist the committee in developing an adjustment program, as stated in section 221 of the Canada Labour Code.

**Timeframe for Appointment**

The members of a joint planning committee must be appointed and must convene for their first sitting within two weeks after the date of the notice given to the Head under section 212, as stated in section 216 of the Canada Labour Code.

question: What are the protections and considerations given to members of a joint planning committee in terms of their work and compensation?
answer:
**Protection of Members' Time**

Members of a joint planning committee are entitled to
"...such time from work as is necessary to attend sittings of the committee or to carry out any other functions as such a member..." This provision ensures that members are not penalized for their participation in the committee's work.

**Compensation for Members' Work**

The time spent by members in carrying out their functions as members is deemed to have been spent at their work, which means that it will be taken into account when calculating their wages (CLC-220). This provision provides a safeguard for members, ensuring that they are not unfairly compensated for their time.

**Procedure for Determining Compensation**

The joint planning committee may determine its own procedure, but it must ensure that members are fairly compensated for their time (CLC-219). The committee's decision on compensation must be made by a majority of the members present at a sitting, with at least half of the majority being representatives of the redundant employees (CLC-219).

**Quorum and Decision-Making**

A majority of the members present at a sitting, with at least half of the majority being representatives of the redundant employees, constitutes a quorum (CLC-219). This ensures that decisions made by the committee are representative of the interests of all parties involved.

**Protection from Vacancy**

A vacancy in the membership of a joint planning committee does not invalidate the constitution of the committee or impair the right of the members of the committee in office to act, if the number of those members is not less than a quorum (CLC-219). This provision provides a safeguard for the committee's continuity and ensures that its decisions are not undermined by vacancies.

**Head's Role**

The Head may
"...monitor and, on request, assist in the establishment and operation of a joint planning committee..." This provision highlights the Head's role in supporting the committee's work and ensuring that it operates effectively.

question: What is the main objective of a joint planning committee when developing an adjustment program in the context of employment termination?
answer:
**Main Objective of a Joint Planning Committee**

The main objective of a joint planning committee is to develop an adjustment program that aims to
"...eliminate the necessity for the termination of employment; or (b) minimize the impact of the termination of employment on the redundant employees and to assist those employees in obtaining other employment."

**Source:** Section 221(1) of the Canada Labour Code

This objective is explicitly stated in the text, highlighting the committee's primary goal of finding alternative solutions to employment termination. The committee's efforts should focus on eliminating the need for termination or minimizing its impact on employees, while also assisting them in finding new employment opportunities.

**Scope of Matters Considered**

The joint planning committee may only consider matters that are normally the subject-matter of collective agreement in relation to employment termination. This means that the committee's focus is on addressing the practical and procedural aspects of employment termination, rather than exploring broader social or economic implications.

**Source:** Section 221(2) of the Canada Labour Code

This section emphasizes the committee's scope of work, ensuring that their efforts are focused on finding practical solutions to employment termination, rather than venturing into areas that may not be directly related to the collective agreement.

**Cooperation and Reasonable Effort**

The members of the joint planning committee are expected to cooperate and make every reasonable effort to develop an adjustment program as expeditiously as possible. This section highlights the importance of collaboration and efficiency in the committee's work, ensuring that they can effectively address the challenges of employment termination.

**Source:** Section 221(3) of the Canada Labour Code

This section underscores the committee's responsibility to work together and make a concerted effort to develop an adjustment program, demonstrating their commitment to finding solutions to employment termination.

answer:
**Application for Arbitrator**

Members of a joint planning committee can apply for the appointment of an arbitrator in relation to the development of an adjustment program for redundant employees under the following circumstances:

**Section 223(1)
"Where all members of a joint planning committee who are representatives of the redundant employees agree to do so or where all members of a joint planning committee who are representatives of the employer agree to do so, those members may, after six weeks from the date of the notice to the Minister under section 212, apply jointly to the Minister for the appointment of an arbitrator if (a) the committee has not then completed developing an adjustment program; or (b) the committee has completed developing an adjustment program, but those members are not satisfied with the program or any part of the program."

The first scenario is when the committee has not completed developing an adjustment program, and the second scenario is when the committee has completed developing an adjustment program but is not satisfied with it. This indicates that the application for an arbitrator can be made when there is a dispute or disagreement regarding the adjustment program.

question: What is the role of an arbitrator appointed under section 224 of the Canada Labour Code, and what are their powers in relation to resolving disputes and assisting in the development of an adjustment program?
answer:
**Role of an Arbitrator under Section 224**

The role of an arbitrator appointed under section 224 of the Canada Labour Code is to assist the joint planning committee in the development of an adjustment program and to resolve any matters in dispute respecting the adjustment program.

According to section 224(1), the Minister may appoint an arbitrator to assist the joint planning committee in the development of an adjustment program and to resolve any matters in dispute respecting the adjustment program.

**Powers of an Arbitrator**

The arbitrator has several powers in relation to resolving disputes and assisting in the development of an adjustment program.

The arbitrator may "consider the matters set out in the statement" (section 224(4)(a)) and render a decision thereon within four weeks after receiving the statement or such longer period as the Minister may specify.

The arbitrator may also "administer oaths and solemn affirmations" (section 224(6)(b)) and
"...receive and accept such evidence and information on oath, affidavit or otherwise as the arbitrator sees fit..."(c)).

Furthermore, the arbitrator may
"...make such examination of documents containing personal information relating to any redundant employee and such inquiries relating to any redundant employee as the arbitrator deems necessary..."(d)).

The arbitrator may also
"...require an employer to post and keep posted in appropriate places any notice that the arbitrator considers necessary to bring to the attention of any redundant employees any matter relating to the proceeding..."(e)).

**Restrictions on the Arbitrator's Powers**

The arbitrator may not
"...review the decision of the employer to terminate the employment of the redundant employees..."(a)) or "delay the termination of employment of the redundant employees" (section 224(5)(b)).

**Duty of the Arbitrator**

The arbitrator has a duty to assist the joint planning committee in the development of an adjustment program and to render a decision within four weeks after receiving the statement or such longer period as the Minister may specify.

The arbitrator must also
"...send a copy of the decision with the reasons therefor to the joint planning committee and to the Minister."(c)).

question: What type of regulatory actions can the Governor in Council take under this Division of the Canada Labour Code, and what are some examples of the regulations that can be made?
answer:
**Regulatory Actions Under Division IX**

The Governor in Council can take the following regulatory actions under Division IX of the Canada Labour Code:

### Exemptions and Exclusions

The Governor in Council may make regulations to exempt employers from the application of this Division in respect of the termination of employment of employees employed on a seasonal or irregular basis.

### Group Termination of Employment

The Governor in Council may make regulations requiring employers employing employees in a particular occupational classification, in a particular industry or in an industrial establishment that is within an area or region described in the regulations, to comply with the provisions of this Division in respect of terminations of employment of groups of employees numbering less than fifty but greater than a number prescribed in the regulations.

### Notice Requirements

The Governor in Council may prescribe information to be set out in a notice referred to in subsection 212(1).

### Lay-off Exceptions

The Governor in Council may prescribe circumstances in which a lay-off of an employee shall not be deemed to be a termination of his employment by his employer.

**Examples of Regulations**

The Governor in Council may make regulations to carry out the purposes and provisions of Division IX, including:

* Exemptions from the application of this Division in respect of the termination of employment of employees employed on a seasonal or irregular basis
* Requirements for employers to comply with the provisions of this Division in respect of terminations of employment of groups of employees
* Information to be set out in a notice referred to in subsection 212(1)
* Circumstances in which a lay-off of an employee shall not be deemed to be a termination of his employment by his employer

**Source:**

question: Under what circumstances can the Minister waive the application of a provision in the CLC related to industrial establishments?
answer:
**Waiver of Application of Division**

The Minister may waive the application of a provision in the CLC related to industrial establishments under certain circumstances.

**Section 228: Waiver of Application**

The Minister may, by order and subject to any terms or conditions specified in the order, waive the application of this Division, or any provision thereof, in respect of any industrial establishment or of any class of employees therein specified in the order if it is shown to the satisfaction of the Minister that the application of this Division, or any provision thereof, as the case may be, in respect of any industrial establishment would be or is:
"...unduly prejudicial to the interests of the employees therein or to any class of employees therein..."
"...unduly prejudicial to the interests of the employer of those employees..."
* "seriously detrimental to the operation of the industrial establishment" (CLC-228(c))
"...not necessary, because measures for the assistance of redundant employees at that establishment that are substantially the same or to the same effect as the measures established by this Division or that provision, as the case may be, have been established by collective agreement or otherwise."

**Source:** CLC-228

**Analysis:** The Minister's power to waive the application of a provision in the CLC related to industrial establishments is subject to certain conditions. The Minister must be satisfied that the application of the provision would be unduly prejudicial to the interests of the employees, the employer, or the operation of the industrial establishment. Alternatively, the Minister must be satisfied that measures for the assistance of redundant employees have been established through collective agreement or otherwise, making the provision not necessary.

question: Under what conditions can sections related to termination of employment not apply to redundant employees represented by a trade union?
answer:
**Conditions for Exemption from Termination of Employment Sections**

**Section 229(1)
"Sections 214 to 226 do not apply in respect of any redundant employees who are represented by a trade union if the trade union and the employer are bound by a collective agreement containing (a) provisions that (i) specify procedures by which any matters relating to the termination of employment in the industrial establishment at which those employees are employed may be negotiated and finally settled, or (ii) are intended to minimize the impact of termination of employment on the employees represented by the trade union and to assist those employees in obtaining other employment; and (b) provisions that specify that those sections do not apply in respect of the employees represented by the trade union."

The conditions for exemption from termination of employment sections are met when the trade union and the employer are bound by a collective agreement that:

* Specifies procedures for negotiating and settling matters related to termination of employment
* Is intended to minimize the impact of termination on employees and assist them in obtaining other employment
* Explicitly states that sections 214 to 226 do not apply to employees represented by the trade union.

**Section 229(2)
"Sections 214 to 226 do not apply in respect of any redundant employees who are represented by a trade union if the termination of the employment of those employees is the result of technological change as defined in subsection 51(1) and sections 52, 54 and 55 apply or would, but for subsection 51(2), apply to the trade union and the employer."

In addition to the conditions outlined in section 229(1), sections 214 to 226 also do not apply to redundant employees represented by a trade union if the termination of their employment is the result of technological change. This exemption applies when the termination is the result of technological change, and sections 52, 54, and 55 would apply to the trade union and the employer.

question: What are the requirements for an employer to terminate an employee's employment in accordance with the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
**Termination Requirements under the Canada Labour Code**

The Canada Labour Code sets out specific requirements for employers to terminate an employee's employment. According to Section 230 of the Canada Labour Code, an employer must give an employee
"...notice in writing of the employer’s intention to terminate their employment on a date specified in the notice, at least the applicable number of weeks set out in subsection (1.1) before that date..."

**Notice Period**

The notice period varies depending on the length of continuous employment with the employer. The applicable number of weeks is as follows:

* Two weeks if the employee has completed at least three consecutive months of continuous employment
* Three weeks if the employee has completed at least three consecutive years of continuous employment
* Four weeks if the employee has completed at least four consecutive years of continuous employment
* Five weeks if the employee has completed at least five consecutive years of continuous employment
* Six weeks if the employee has completed at least six consecutive years of continuous employment
* Seven weeks if the employee has completed at least seven consecutive years of continuous employment
* Eight weeks if the employee has completed at least eight consecutive years of continuous employment (CLC-230).

**Severance Pay**

In addition to notice, an employer must also provide severance pay to an employee who has completed at least 12 consecutive months of continuous employment. The amount of severance pay is the greater of:

* 2 days wages, at the employee's regular rate of wages, for each full year that an employee has worked for an employer before they were terminated
* 5 days wages at the employee's regular rate of wages (CLC-231).

**Exceptions**

There are exceptions to the termination requirements, including:

* If the employee's lay-off does not result in a termination of employment
* If the employee's employment contract contains an end date and the contract ends
* If the employee is dismissed for just cause
* If the employee terminates their own employment (CLC-231).

**Notice to Trade Unions**

If an employer is bound by a collective agreement that contains a provision authorizing an employee whose position becomes redundant to displace another employee on the basis of seniority, the employer must give at least the applicable number of weeks' notice set out in subsection (1.1) in writing to the trade union that is a party to the collective agreement and to the employee that the employee's position has become redundant (CLC-230).

**Statement of Benefits**

An employer must give any employee whose employment is terminated a statement in writing that sets out their vacation benefits, wages, severance pay, and any other benefits and pay arising from their employment with the employer as at the date of the statement (CLC-230).

question: What are the main restrictions and obligations placed on an employer after giving notice of termination to an employee under the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
**Restrictions on the Employer**

After giving notice of termination to an employee, the employer is restricted from making certain changes to the employee's employment conditions.
"...the employer (a) shall not thereafter reduce the rate of wages or alter any other term or condition of employment of the employee to whom the notice was given except with the written consent of the employee..."

This restriction applies to the period between the time the notice is given and the date specified in the notice. The employer must pay the employee their regular rate of wages for their regular hours of work during this period.

**Obligations of the Employer**

The employer has several obligations after giving notice of termination to an employee.
"...employer must give any employee whose employment is terminated a statement in writing that sets out their vacation benefits, wages, severance pay and any other benefits and pay arising from their employment with the employer as at the date of the statement."

This statement must be given to the employee within two weeks before the date of termination, or on the date of termination if the employee receives wages in lieu of notice.

**Notice Period**

The notice period is determined by the length of the employee's continuous employment with the employer.
"The applicable number of weeks for the purposes of subsections (1) and (2) is (a) two weeks, if the employee has completed at least three consecutive months of continuous employment with the employer; (b) three weeks, if the employee has completed at least three consecutive years of continuous employment with the employer; (c) four weeks, if the employee has completed at least four consecutive years of continuous employment with the employer; (d) five weeks, if the employee has completed at least five consecutive years of continuous employment with the employer; (e) six weeks, if the employee has completed at least six consecutive years of continuous employment with the employer; (f) seven weeks, if the employee has completed at least seven consecutive years of continuous employment with the employer; and (g) eight weeks, if the employee has completed at least eight consecutive years of continuous employment with the employer."

**Severance Pay**

The employer is also required to provide severance pay to the employee if they have completed at least 12 consecutive months of continuous employment.
"Severance pay is the greater of the following:  2 days wages, at the employee’s regular rate of wages, for each full year that an employee has worked for an employer before they were terminated, or 5 days wages at the employee’s regular rate of wages..."

The employer must pay severance pay in instances of individual and group termination of employment.

question: What are the conditions that must be met for an employer to terminate an employee's employment if the employee continues to work more than two weeks after the date specified in the initial termination notice?
answer:
**Termination Conditions**

For an employer to terminate an employee's employment after the employee continues to work more than two weeks after the date specified in the initial termination notice, the employer must meet the following conditions:

**Written Consent of the Employee**

The employer must obtain the written consent of the employee before terminating their employment. This is stated in Section 232 of the Canada Labour Code:
"Section 232 Where an employee to whom notice is given by his employer pursuant to subsection 230(1) continues to be employed by the employer for more than two weeks after the date specified in the notice, his employment shall not, except with the written consent of the employee, be terminated except by way of dismissal for just cause unless the employer again complies with subsection 230(1) in respect of the employee."

**Source:** Canada Labour Code, Section 232

**Notice Requirements**

The employer must also comply with the initial termination notice requirements, as stated in Section 230(1) of the Canada Labour Code:

"230(1) Where an employer intends to terminate the employment of an employee, the employer must give the employee written notice of the termination, in the manner and form prescribed by the regulations."

**Source:** Canada Labour Code, Section 230(1)

**Just Cause**

The termination must be for just cause, meaning that the employer must have a valid reason for terminating the employee's employment. This is stated in Section 232 of the Canada Labour Code:
"Section 232 Where an employee to whom notice is given by his employer pursuant to subsection 230(1) continues to be employed by the employer for more than two weeks after the date specified in the notice, his employment shall not, except with the written consent of the employee, be terminated except by way of dismissal for just cause unless the employer again complies with subsection 230(1) in respect of the employee."

**Source:** Canada Labour Code, Section 232

question: What are the conditions under which an employer in Canada must pay an employee upon termination of employment, and how is the amount of pay calculated?
answer:
**Termination of Employment and Severance Pay**

**Conditions for Payment**

According to the Canada Labour Code, an employer must pay an employee severance pay upon termination of employment under certain conditions. The conditions include:

*   The employee has completed at least 12 consecutive months of continuous employment with the employer.
*   The termination is not due to just cause, such as misconduct or poor performance.
*   The employee is not terminating their own employment.

**Calculation of Severance Pay**

The amount of severance pay is calculated based on the employee's regular rate of wages. The employer must pay the employee the greater of:

*   2 days wages at the employee's regular rate of wages for each completed year of employment that is within the term of the employee's continuous employment by the employer.
*   5 days wages at the employee's regular rate of wages for their regular hours of work.

**Example**

For example, if an employee has completed 12 consecutive months of continuous employment with an employer, the employer must pay the employee the greater of 2 days wages or 5 days wages, depending on the employee's regular rate of wages.

**Source**

{"id": "CLSR-23.1", "type": "Canada Labour Standards Regulations", "title": "Reimbursement of Reasonable Work-Related Expenses", "section": "23.1"}, "text": "Section 23.1 (1) For the purposes of subsection 238.1(1) of the Act, the factors to consider in determining whether or not an expense is work-related are (a) whether the expense is connected to the employee’s performance of work; (b) whether the expense enables an employee to perform work; (c) whether incurring the expense is required by the employer as a condition of employment or continued employment; (d) whether the expense satisfies a requirement for the employee’s work imposed by an occupational health or safety standard; and (e) whether the expense is incurred for a legitimate business purpose and not for personal use or enjoyment. (2) For the purposes of subsection 238.1(1) of the Act, the factors to consider in determining whether or not an expense is reasonable are (a) whether the expense is connected to the employee’s performance of work; (b) whether the expense is incurred to enable an employee to perform work; (c) whether it is incurred at the request of the employer; (d) whether any amount of expense is incurred beyond the amount necessary to enable the performance of the work; (e) whether the expense is one that is normally reimbursed by employers in similar industries; (f) whether the employer authorized the expense in advance; (g) whether the expense is incurred by the employee in good faith; and (h) whether the claim includes documentation, such as a receipt or invoice, that indicates that the expense was incurred. (3) For the purposes of paragraph 238.1(3)(c) of the Act, the time limit for the employer to pay the employee any amount that is payable is 30 days after the day on which the employee submits the claim for payment. SOR/2023-79, s. 2"

question: What are the conditions under which an employer is required to reimburse an employee for work-related expenses, and are there any exceptions to this rule?
answer:
**Eligibility Criteria for Reimbursement of Work-Related Expenses**

According to the Canada Labour Code (CLC), an employee is entitled to reimbursement of reasonable work-related expenses (CLC-238.1(1)). The employer shall provide reimbursement when the expense meets all eligibility criteria.

**Factors to Consider in Determining Work-Related Expenses**

To determine if an expense is work-related, the employer must consider the following factors:
"...whether the expense is connected to the employee’s performance of work..."
* "Whether the expense enables an employee to perform work;"
"...whether incurring the expense is required by the employer as a condition of employment or continued employment..."
"...whether the expense satisfies a requirement for the employee’s work imposed by an occupational health or safety standard..."
"...whether the expense is incurred for a legitimate business purpose and not for personal use or enjoyment."

These factors are outlined in the Canada Labour Standards Regulations (CLSR-23.1(1)).

**Reasonableness of Work-Related Expenses**

In addition to being work-related, the expense must also be reasonable. The employer must consider the following factors to determine if an expense is reasonable:
"...whether the expense is connected to the employee’s performance of work..."
"...whether the expense is incurred to enable an employee to perform work..."
"...whether it is incurred at the request of the employer..."
"...whether any amount of expense is incurred beyond the amount necessary to enable the performance of the work..."
"...whether the expense is one that is normally reimbursed by employers in similar industries..."
* "Whether the employer authorized the expense in advance;"
"...whether the expense is incurred by the employee in good faith..."
"...whether the claim includes documentation, such as a receipt or invoice, that indicates that the expense was incurred."

These factors are also outlined in the Canada Labour Standards Regulations (CLSR-23.1(2)).

**Exceptions to the Rule**

There are exceptions to the rule, including:

* An expense that is ineligible under any regulation made under Division XII.1 of the Canada Labour Code (CLC-238.1(2)(a)).
* An expense that the employee is required to pay in accordance with a collective agreement or any other written agreement between the trade union and the employer (CLC-238.1(2)(b)).
* An expense that the employee is required to pay in accordance with any written agreement between themselves and the employer (CLC-238.1(2)(c)).

In these cases, the employer is not required to reimburse the employee for the expense.

question: What are the circumstances under which an employee is entitled to take a medical leave of absence, and what protections are afforded to them during this time?
answer:
**Entitlement to Medical Leave of Absence**

According to Section 239(1) of the Canada Labour Code, an employee is entitled to take a medical leave of absence from employment of up to 27 weeks due to:

* Personal illness or injury
* Organ or tissue donation
* Medical appointments during working hours
* Quarantine
"Every employee is entitled to and shall be granted a medical leave of absence from employment of up to 27 weeks as a result of (a) personal illness or injury; (b) organ or tissue donation; (c) medical appointments during working hours; or (d) quarantine."

**Protections During Medical Leave**

During this time, the employee is entitled to:

* Earn medical leave of absence with pay, subject to certain conditions
* Have their pension, health and disability benefits, and seniority accumulate during the entire period of the medical leave
* Be informed of every employment, promotion, or training opportunity that arises during the period of medical leave
* Not be dismissed, suspended, laid off, demoted, or disciplined because of their medical leave
"An employee is entitled, on written request, to be informed in writing of every employment, promotion or training opportunity that arises during the period when the employee is on a medical leave of absence under this Division and for which the employee is qualified, and on receiving that request, the employer must provide the information to the employee."

**Employer Obligations**

Employers are required to:

* Provide a certificate from a health care practitioner certifying the employee's incapacity to work
* Pay contributions to the employee's pension, health and disability benefits, and seniority during the medical leave
* Not dismiss, suspend, lay off, demote, or discipline the employee because of their medical leave
"An employer who pays contributions in respect of a benefit referred to in subsection (8) must continue to pay those contributions during an employee’s medical leave of absence in at least the same proportion as if the employee were not absent, unless the employee does not pay the employee’s contributions, if any, within a reasonable time."

**Regulations**

The Governor in Council may make regulations to define terms, modify certain subsections, and provide for employees to earn medical leave of absence with pay in other ways.
"The Governor in Council may make regulations (a) defining terms for the purposes of this Division, including “regular rate of wages” and “normal hours of work”; (b) modifying subsection (1.2), (1.21) or (1.4) if, in the opinion of the Governor in Council, employees or classes of employees will, despite the modification, earn periods of medical leave of absence with pay that are substantially equivalent to the period provided for in subsection (1.21); and (c) providing for employees or classes of employees to earn periods of medical leave of absence with pay other than in accordance with subsection (1.2) if, in the opinion of the Governor in Council, the periods of medical leave of absence with pay are substantially equivalent to the period provided for in subsection (1.21)."

question: What are the obligations of an employer towards an employee who is absent from work due to a work-related illness or injury, and what benefits should continue to accumulate during the absence?
answer:
**Work-related Illness and Injury Obligations**

An employer's obligation towards an employee absent from work due to a work-related illness or injury is outlined in Section 239.1 of the Canada Labour Code.

**Subscription to a Wage Replacement Plan**

The employer
"...shall subscribe to a plan that provides an employee who is absent from work due to work-related illness or injury with wage replacement, payable at an equivalent rate to that provided for under the applicable workers’ compensation legislation in the employee’s province of permanent residence."

**Return to Work**

The employer
"...shall, where reasonably practicable, return an employee to work after the employee’s absence due to work-related illness or injury."

**Accumulation of Benefits**

The pension, health and disability benefits, and seniority of the employee "shall accumulate during the entire period of the absence" (CLC-239.1(5)).

**Contributions by Employee and Employer**

The employee is responsible for paying contributions for the period of absence, and the employer shall continue to pay contributions in the same proportion as if the employee were not absent (CLC-239.1(6) and (7)).

**Failure to Pay Contributions**

If contributions are not paid, the benefits shall not accumulate during the absence, and employment on the employee's return to work shall be deemed to be continuous with employment before the employee's absence (CLC-239.1(8)).

**Regulations**

The Governor in Council may make regulations for carrying out the purposes of this Division, including determining the duration of the employer's obligation under subsection (3) and providing terms and conditions applicable to the employer in the event of any termination of employment, lay-off, or discontinuance of a function (CLC-239.1(10)).

question: What are the requirements for an employer's long-term disability plan under the Canada Labour Code, and are there any exceptions to these requirements?
answer:
**Employer's Obligation for Long-term Disability Plans**

According to the Canada Labour Code, every employer that provides benefits to its employees under a long-term disability plan must insure the plan with an entity that is licensed to provide insurance under the laws of a province.
"Every employer that provides benefits to its employees under a long-term disability plan must insure the plan with an entity that is licensed to provide insurance under the laws of a province."

This means that employers must ensure that their long-term disability plans are insured by a licensed insurance company to provide adequate protection for their employees in case of a medical event that renders them unable to work for an extended period.

**Exceptions to the Requirements**

However, there are exceptions to this requirement. An employer may provide benefits under a long-term disability plan that is not insured, in the circumstances and subject to the conditions provided for in the regulations.
"However, an employer may provide those benefits under a long-term disability plan that is not insured, in the circumstances and subject to the conditions provided for in the regulations."

This exception allows employers to provide benefits under a non-insured plan, but only under specific circumstances and subject to certain conditions. The regulations governing these exceptions are outlined in Section 239.3 of the Canada Labour Code.

**Regulations for Long-term Disability Plans**

The Governor in Council may make regulations respecting long-term disability plans, including regulations specifying what constitutes a long-term disability plan and the circumstances and conditions referred to in subsection 239.2(2).
"Section 239.3 The Governor in Council may make regulations respecting long-term disability plans, including regulations (a) specifying what constitutes a long-term disability plan; and (b) specifying the circumstances and conditions referred to in subsection 239.2(2)."

question: What are the conditions and time limitations for an employee to file a complaint about an unjust dismissal under the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
**Eligibility for Filing a Complaint**

To file a complaint about an unjust dismissal under the Canada Labour Code, an employee must meet the following conditions:
"...have been dismissed by your employer (including a situation of constructive dismissal) have at least 12 consecutive months of employment with the same employer not be covered by a collective agreement, and  not be a manager..."

**Source:** CLC-240

**Time Limitations for Filing a Complaint**

The time limitations for filing a complaint about an unjust dismissal under the Canada Labour Code are as follows:

* For a complaint about non-payment of wages or other amounts to which the employee is entitled, the complaint must be filed within 6 months from the last day on which the employer was required to pay those wages or other amounts.
* For any other complaint, the complaint must be filed within 6 months from the day on which the subject-matter of the complaint arose.

**Source:** CLC-251.01(2)(a) and (b)

**Extension of Time Limitations**

In certain circumstances, the Head may extend the time limitations for filing a complaint. For example, if a complaint was made to a government official who had no authority to deal with the complaint, the Head may extend the time limitations if they are satisfied that the complaint was made within the original time period.

**Source:** CLC-251.01(3)(a)

**Limitation on Filing Multiple Complaints**

An employee shall not make a complaint about an unjust dismissal if they have made a complaint that is based on substantially the same facts under subsections 246.1(1) or 247.99(1), unless that complaint has been withdrawn.

**Source:** CLC-240(1.1)

question: What are the steps and obligations for an employer and the Head when handling a complaint related to the dismissal of a person described in subsection 240(1) of the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
**Complaint Handling Process**

When an employer dismisses a person described in subsection 240(1) of the Canada Labour Code, the employer and the Head have specific obligations and steps to follow when handling the complaint.

**Request for Reasons for Dismissal**

The employer must provide a written statement giving the reasons for the dismissal to the person who was dismissed or to the Head, within 15 days after the request is made.
"If an employer dismisses a person described in subsection 240(1), the person who was dismissed or the Head may make a request in writing to the employer to provide a written statement giving the reasons for the dismissal, and any employer who receives such a request must provide the person who made the request with such a statement within 15 days after the request is made."

**Assistance by the Head**

The Head must endeavour to assist the parties to the complaint to settle the complaint.
"On receipt of a complaint made under subsection 240(1), the Head must endeavour to assist the parties to the complaint to settle the complaint."

**Referral to the Board**

If the complaint is not settled within a reasonable time, the Head must deliver to the Board the complaint, any written statement giving the reasons for the dismissal, and any other statements or documents that the Head has that relate to the complaint.
"If a complaint is not settled under subsection (2) within the period that the Head considers to be reasonable in the circumstances, the Head must, on the written request of the person who made the complaint that the complaint be referred to the Board, deliver to the Board the complaint made under subsection 240(1), any written statement giving the reasons for the dismissal provided under subsection (1) and any other statements or documents that the Head has that relate to the complaint."

**Notice and Time Limit**

The Head may give written notice to the person who made the complaint that they have a period of 30 days, or any longer period that may be prescribed by regulation, to make a written request that the complaint be referred to the Board.
"If the person who made the complaint does not reply to a written communication from the Head within a period that the Head considers to be reasonable in the circumstances and a period of at least 30 days, or any longer period that may be prescribed by regulation, have elapsed from the day on which the complaint was made, the Head may give written notice to the person who made the complaint that they have the period of 30 days, or any longer period that may be prescribed by regulation, set out in the notice to make a written request that the complaint be referred to the Board."

**Withdrawal of Complaint**

If the person who made the complaint does not make a written request that the complaint be referred to the Board within the specified period, the Head may deem the complaint to be withdrawn.
"Subject to the regulations, if the person who made the complaint does not, within the period set out in the notice, make a written request that the complaint be referred to the Board, the Head may deem the complaint to be withdrawn."
