question: Under what circumstances can the Board suspend or reject a complaint, and what steps must it take in these situations?
answer:
**Suspension of Complaint**

The Board may suspend a complaint under the following circumstances:

* If the Board is satisfied that the employee must take measures before the Board may continue to deal with the complaint, it may suspend consideration of the complaint, in whole or in part. (
"If the Board is satisfied that the employee must take measures before the Board may continue to deal with the complaint made under subsection 246.1(1), it may, at any time, suspend consideration of the complaint, in whole or in part." - CLC-246.2(1))

The Board must notify the employee in writing and specify the measures that the employee must take and the period within which they must take those measures. (
"If the Board suspends a complaint, the Board shall notify the employee in writing and specify in the notice (a) the measures that the employee must take; and (b) the period of time within which the employee must take those measures." - CLC-246.2(2))

The suspension ends when, in the Board's opinion, the measures specified in the notice have been taken. (
"The suspension ends when, in the Board’s opinion, the measures specified in the notice have been taken." - CLC-246.2(3))

**Rejection of Complaint**

The Board may reject a complaint under the following circumstances:

* If the Board is satisfied that the complaint is not within its jurisdiction, the complaint is frivolous, vexatious or not made in good faith, the complaint has been settled in writing between the employer and the complainant, there are other means available to the complainant to resolve the subject matter of the complaint that the Board considers should be pursued, or the subject matter of the complaint has been adequately dealt with through recourse obtained before a court, tribunal, arbitrator or adjudicator, the Board may reject the complaint, in whole or in part. (
"The Board may reject a complaint referred to it under subsection 241(3), in whole or in part, (a) if the Board is satisfied that (i) the complaint is not within its jurisdiction, (ii) the complaint is frivolous, vexatious or not made in good faith, (iii) the complaint has been settled in writing between the employer and the complainant, (iv) there are other means available to the complainant to resolve the subject matter of the complaint that the Board considers should be pursued, or (v) the subject matter of the complaint has been adequately dealt with through recourse obtained before a court, tribunal, arbitrator or adjudicator..." - CLC-241.2(1))

The Board must notify the complainant in writing, with reasons, if it rejects a complaint. (
"If the Board rejects a complaint, it shall notify the complainant in writing, with reasons." - CLC-241.2(2))

LABOUR-REPORTS-9_8:

{"id": "LABOUR-REPORTS-9_8", "type": "canada.ca", "title": "Unjust dismissal - A guide to the hearing process", "section": "N/A"}, "text": "WHAT DOES THE ADJUDICATOR CONSIDER WHEN MAKING HIS OR HER DECISION? Adjudicators will consider a number of factors when deciding whether or not the dismissal was justified. For example, he or she may consider:   Seriousness of the problem: Did the action/inaction of the employee have serious or only minor consequences for the employer?  Degree of orientation: Had the workplace rules been clearly explained? Was the employee informed about the employer's job performance expectations?  Past discipline: Has the employee been disciplined for improper workplace behaviour in the past?  Employee's work history: Has the employee's work performance been satisfactory in the past?  History of organization's disciplinary practice: Have other employees who engaged in similar improper conduct been disciplined for it?  Extenuating circumstances or mitigating factors: Was the employee facing pressures such as personal problems or provocation which may have led to the improper behaviour?  Adjudicators might also rely on past unjust dismissal adjudication decisions when deciding your case. They are not obligated to follow those decisions, but they can serve as helpful guides. You do not have to refer to past decisions when making your arguments, but can if you like. Past adjudication decisions can be found at your local Labour Program office or in on-line legal databases such as LexisNexis and SOQUIJ, which can be subscribed to for a fee. Information about past unjust dismissal decisions can also be found in labour and employment law textbooks, which may be available at your local library.  WHAT HAPPENS AFTER THE HEARING? After hearing the evidence and the arguments, the adjudicator will make a decision. It is possible that the adjudicator may not make a decision on the day of the hearing. Rather, the adjudicator may reserve judgment, meaning that he or she wants more time to review the facts, evidence and law before making a decision. In that case, the adjudicator will mail or fax a copy of the written decision to both parties and the Minister of Labour once it is made."

question: What actions can the Board take if it decides that a person has been unjustly dismissed, and what factors might it consider in making its decisions?
answer:
**Actions of the Board**

If the Board decides that a person has been unjustly dismissed, it may take the following actions:

The Board may, by order, require the employer who dismissed the complainant to
"...pay the complainant compensation, not higher than the amount of money that is equal to what would have been paid by the employer if they had not dismissed them..." The Board may also require the employer to "reinstate the complainant in their employment" (CLC-242(4)). Additionally, the Board may order the employer to
"...do any other like thing that it is equitable to require the employer to do in order to remedy or counteract any consequence of the dismissal."

**Factors Considered by the Board**

When making its decisions, the Board may consider the following factors:

The Board will consider
"Seriousness of the problem: Did the action/inaction of the employee have serious or only minor consequences for the employer?" The Board will also consider
"...the employer?  Degree of orientation: Had the workplace rules been clearly explained? Was the employee informed about the employer's job performance expectations?" Furthermore, the Board may consider
"Past discipline: Has the employee been disciplined for improper workplace behaviour in the past?" The Board may also consider
"...the past?  Employee's work history: Has the employee's work performance been satisfactory in the past?" Additionally, the Board may consider
"History of organization's disciplinary practice: Have other employees who engaged in similar improper conduct been disciplined for it?"

question: What is the status of the Board's orders in relation to judicial review?
answer:
**Status of Board's Orders**

**Finality of Orders**

The Board's orders are final and shall not be questioned or reviewed in any court, except in accordance with the Federal Courts Act on the grounds referred to in paragraph 18.1(4)(a), (b) or (e) of that Act.

Source: CLC-22

**No Judicial Review
"Except as permitted by subsection (1), no order, decision or proceeding of the Board made or carried on under or purporting to be made or carried on under this Part shall (a) be questioned, reviewed, prohibited or restrained, or (b) be made the subject of any proceedings in or any process of any court, whether by way of injunction, certiorari , prohibition, quo warranto or otherwise, on any ground, including the ground that the order, decision or proceeding is beyond the jurisdiction of the Board to make or carry on or that, in the course of any proceeding, the Board for any reason exceeded or lost its jurisdiction."

Source: CLC-22

**No Review by Certiorari, etc.**

The Board has standing to appear in proceedings referred to in subsection (1) for the purpose of making submissions regarding the standard of review to be used with respect to decisions of the Board and the Board's jurisdiction, policies and procedures.

Source: CLC-22

**No Review by Federal Courts**

No order shall be made, process entered or proceeding taken in any court, whether by way of injunction, certiorari, prohibition, quo warranto or otherwise, to question, review, prohibit or restrain the Board in any proceedings under this Part.

Source: CLC-22

question: How can an order of the Board be enforced in the Federal Court?
answer:
**Enforcement of Orders in the Federal Court**

**Section 246.6 of the Canada Labour Code**

Any person affected by an order of the Board under section 246.4, or the Head on the request of such a person, may, after 14 days from the day on which the order is made, or from the day provided in the order for compliance, whichever is later, file in the Federal Court a copy of the order, exclusive of reasons.

**Registration of the Order**

On filing in the Federal Court under subsection (1), an order of the Board shall be registered in the Court and, when registered, has the same force and effect, and all proceedings may be taken in respect of it, as if the order were a judgment obtained in that Court.

**Source:** CLC-246.6, Canada Labour Code

**Section 23 of the Canada Labour Code**

The Board shall, on the request in writing of any person or organization affected by any order or decision of the Board made under this Part, file a copy of the order or decision, exclusive of reasons, in the Federal Court, unless, in the opinion of the Board, (a) there is no indication of failure or likelihood of failure to comply with the order or decision; or (b) there is other good reason why the filing of the order or decision in the Federal Court would serve no useful purpose.

**Registration of the Order**

Where the Board files a copy of any order or decision in the Federal Court pursuant to subsection (1), it shall specify in writing to the Court that the copy of the order or decision is filed pursuant to that subsection and, where the Board so specifies, the copy of the order or decision shall be accepted for filing by, and registered in, the Court without further application or other proceeding.

**Effect of Registration**

When a copy of any order or decision of the Board is registered pursuant to subsection (2), the order or decision has the same force and effect as a judgment obtained in the Federal Court and, subject to this section and the Federal Courts Act, all proceedings may be taken thereon by any person or organization affected thereby as if the order or decision were a judgment of that Court.

**Source:** CLC-23, Canada Labour Code

question: What type of regulations can the Governor in Council make for the purposes of Division 11 of the Canada Labour Code, and what aspects of employment complaints can these regulations address?
answer:
**Regulatory Powers of the Governor in Council**

The Governor in Council has the power to make regulations for the purposes of Division 11 of the Canada Labour Code.

**Section 121.1: Application of Provincial Laws**

The Governor in Council may by regulation direct that Division 11 of the Canada Labour Code applies in respect of any employment, or any class or classes of employment, on or in connection with a work or undertaking set out in the regulation that is, or is part of, a corporation that is an agent of Her Majesty in right of a province and whose activities are regulated, in whole or in part, pursuant to the Nuclear Safety and Control Act.

**Section 266: Exclusion from Application**

The Governor in Council may by regulation exclude, in whole or in part, from the application of any of the provisions of Division 11 any employment, or any class or classes of employment, on or in connection with a work or undertaking set out in the regulation whose activities are regulated, in whole or in part, pursuant to the Nuclear Safety and Control Act.

**Regulatory Aspects of Employment Complaints**

The Governor in Council may make regulations relating to labour standards in relation to employment that is subject to a regulation made pursuant to section 266.

**Regulatory Aspects of Division 11**

The Governor in Council may make regulations defining the absences from employment that shall be deemed not to have interrupted continuity of employment, prescribing circumstances for the purposes of paragraph 240(3)(b), prescribing periods for the purposes of subsection 241(4), prescribing the circumstances under which a complaint is not to be deemed to be withdrawn under subsection 241(5), and prescribing the conditions that are to be met before a complaint may be deemed to be withdrawn under subsection 241(5).

question: What is the effect of sections 240 to 245 on an employee's civil remedies against their employer?
answer:
**Effect of Sections 240 to 245 on Civil Remedies**

**Section 246: No Suspension of Civil Remedies**

The effect of sections 240 to 245 on an employee's civil remedies against their employer is that
"No civil remedy of an employee against his employer is suspended or affected..." This means that the provisions of sections 240 to 245 do not impact the employee's ability to pursue civil remedies against their employer.

**Application of Section 189**

The provisions of sections 240 to 245 are subject to the application of section 189, which "applies for the purposes of this Division" (CLC-246.1(2)). This suggests that section 189 provides a framework for understanding the relationship between sections 240 to 245 and the employee's civil remedies.

**No Impact on Civil Remedies**

The fact that sections 240 to 245 do not affect the employee's civil remedies is further emphasized by the statement that
"...not (a) affect the employee’s rights under this Division..." This indicates that the provisions of sections 240 to 245 do not impact the employee's ability to pursue civil remedies against their employer.

**No Suspension of Civil Remedies**

The phrase
"No civil remedy of an employee against his employer is suspended or affected..." is a clear indication that sections 240 to 245 do not suspend or affect the employee's civil remedies. This means that the employee can still pursue civil remedies against their employer, even if they have made a complaint under sections 240 to 245.

question: What recourse do employees have under the Canada Labour Code if they believe their employer has taken disciplinary action against them in response to certain protected activities, such as filing a complaint or providing information to authorities?
answer:
**Complaints Relating to Reprisals**

Employees who believe their employer has taken disciplinary action against them in response to certain protected activities, such as filing a complaint or providing information to authorities, have recourse under the Canada Labour Code.

**Section 246.1: Complaint to Board**

Any employee may make a complaint in writing to the Board if they believe that their employer has taken any of the following reprisals against them:
"...the employer has taken action against the employee in contravention of subsection 173.01(5), 174.1(4) or 177.1(7) or of section 208, 209.3, 238, 239, 239.1 or 247.96..." This section outlines the specific grounds for making a complaint to the Board.

**Section 246.1: Limitation**

An employee shall not make a complaint under subsection (1) if they have made a complaint that is based on substantially the same facts under either subsection 240(1) or 247.99(1), unless that complaint has been withdrawn. (CLC-246.1(3)) This section sets a time limit for making a complaint, which must be made within 90 days after the day on which the employee knew or, in the Board's opinion, ought to have known of the action or circumstances giving rise to the complaint.

**Section 246.4: Board Orders**

If the Board determines that a complaint under subsection 246.1(1) is justified, the Board may, by order, require the employer to cease engaging in or to rescind the reprisal and, if applicable, to
"...permit the employee who has made the complaint to return to the duties of their employment; (b) reinstate the employee; (c) pay to the employee compensation not exceeding the sum that, in the Board’s opinion, is equivalent to the remuneration that would, but for the reprisal, have been paid by the employer to the employee; (d) pay to the employee compensation not exceeding the sum that, in the Board’s opinion, is equivalent to any financial or other penalty imposed on the employee by the employer..." This section outlines the potential remedies available to employees who have been subjected to reprisals.

**Section 246.4: Decisions Final**

Every decision of the Board made under this Division is final and shall not be questioned or reviewed in any court. (CLC-246.5(1)) This section establishes the finality of Board decisions, which means that employees who have made a complaint to the Board cannot appeal the decision to a court.

**Section 246.4: Enforcement of Orders**

No order shall be made, process entered or proceeding taken in any court, whether by way of injunction, certiorari, prohibition, quo warranto or otherwise, to question, review, prohibit or restrain the Board in any proceedings under this Division. (CLC-246.5(2)) This section prohibits courts from reviewing or interfering with Board decisions, ensuring that the Board's decisions are enforced.

In summary, employees who believe their employer has taken disciplinary action against them in response to certain protected activities have recourse under the Canada Labour Code by making a complaint to the Board. The Board may then make an order requiring the employer to cease engaging in or to rescind the reprisal, and the decision is final and cannot be reviewed in court.

Marginal note: Notice of rejection of complaint (2) If the Board rejects a complaint, it shall notify the employee in writing, with reasons. 2017, c. 20, s. 356 2018, c. 27, s. 506 Marginal note: Board orders"

question: Under what circumstances can the Board reject a complaint made under subsection 246.1(1) of the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
**Rejection of Complaint under Section 246.3**

The Board may reject a complaint made under subsection 246.1(1) of the Canada Labour Code under the following circumstances:

* The complaint is not within the Board's jurisdiction.
* The complaint is frivolous, vexatious, or not made in good faith.
* The complaint has been settled in writing between the employer and the employee.
* There are other means available to the employee to resolve the subject matter of the complaint that the Board considers should be pursued.
* The subject matter of the complaint has been adequately dealt with through recourse obtained before a court, tribunal, arbitrator, or adjudicator.
* In respect of a complaint made by an employee who is subject to a collective agreement, the collective agreement covers the subject matter of the complaint and provides a third-party dispute resolution process.

**Examples of Rejection**

The Board may reject a complaint if it determines that other means are available to the employee to resolve the complaint. For example, if an employee files a complaint for termination and severance pay, but the underlying subject-matter of the complaint is to challenge the dismissal, the allegations related to termination and severance pay should be rejected because there are other means available to the employee to resolve the real subject-matter of the complaint, namely, challenging the dismissal through their collective agreement.

**Notice of Rejection**

If the Board rejects a complaint, it shall notify the employee in writing, with reasons.

question: How can an order of the Board be enforced in the Federal Court?
answer:
**Enforcement of Orders in the Federal Court**

**Filing in the Federal Court**

According to Section 244(1) of the Canada Labour Code,
"Any person affected by an order of the Board under subsection 242(4), or the Head on the request of such a person, may, after 14 days from the day on which the order is made, or from the day provided in the order for compliance, whichever is later, file in the Federal Court a copy of the order, exclusive of reasons."

This section outlines the process for filing an order of the Board in the Federal Court, which has the same force and effect as a judgment obtained in that Court.

**Registration of the Order**

On filing in the Federal Court, the order of the Board shall be registered in the Court, as stated in Section 244(2):
"On filing in the Federal Court under subsection (1), an order of the Board shall be registered in the Court and, when registered, has the same force and effect, and all proceedings may be taken in respect of it, as if the order were a judgment obtained in that Court."

**Effect of Registration**

When an order of the Board is registered in the Federal Court, it has the same force and effect as a judgment obtained in that Court, and all proceedings may be taken in respect of it, as stated in Section 244(2).

**Alternative Option: Filing in Provincial Superior Court**

Section 23 of the Canada Labour Code provides an alternative option for filing an order of the Board in a provincial superior court:
"The Board may, on application by a person or organization affected by an order or decision of the Board made under this Part, file a copy of the order or decision, exclusive of reasons, in the superior court of a province."

However, this section does not provide the same level of force and effect as registration in the Federal Court.

question: What are the notice and communication requirements for an employee taking a leave of absence under this Division of the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
**Notice Requirements for Leave of Absence**

The Canada Labour Code requires employees taking a leave of absence to provide notice to their employer. The notice requirements are outlined in Section 247.6 of the Canada Labour Code.

**Giving Notice**

An employee who takes a leave of absence under this Division
"...shall (a) unless there is a valid reason for not doing so, give at least four weeks notice in writing to the employer before the day on which the leave is to begin..." This means that the employee must provide written notice to the employer at least four weeks before the start of the leave.

**Change in Length of Leave**

If the employee's leave is changed, they must notify the employer of the change at least four weeks before the new end date of the leave. This is stated in Section 247.6(3) of the Canada Labour Code:
"Unless there is a valid reason for not doing so, an employee who takes a leave of absence under this Division shall notify the employer of any change in the length of the leave at least four weeks before (a) the new day on which the leave is to end, if the employee is taking a shorter leave; or (b) the day that was most recently indicated for the leave to end, if the employee is taking a longer leave."

**Written Notice**

The notice must be in writing, as stated in Section 247.6(4) of the Canada Labour Code:
"Unless there is a valid reason for not doing so, any notice or other information to be provided by the employee to the employer under this section is to be in writing."

question: What are the responsibilities of an employee who takes a leave of absence for military purposes in terms of providing documentation to their employer and notifying them of their return to work?
answer:
**Documentation Requirements**

According to the Canada Labour Code, Section 247.97, the Governor in Council may make regulations for carrying out the purposes of Division XV.2, which includes the requirements for documentation. However, in the absence of prescribed or approved documentation, an employee must provide their employer with a document from their commanding officer specifying that they are taking part in an operation or activity referred to in paragraphs 247.5(1)(a) to (g). [CLC-247.97]

**Notification of Return to Work**

An employee who takes a leave of absence for military purposes must notify their employer at least four weeks before the day on which the leave is to end. If the employee does not notify their employer in accordance with this requirement, their employer may postpone their return to work for a period of up to four weeks after the day on which the employee informs their employer of the end date of the leave. [CLC-247.7(1)]

**Consequences of Failure to Notify**

If an employee fails to notify their employer of their return to work, their employer may postpone their return to work, which is deemed to be part of the leave. This means that the employee is not entitled to return to work until the day indicated by the employer. [CLC-247.7(3)]

**Employer's Obligations**

The employer is required to reinstate the employee in their former position or give them a comparable position in the same location and with the same wages and benefits upon their return to work. If the employee is no longer able to perform the function of the original position, or those of a comparable position, the employer may assign them to a different position with different terms and conditions of employment. [LABOUR-STANDARDS-5_20]

**No Contribution to Pension Plans or Benefits**

The employer is not required to contribute to pension plans, health insurance, disability insurance, or other employee benefits while the employee is on leave for military purposes. [LABOUR-STANDARDS-5_20]

question: What happens to an employee's employment status and position when they return to work after taking a leave of absence under this Division?
answer:
**Return to Work After Leave of Absence**

When an employee returns to work after taking a leave of absence under this Division, their employment status and position are affected in the following ways.

**Reinstatement in Original Position**

The employer is required to reinstate the employee in the position that the employee occupied on the day before the day on which the leave begins. [1]
"...employer shall reinstate the employee in the position that the employee occupied on the day before the day on which the leave begins."

**Comparable Position**

If the employer is unable to reinstate the employee in the original position, they must reinstate the employee in a comparable position with the same wages and benefits and in the same location. [2]
"If for a valid reason an employer is not able to reinstate the employee in that position, they shall reinstate the employee in a comparable position with the same wages and benefits and in the same location."

**Assignment to Different Position**

If the employee is unable to perform the functions of their original position or a comparable position, the employer may assign them to a position with different terms or conditions of employment. [3]
"Subject to the regulations, if an employee is not able to perform the functions of the position that they occupy before the leave begins — or those of a comparable position, with the same wages and benefits and in the same location — the employer may assign them to a position with different terms or conditions of employment."

In summary, when an employee returns to work after taking a leave of absence under this Division, they are entitled to be reinstated in their original position or a comparable position with the same wages and benefits and in the same location. If they are unable to perform the functions of their original position or a comparable position, the employer may assign them to a position with different terms or conditions of employment.

References:

[1] CLC-247.93(1)

[2] CLC-247.93(2)

[3] CLC-247.94

question: What protections are provided to employees who are members of the reserve force and take a leave of absence under the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
**Entitlement to Leave**

Employees who are members of the reserve force and have completed at least three consecutive months of continuous employment with an employer are entitled to a leave of absence under the Canada Labour Code. This entitlement is outlined in Section 247.5 of the Code.
"An employee who is a member of the reserve force and has completed at least three consecutive months of continuous employment with an employer — or a shorter period that is prescribed for a class of employees to which the employee belongs — is entitled to and shall be granted a leave of absence from employment to take part in the following operations or activities: (a) an operation in Canada or abroad — including preparation, training, rest or travel from or to the employee’s residence — that is designated by the Minister of National Defence; (b) an activity set out in the regulations; (c) Canadian Armed Forces military skills training; (d) training that they are ordered to take under paragraph 33(2)(a) of the National Defence Act ; (e) duties that they are called out on service to perform under paragraph 33(2)(b) of the National Defence Act ; (f) service in aid of a civil power for which they are called out under section 275 of the National Defence Act ; or (g) treatment, recovery or rehabilitation in respect of a physical or mental health problem that results from service in an operation or activity referred to in this subsection."

**Continuity of Employment**

The leave of absence is deemed to be continuous with the employee's employment before the leave, and the employee's seniority accumulates during the leave. This means that the employee's employment is not interrupted, and they are entitled to the same benefits and wages as they would have received if they had not taken the leave.
"Section 247.91 (1) For the purposes of calculating the benefits of an employee who takes a leave of absence under this Division, employment on the employee’s return to work is deemed to be continuous with their employment before the leave."

**Reinstatement**

The employer is required to reinstate the employee in the same position or a comparable position with the same wages and benefits. If the employee is unable to perform the functions of their original position, the employer may assign them to a different position with different terms and conditions of employment.
"Section 247.93 (1) At the end of a leave of absence that is taken under this Division, the employer shall reinstate the employee in the position that the employee occupied on the day before the day on which the leave begins."

**Protection from Dismissal**

The Canada Labour Code also provides protection from dismissal for employees who are members of the reserve force. Employers are prohibited from dismissing, suspending, laying off, demoting, or disciplining an employee because they are a member of the reserve force or intend to take or have taken a leave of absence under the Code.
"No employer may dismiss, suspend, lay off, demote or discipline an employee because they are a member of the reserve force or intend to take or have taken a leave of absence under this Division or take into account the fact that an employee is a member of the reserve force or intends to take or has taken a leave of absence under this Division in a decision to promote or train them."

question: What is the purpose of the regulations that the Governor in Council may make under section 247.97 of the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
**Purpose of Regulations under Section 247.97**

The purpose of the regulations that the Governor in Council may make under section 247.97 of the Canada Labour Code is to "carry out the purposes of this Division".

**Specific Purposes of the Regulations**

The regulations may specify various aspects of leave of absence for members of the Reserve Force, including:

* Absences that are deemed not to interrupt continuity of employment
* What constitutes or does not constitute an operation for the purposes of the definition of "operation"
* Activities for the purposes of the definition of "operation"
* Definition of "military skills training" for the purposes of the definition of "operation"
* Limiting the duration of treatment, recovery, or rehabilitation
* Specifying what constitutes or does not constitute undue hardship
* Specifying what constitutes or does not constitute a valid reason for certain provisions

**Source of the Quote**

Source: Section 247.97 of the Canada Labour Code.

question: What protections does the Canada Labour Code provide to employees regarding genetic testing and the disclosure of genetic test results?
answer:
**Protection from Genetic Testing**

The Canada Labour Code provides several protections to employees regarding genetic testing. According to Section 247.98(2),
"Every employee is entitled not to undergo or be required to undergo a genetic test."

**Protection from Disclosure of Genetic Test Results**

The Code also protects employees from being required to disclose the results of a genetic test. Section 247.98(3) states,
"Every employee is entitled not to disclose or be required to disclose the results of a genetic test."

**Protection from Disciplinary Action**

Employees are also protected from disciplinary action taken by their employer based on their refusal to undergo or disclose genetic testing. Section 247.98(4) states,

question: What steps can an employee take if they believe their employer has taken action against them in contravention of subsection 247.98(4), and what is the role of the Head and the Board in handling the complaint?
answer:
**Complaint Procedure**

If an employee believes their employer has taken action against them in contravention of subsection 247.98(4), they can make a complaint in writing to the Head. According to CLC-247.99,
"An employee who alleges that an employer has taken action against the employee in contravention of subsection 247.98(4) may make a complaint in writing to the Head." 

**Role of the Head**

The Head's role is to assist the parties to the complaint to settle the complaint. However, if the complaint is not settled within a reasonable time, the Head must deliver the complaint to the Board. The Head may also give written notice to the employee that they have 30 days to make a written request that the complaint be referred to the Board. If the employee does not make a written request within the specified period, the Head may deem the complaint to be withdrawn.

**Role of the Board**

The Board's role is to consider whether the employer has contravened subsection 247.98(4) and render a decision on it. If the Board decides that the employer has contravened subsection 247.98(4), it may make an order requiring the employer to cease contravening that subsection and may also require the employer to pay compensation to the employee. The Board may also reject a complaint if it is deemed frivolous, vexatious, or not made in good faith, or if there are other means available to the employee to resolve the subject matter of the complaint.

**Suspension of Complaint**

The Board may suspend consideration of a complaint if it is satisfied that the complainant must take measures before the Board can continue to deal with the complaint. The suspension ends when the measures specified in the notice have been taken. The Board must notify the complainant in writing and specify the measures that must be taken and the period within which they must take those measures.

**Notice of Rejection of Complaint**

If the Board rejects a complaint, it must notify the employee in writing, with reasons. The Board's decision is final and binding on the parties to the complaint.

question: What is the effect of an order made by the Board under section 247.99 of the Canada Labour Code, and how does it interact with the court system?
answer:
**Effect of an Order Made by the Board**

An order made by the Board under section 247.99 of the Canada Labour Code has the following effect:
"Any person affected by an order of the Board under subsection 247.99(8), or the Head on the request of such a person, may, after 14 days from the day on which the order is made, or from the day provided in the order for compliance, whichever is later, file a copy of the order in the Federal Court, exclusive of reasons."

This means that the order has the same force and effect as a judgment obtained in the Federal Court, and all proceedings may be taken in respect of it.

**Interaction with the Court System**

The order made by the Board is final and shall not be questioned or reviewed in any court, except in certain circumstances.
"No order shall be made, process entered or proceeding taken in any court, whether by way of injunction, certiorari , prohibition, quo warranto or otherwise, to question, review, prohibit or restrain the Board in any proceedings under section 247.99."

However, a person affected by the order may file a copy of the order in the Federal Court, exclusive of reasons, after 14 days from the day on which the order is made.
"Any person affected by an order of the Board under subsection 242(4), or the Head on the request of such a person, may, after 14 days from the day on which the order is made, or from the day provided in the order for compliance, whichever is later, file in the Federal Court a copy of the order, exclusive of reasons."

This means that the order can be registered in the Federal Court and has the same force and effect as a judgment obtained in that Court.

question: What actions can the Minister take to investigate employment in industrial establishments, and who can be appointed to carry out this investigation?
answer:
**Investigation Actions**

The Minister can take several actions to investigate employment in industrial establishments. According to Section 248 of the Canada Labour Code:
"The Minister may, (a) for any of the purposes of this Part, cause an inquiry to be made into and concerning employment in any industrial establishment; and (b) appoint one or more persons to hold the inquiry."

This indicates that the Minister has the authority to initiate an inquiry into employment in industrial establishments.

**Appointment of Investigators**

The Minister can appoint one or more persons to carry out the investigation. As stated in Section 248 of the Canada Labour Code:
"A person appointed pursuant to subsection (1) has all of the powers of a person appointed as a commissioner under Part I of the Inquiries Act..."

This means that the appointed person will have the same powers and authority as a commissioner under the Inquiries Act, allowing them to conduct a thorough investigation into the employment in industrial establishments.

**Powers of Investigators**

The appointed person will have the power to:
"...issue a summons requiring any person to appear at the time and place mentioned in the summons to testify about all matters within that person’s knowledge relative to the inquiry and to produce any document or thing relative to the inquiry..."

This power allows the investigator to gather information and testimony from individuals involved in the industrial establishment.

**Staff Support**

The Minister can also engage the services of counsel and other persons having technical or specialized knowledge to assist the investigator in conducting the inquiry (Section 12.10 of the Canada Labour Code). This support can be crucial in gathering accurate and relevant information during the investigation.

question: What powers does the Head have to gather information and conduct inspections under the Canada Labour Code, and who can assist or be delegated these powers?
answer:
**Powers of the Head**

The Head has the power to gather information and conduct inspections under the Canada Labour Code. According to Section 249 of the Code, the Head may:
"...inspect and examine all books, payrolls and other records of an employer that relate to the wages, hours of work or conditions of employment affecting any employee..."
"...require any employer to make or furnish full and correct statements, either orally or in writing, in such form as may be required, respecting the wages paid to all or any of his employees, and the hours of work and conditions of their employment..."
"...require any party to a complaint made under subsection 240(1) to make or furnish full and correct statements, either orally or in writing, in such form as may be required, respecting the circumstances of the dismissal in respect of which the complaint was made."

These powers are granted to the Head under Section 249 of the Code, which states that the Head may delegate to any qualified person or class of persons any of the powers the Head is authorized to exercise or any of the duties or functions the Head is authorized to perform.

**Delegation of Powers**

The Head may delegate its powers to conduct inspections and gather information to qualified persons or classes of persons. According to Section 249 of the Code, the Head shall furnish to every person to whom powers, duties or functions are delegated a certificate of authority.

**Assistance and Accompaniment**

The person in charge of any federal work, undertaking or business and every person employed in it or in connection with its operation shall give the Head all reasonable assistance to enable the Head to carry out its duties and functions under this Part or the regulations.

The Head may also be accompanied or assisted by any persons that the Head considers necessary in carrying out its duties and functions.

**Limitations on Liability**

Neither the Head nor a person to whom powers, duties or functions have been delegated under subsection (1) is personally liable for anything done or omitted to be done by them in good faith under the authority or purported authority of this Part.

question: What happens if an employer is found to have failed to pay an employee the wages or other amounts they are entitled to under the Canada Labour Code, and how does this impact potential prosecution?
answer:
**Section 251.14: Deposit of Moneys**

If the Head receives moneys under this Division, the Head shall deposit those moneys to the credit of the Receiver General in the account known as the “Labour Standards Suspense Account” or in any other special account created for the purposes of this section and may authorize payments out of that account to any employee or other person who is entitled to that money. (
"Marginal note: Consolidated Revenue Fund (1.1) The moneys that are equal to the administrative fees paid to the Head under this Part with respect to matters that are the subject of a final decision shall be debited from the account referred to in subsection (1) and credited to the Consolidated Revenue Fund no later than the fiscal year following the fiscal year in which the final decision is made.")

**Section 251.14: Payment of Underpayment**

If the Head determines that there is a difference between the wages or other amounts actually paid to an employee and the wages or other amounts to which the employee is entitled, the employer must pay the amount to the employee or to the Head. If an employer pays the amount to the Head, the Head must, without delay after receiving it, pay it over to the employee who is entitled to the amount. (
"...amount paid to Head (3) If an employer pays the amount under subsection (2) to the Head, the Head must, without delay after receiving it, pay it over to the employee who is entitled to the amount.")

**Section 251.14: Minister’s Consent Required for Prosecution**

No prosecution for failure to pay an employee the wages or other amounts that were the subject of the complaint may be instituted against an employer, without the written consent of the Minister, if the employer has paid the amounts referred to in subsection (1) to the employee or the Head.

**Section 251.1: Payment Order**

If the Head finds that an employer has not paid an employee wages or other amounts to which the employee is entitled under this Part, the Head may issue a written payment order to the employer, or, subject to section 251.18, to a director of a corporation referred to in that section, ordering the employer or director to pay the amount in question, and the Head shall send a copy of any such payment order to the employee at the employee’s latest known address. (
"Marginal note: Limitation (1.1) A payment order must not relate to wages or other amounts to which the employee is entitled for the period preceding (a) in the case where the employee made a complaint under subsection 251.01(1) that was not rejected under subsection 251.05(1), the 24 months, plus any extension of the period for making the complaint that is granted by the Head under subsection 251.01(3), immediately before the day on which the complaint was made or, if there was a termination of employment prior to the complaint being made, the 24 months immediately before the date of termination...")

**Section 251.04: Settlement of Amounts Due**

If an employer and an employee who has made a complaint relating to the non-payment of wages or other amounts to which they are entitled under this Part reach a settlement in writing on the wages or other amounts to be paid, the employer may pay those amounts to the employee or to the Head. (
"Marginal note: If amount paid to Head (2) If an employer pays the amounts to the Head, the Head must, without delay after receiving them, pay them over to the employee who is entitled to the amounts.")

In summary, if an employer is found to have failed to pay an employee the wages or other amounts they are entitled to under the Canada Labour Code, the Head may issue a payment order or a notice of unfounded complaint, and the employer may be required to pay the amount to the employee or the Head. If the employer pays the amount to the Head, the Head must pay it over to the employee. The Minister's consent is required for prosecution if the employer has paid the amounts referred to in subsection (1) to the employee or the Head.

question: What are the circumstances under which the Head may order an employer to conduct an internal audit of its practices and records, and what information must be included in the report?
answer:
**Internal Audit Order**

The Head may order an employer to conduct an internal audit of its practices and records under Section 251.001 of the Canada Labour Code.

**Circumstances for Ordering an Internal Audit**

The Head may order an internal audit
"...for the purpose of verifying compliance or preventing non-compliance with this Part..." This implies that the Head may order an internal audit in situations where there is a concern about an employer's compliance with the Canada Labour Code.

**Information to be Included in the Report**

The report resulting from the internal audit must include the following information:

* The industrial establishment and class of employees to which the order applies (CLC-251.001(2)(a))
* The period of time to be covered by the internal audit (CLC-251.001(2)(b))
* The provisions of the Canada Labour Code or regulations with respect to which the internal audit was ordered (CLC-251.001(2)(c))
* The date by which the employer must provide the report (CLC-251.001(2)(d))
* The form of the report (CLC-251.001(2)(e))

Additionally, the report may also include any other information that the Head considers appropriate (CLC-251.001(3)).

question: What is the process and timeframe for employees to make complaints about potential contraventions of the Canada Labour Code by their employer?
answer:
**Eligibility and Timeframe for Filing a Complaint**

Employees must make a complaint in writing to the Board of the alleged contravention within 90 days after the date on which the complainant knew, or in the Board's opinion ought to have known, of the action or circumstances giving rise to the complaint. ("Section 133(2) Canada Labour Code")

**Completing the Complaint Form**

The complaint must be made in writing, and the employee must provide records to support their claim. The Labour Program will accept and investigate the complaint if filed within 6 months from the last day the employer was required to pay wages or other amounts.

**Restrictions on Filing a Complaint**

A complaint in respect of the exercise of a right under section 128 or 129 may not be made unless the employee has complied with subsection 128(6) or the Head has received the reports referred to in subsection 128(16), as the case may be. ("Section 133(3) Canada Labour Code")

**Exclusion of Arbitration**

A complaint made under this section may not be referred by an employee to arbitration or adjudication. ("Section 133(4) Canada Labour Code")

**Process for Filing a Complaint**

If the employee believes that an employer has contravened any provision of the Canada Labour Code or any order, they may make a complaint in writing to the Head. The complaint must be made within 6 months from the day on which the subject-matter of the complaint arose. ("Section 251.01(2) Canada Labour Code")

**Extension of Time**

The Head may extend the period set out in subsection (2) if the Head is satisfied that a complaint was made within that period to a government official who had no authority to deal with the complaint and that the person making the complaint believed the official had that authority. ("Section 251.01(3) Canada Labour Code")

**Limitation on Filing a Complaint**

An employee shall not make a complaint under subsection (1) if they have made a complaint that is based on substantially the same facts under any of subsections 240(1), 246.1(1) and 247.99(1), unless that complaint has been withdrawn. ("Section 251.01(3.1) Canada Labour Code")

question: Under what circumstances can the Head suspend consideration of a complaint made by an employee, and what are the requirements for the Head's decision to be implemented?
answer:
**Suspension of Complaint Consideration**

The Head may suspend consideration of a complaint made by an employee under Section 251.02 of the Canada Labour Code.

**Circumstances for Suspension**

The Head may suspend consideration of a complaint if they are satisfied that the employee must take measures before the Head may continue to deal with the complaint. This is stated in Section 251.02(1) of the Code:
"If the Head is satisfied that the employee must take measures before the Head may continue to deal with the complaint made under section 251.01, the Head may, at any time, suspend consideration of the complaint, in whole or in part."

**Requirements for Suspension**

If the Head decides to suspend consideration of a complaint, they must notify the employee in writing and specify the measures that the employee must take and the period of time within which the employee must take those measures. This is stated in Section 251.02(2) of the Code:
"If the Head suspends consideration of a complaint, the Head must notify the employee in writing and specify in the notice (a) the measures that the employee must take; and (b) the period of time within which the employee must take those measures."

**End of Suspension**

The suspension ends when, in the Head's opinion, the measures specified in the notice have been taken. This is stated in Section 251.02(4) of the Code:
"The suspension ends when, in the Head’s opinion, the measures specified in the notice have been taken."

**Extension of Time
"The Head may, upon request, extend the time period specified in the notice." This is stated in Section 251.02(3) of the Code:
"The Head may, upon request, extend the time period specified in the notice."

**Implementation of Suspension**

The suspension must be implemented in accordance with the notice specified by the Head. The employee must take the specified measures within the specified period of time, and the Head must verify that the measures have been taken before ending the suspension.

question: What happens when an employer and employee reach a settlement regarding non-payment of wages or other amounts under the Canada Labour Code, and how does this affect potential prosecution?
answer:
**Settlement of Amounts Due**

When an employer and an employee reach a settlement in writing on the wages or other amounts to be paid, the employer may pay those amounts to the employee or to the Head, as stated in Section 251.04 of the Canada Labour Code.
"If an employer and an employee who has made a complaint relating to the non-payment of wages or other amounts to which they are entitled under this Part reach a settlement in writing on the wages or other amounts to be paid, the employer may pay those amounts to the employee or to the Head."

This settlement can prevent prosecution for failure to pay an employee the wages or other amounts that were the subject of the complaint, as long as the employer has paid the amounts referred to in subsection (1) to the employee or the Head.
"No prosecution for failure to pay an employee the wages or other amounts that were the subject of the complaint may be instituted against an employer, without the written consent of the Minister, if the employer has paid the amounts referred to in subsection (1) to the employee or the Head."

**Consequences of Settlement**

The settlement can have significant consequences for both the employer and the employee. The employer is relieved of the obligation to pay the wages or other amounts, and the employee receives the compensation they are entitled to. The settlement also provides a mechanism for resolving disputes and avoiding further action by the Labour Program.

**Minister's Consent**

The Minister's consent is required for prosecution to proceed, as long as the employer has paid the amounts referred to in subsection (1) to the employee or the Head. This ensures that the settlement is effective and that the employer is not prosecuted for failure to pay the wages or other amounts.

**Payment to the Head**

If the employer pays the amounts to the Head, the Head must pay them over to the employee without delay. This ensures that the employee receives the compensation they are entitled to, and that the settlement is effective.

**Source**

The information provided is based on Section 251.04 of the Canada Labour Code.

question: Under what conditions can the Head reject a complaint made under section 251.01, and what steps must be taken after a complaint is rejected?
answer:
**Conditions for Rejecting a Complaint**

The Head may reject a complaint made under section 251.01, in whole or in part, under the following conditions:

* The complaint is not within the Head's jurisdiction (CLC-251.05(1)(a)(i))
* The complaint is frivolous, vexatious, or not made in good faith (CLC-251.05(1)(a)(ii))
* The complaint has been settled in writing between the employer and the employee (CLC-251.05(1)(a)(iii))
* There are other means available to the employee to resolve the subject-matter of the complaint that the Head considers should be pursued (CLC-251.05(1)(a)(iv))
* The subject-matter of the complaint has been adequately dealt with through recourse obtained before a court, tribunal, arbitrator, or adjudicator (CLC-251.05(1)(a)(v))
* In respect of a complaint other than a complaint of non-payment of wages or other amounts to which the employee is entitled under this Part, there is insufficient evidence to substantiate the complaint (CLC-251.05(1)(a)(vi))
* In respect of a complaint made by an employee who is subject to a collective agreement, the collective agreement covers the subject-matter of the complaint and provides a third party dispute resolution process (CLC-251.05(1)(a)(vii))

**Steps After a Complaint is Rejected**

If a complaint is rejected, the following steps must be taken:

* The Head shall notify the employee in writing, with reasons, of the rejection of the complaint (CLC-251.05(2))
* The employee may request in writing, with reasons, that the Head review the decision within 15 days after the day on which the employee is notified of the rejection (CLC-251.05(3))
* The Head may confirm the decision, or rescind it and re-examine the complaint (CLC-251.05(4))
* The Head shall notify the employee in writing of the Head's decision (CLC-251.05(5))
* The Head's confirmation or rescission is final and conclusive and is not subject to appeal to or review by any court (CLC-251.05(6))

question: What actions can the Head take if an employer has not paid an employee wages or other amounts to which the employee is entitled under the Canada Labour Code, and what are the limitations and procedures involved?
answer:
**Actions the Head Can Take**

If an employer has not paid an employee wages or other amounts to which the employee is entitled under the Canada Labour Code, the Head can take the following actions:

* Issue a written payment order to the employer, or to a director of a corporation, ordering the employer or director to pay the amount in question. (
"If the Head finds that an employer has not paid an employee wages or other amounts to which the employee is entitled under this Part, the Head may issue a written payment order to the employer, or, subject to section 251.18, to a director of a corporation referred to in that section, ordering the employer or director to pay the amount in question, and the Head shall send a copy of any such payment order to the employee at the employee’s latest known address.") (CLC-251.1(1))

**Limitations**

A payment order must not relate to wages or other amounts to which the employee is entitled for the period preceding:

* 24 months, plus any extension of the period for making the complaint that is granted by the Head under subsection 251.01(3), immediately before the day on which the complaint was made, if the employee made a complaint under subsection 251.01(1) that was not rejected under subsection 251.05(1). (
"A payment order must not relate to wages or other amounts to which the employee is entitled for the period preceding (a) in the case where the employee made a complaint under subsection 251.01(1) that was not rejected under subsection 251.05(1), the 24 months, plus any extension of the period for making the complaint that is granted by the Head under subsection 251.01(3), immediately before the day on which the complaint was made or, if there was a termination of employment prior to the complaint being made, the 24 months immediately before the date of termination...") (CLC-251.1(1.1))

**Procedures**

The Head must notify the employee in writing that their complaint is unfounded if the Head concludes that the employer has paid to the employee all wages and other amounts to which the employee is entitled under the Canada Labour Code for the period of six months, plus any extension of the period for making the complaint that is granted by the Head under subsection 251.01(3), immediately before the day on which the complaint was made. (
"If the Head deals with a complaint of non-payment of wages or other amounts to which an employee is entitled under this Part, the Head must notify the employee in writing that their complaint is unfounded if the Head concludes that the employer has paid to the employee all wages and other amounts to which the employee is entitled under this Part for the period of six months, plus any extension of the period for making the complaint that is granted by the Head under subsection 251.01(3), immediately before the day on which the complaint was made.") (CLC-251.2(2))

question: What is the process for an employer or affected person to dispute a compliance order, payment order, or notice of unfounded complaint or voluntary compliance issued under the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
**Request for Review**

To dispute a compliance order, payment order, or notice of unfounded complaint or voluntary compliance issued under the Canada Labour Code, an employer or affected person must send a written request with reasons to the Head for a review of the decision.
"An employer to whom a compliance order has been issued or a person who is affected by a payment order, a notice of unfounded complaint or a notice of voluntary compliance may send a written request with reasons to the Head for a review of the Head’s decision (a) subject to paragraph (b), within 15 days after the day on which the order or a copy of the order or the notice is served; or (b) if a compliance order is served with a notice of violation issued under subsection 276(1) for the same contravention, within 30 days after the day on which they are served."

**Payment of Amount and Administrative Fee**

To request a review of a payment order, an employer or director of a corporation must pay the amount indicated in the payment order and the administrative fee specified in the payment order.
"An employer or a director of a corporation is not permitted to request a review of a payment order unless the employer or director pays to the Head the amount indicated in the payment order and, in the case of an employer, the administrative fee specified in the payment order in accordance with subsection 251.131(1), subject to, in the case of a director, the maximum amount of the director’s liability under section 251.18."

**Review Process**

Upon receipt of the request for review, the Head may confirm, rescind, or vary the payment order or compliance order, or confirm the notice of unfounded complaint or notice of voluntary compliance, or rescind the notice.
"On receipt of the request for review, the Head may, in writing, (a) confirm, rescind or vary, in whole or in part, the payment order or the compliance order; or (b) confirm the notice of unfounded complaint or the notice of voluntary compliance, or rescind the notice, in which case the Head shall re-examine the complaint."

**Service of Documents**

The decision made under subsection (3) must be served by personal service, registered mail, or any other means prescribed by regulation.
"Service of a decision made under subsection (3) shall be by personal service, by registered mail or by any other means prescribed by regulation on any person who is affected by the payment order, the notice of unfounded complaint or the notice of voluntary compliance or, in the case of a compliance order, on the employer."

question: Who can appeal a decision made under subsection 251.101(3) of the Canada Labour Code, and what are the conditions for doing so?
answer:
**Appeal Process**

The Canada Labour Code allows for an appeal of a decision made under subsection 251.101(3) to be made by a person who is affected by the decision.

**Who Can Appeal**

According to section 251.11(1),
"...a person who is affected by a decision made under subsection 251.101(3), other than a decision to rescind a notice of unfounded complaint or a notice of voluntary compliance, may appeal the decision to the Board, in writing, within 15 days after the day on which the decision is served."

This means that anyone who is affected by the decision, except for the employer in the case of a compliance order, can appeal the decision.

**Conditions for Appealing**

The appeal must be made in writing within 15 days after the decision is served. The request for appeal must also contain a statement of the grounds of appeal.

Additionally, the employer or director of a corporation may not appeal a decision confirming or varying a payment order unless they pay to the Head the amount indicated in the decision, less any amount and administrative fee paid under subsection 251.101(2).

**Security for Payment**

The Head may allow an employer or director of a corporation to give security, in a form satisfactory to the Head and on any conditions specified by the Head, for all or part of the amount and fee referred to in subsection (3).

**Limitation for Directors**

In the case of a director, subsection (3) applies subject to the maximum amount of the director's liability under section 251.18.

question: What are the responsibilities of the Head and the Board in terms of document provision and participation in an appeal under the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
**Document Provision**

The Head and the Board have specific responsibilities when it comes to document provision in an appeal under the Canada Labour Code.

**Head's Responsibilities**

The Head is required to provide documents to the Board upon request. For example, the Head
"...shall, on request of the Board, provide to the Board a copy of any document that the Head relied on for the purpose of making the decision being appealed." This ensures that the Board has access to all relevant information that the Head relied on when making the decision.

**Board's Responsibilities**

The Board also has a responsibility to inform the Head in writing when an appeal is brought under subsection 285(1) and provide the Head with a copy of the request for appeal (CLC-286(1)). Additionally, the Board may request documents from the Head, such as
"...any document that the Head relied on for the purpose of making the decision being appealed."

**Participation in an Appeal**

The Head may also participate in an appeal by presenting evidence and making representations to the Board. For example, the Head
"...may, in an appeal, present evidence and make representations to the Board."

**Delegation of Powers**

The Head may delegate powers and duties to qualified persons or classes of persons, but the Head must still provide a certificate of authority to the person or persons to whom the powers are delegated (CLC-249(1.1)). This ensures that the person or persons to whom the powers are delegated have the necessary authority to carry out the Head's duties and functions.

**No Liability for Documents**

Neither the Head nor a person to whom powers, duties or functions have been delegated under subsection (1) is personally liable for anything done or omitted to be done by them in good faith under the authority or purported authority of this Part (CLC-249(8)). This means that the Head and delegated persons are not liable for providing documents or participating in an appeal.

question: What are the possible outcomes and implications when the Board makes a decision in an appeal under this Part of the Canada Labour Code (PART III - Standard Hours, Wages, Vacations and Holidays)?
answer:
**Possible Outcomes of a Board Decision**

The Board may make several outcomes in an appeal under this Part of the Canada Labour Code.

**Confirmation, Rescission, or Variation of the Decision**

The Board may confirm, rescind, or vary, in whole or in part, the decision being appealed. This means that the Board may uphold the original decision, overturn it entirely, or modify it to some extent. (
"The Board may, in an appeal under this Part, make any order that is necessary to give effect to its decision, including an order to (a) confirm, rescind or vary, in whole or in part, the decision being appealed...")

**Payment of Wages or Other Amounts**

The Board may direct payment to any specified person of any wages or other amounts held in trust by the Receiver General that relate to the appeal. This implies that the Board may order the payment of wages or other amounts that were previously withheld or held in trust. (
"The Board may, in an appeal under this Part, make any order that is necessary to give effect to its decision, including an order to (a) confirm, rescind or vary, in whole or in part, the decision being appealed; (b) direct payment to any specified person of any wages or other amounts held in trust by the Receiver General that relate to the appeal...")

**Award of Costs**

The Board may award costs in the proceedings. This means that the Board may order one party to pay the costs incurred by the other party in the appeal process. (
"The Board may, in an appeal under this Part, make any order that is necessary to give effect to its decision, including an order...")

**Order to Pay Expenses**

The Board may order a party, whose conduct in the proceedings has, in the Board's opinion, unduly delayed the determination of the appeal, to pay to the Receiver General an amount that is equal to all or part of the expenses incurred in the proceedings by the Board. This implies that the Board may order a party to pay expenses incurred by the Board in the appeal process. (
"(d) order a party, whose conduct in the proceedings has, in the Board’s opinion, unduly delayed the determination of the appeal, to pay to the Receiver General an amount that is equal to all or part of the expenses incurred in the proceedings by the Board.")

**Implications of a Board Decision**

The decision of the Board is final and conclusive, and is not subject to appeal to or review by any court. This means that the decision of the Board is binding and cannot be challenged in court. (
"The order of the Board is final and shall not be questioned or reviewed in any court.")

The decision of the Board may also have implications for the parties involved in the appeal. For example, if the Board orders payment of wages or other amounts, the employer may be required to pay these amounts to the employee. Similarly, if the Board awards costs, the losing party may be required to pay these costs to the winning party.

question: Under what circumstances can the Head issue a written order to a person who owes money to an employer or a director of a corporation?
answer:
**Issuance of Written Order to Debtor**

The Head can issue a written order to a person who owes money to an employer or a director of a corporation under the following circumstances:

The Head may issue a written order to a person who is or is about to become indebted to an employer to whom a payment order has been issued under subsection 251.1(1), to pay any amount owing to the employer, up to the amount and the administrative fee indicated in the payment order, directly to the Head within 15 days, in satisfaction of the payment order.

This is stated in section 251.13(1) of the Canada Labour Code.

The Head may issue a written order to a person who is or is about to become indebted to a director of a corporation to whom a payment order has been issued under subsection 251.1(1) to pay any amount owing to the director of the corporation, up to the amount indicated in the payment order, directly to the Head within 15 days, in satisfaction of the payment order.

This is stated in section 251.13(1.1) of the Canada Labour Code.

**Eligible Parties**

The written order can be issued to a person who is indebted to an employer or a director of a corporation, including banks or other financial institutions that have money on deposit to the credit of an employer or a director of a corporation.

This is stated in section 251.13(2) of the Canada Labour Code.

question: What happens to an employer's administrative fee if it is overpaid, and what is the status of an unpaid administrative fee?
answer:
**Administrative Fee Overpayment**

If an employer is overpaid, they are entitled to a reimbursement of the excess amount. According to Section 251.132 of the Canada Labour Code:
"The Head, after a final decision has been made in respect of which security was given, (a) may apply, in whole or in part, the security given under subsection 251.101(2.1) or 251.11(3.1) toward any amounts — and, if the security was given by an employer, any administrative fee — owing under the final decision by the employer or a director of a corporation who gave the security..."

This indicates that the employer can apply the overpaid administrative fee towards any amounts owing under the final decision.

**Unpaid Administrative Fee**

An unpaid administrative fee constitutes a debt due to Her Majesty in right of Canada and is recoverable as such in the Federal Court or any other court of competent jurisdiction. According to Section 251.131 of the Canada Labour Code:
"An administrative fee constitutes a debt due to Her Majesty in right of Canada and is recoverable as such in the Federal Court or any other court of competent jurisdiction or in any other manner provided under this Act, including under subsection 251.13(1) and section 251.15."

This means that the employer is liable to pay the administrative fee, and if it is not paid, the Labour Program can take collection action, including collection from the employer's debtors or financial institution.

question: What happens to the money received by the Head under the Labour Standards division, and how are administrative fees handled?
answer:
**Deposit of Moneys**

The money received by the Head under the Labour Standards division is deposited into a special account, which may be the "Labour Standards Suspense Account" or another account created for this purpose.

According to Section 251.14(1) of the Canada Labour Code,
"If the Head receives moneys under this Division, the Head shall deposit those moneys to the credit of the Receiver General in the account known as the “Labour Standards Suspense Account” or in any other special account created for the purposes of this section and may authorize payments out of that account to any employee or other person who is entitled to that money."

**Administrative Fees**

Administrative fees are handled in a specific way when it comes to payment orders.

According to Section 251.131(1) of the Canada Labour Code,
"A payment order made to an employer under subsection 251.1(1), and any decision made under subsection 251.101(3) or section 251.12 with respect to that payment order ordering the employer to pay wages or other amounts to an employee, shall specify the amount of the administrative fee — which is equal to the greater of $200 and 15% of the amounts indicated in the payment order or decision — that the employer is to pay."

This means that the administrative fee is either \$200 or 15% of the total amount owed, whichever is greater. The employer is liable only for the administrative fee that is specified in a final decision and shall pay it to the Head, less any administrative fee paid under subsection 251.101(2) or 251.11(3).

question: What happens to a payment order or Board order under the Canada Labour Code once it is filed in the Federal Court, and what are the implications for enforcement?
answer:
**Enforcement of Orders in the Federal Court**

Once a payment order or Board order is filed in the Federal Court, it has the same force and effect as a judgment obtained in that Court.

**Registration of Orders**

On the filing of a copy of an order in the Federal Court, the order shall be registered in the Court and, when registered, has the same force and effect, and all proceedings may be taken thereon, as if the order were a judgment obtained in that Court.

**Source:**
CLC-251.15(3)

This means that the payment order or Board order becomes a binding judgment in the Federal Court, and all parties affected by it must comply with its terms. The Federal Court can then enforce the order through various means, such as issuing warrants or making orders for the payment of wages or other amounts.

**Implications for Enforcement**

The registration of the order in the Federal Court provides a formal mechanism for enforcing the payment order or Board order. This can help to ensure that employers and employees comply with the terms of the order, and that wages and other amounts are paid in accordance with the law.

**Source:**
CLC-251.15(3)

In the event of non-compliance, the Federal Court can take enforcement action, such as issuing a warrant for the payment of wages or other amounts. This can help to ensure that employers and employees comply with the terms of the order, and that the rights of employees are protected.

**Source:**
CLC-251.15(3)

Overall, the filing of a payment order or Board order in the Federal Court provides a formal mechanism for enforcing the terms of the order, and helps to ensure that employers and employees comply with the law.

question: Can directors of a corporation be held personally liable for unpaid wages and other amounts owed to employees?
answer:
**Directors' Liability Under the Canada Labour Code**

According to Section 251.18 of the Canada Labour Code, directors of a corporation are jointly and severally liable for wages and other amounts to which an employee is entitled under the Act, to a maximum amount equivalent to six months' wages.
"Directors of a corporation are jointly and severally liable for wages and other amounts to which an employee is entitled under this Part, to a maximum amount equivalent to six months’ wages, to the extent that (a) the entitlement arose during the particular director’s incumbency; and (b) recovery of the amount from the corporation is impossible or unlikely."

This means that if an employee is owed wages or other amounts by a corporation, and the corporation is unable to pay, the directors of the corporation may be held personally liable for the amount. This liability is limited to six months' wages, and only applies if the entitlement arose during the director's incumbency and recovery from the corporation is impossible or unlikely.

**Limitation of Liability**

However, it is worth noting that the Chairperson, Vice-Chairpersons, other members, and external adjudicators of the Board are not personally liable, either civilly or criminally, for anything done or omitted to be done by them in good faith in the exercise or purported exercise of any power, or in the performance or purported performance of any duty or function, conferred on them under the Act.
"Section 12.051 The Chairperson, Vice-Chairpersons, other members and external adjudicators are not personally liable, either civilly or criminally, for anything done or omitted to be done by them in good faith in the exercise or purported exercise of any power, or in the performance or purported performance of any duty or function, conferred on them under this Act."

This provision does not apply to directors of a corporation, and their liability for unpaid wages and other amounts owed to employees remains under Section 251.18.
